  [`PermissionPolicyProvider`](#permissionpolicyprovider) (decode).

### PermissionRequirement
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionRequirement.cs:10` · Level 0 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: an ASP.NET Core `IAuthorizationRequirement` carrying the single permission a
  principal must hold for a given policy to succeed.
- **Depends on**: `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.IAuthorizationRequirement` (framework).
- **Concept introduced, the requirement/handler pair.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` and `[Rubric §2,
  Design Patterns]` (assesses whether the ASP.NET Core authorization model is used as designed: it
  splits *what is required* from *how it is checked*). A requirement is a passive data object; a
  matching `AuthorizationHandler<T>` decides whether it is satisfied. This type is the passive half;
  [`PermissionAuthorizationHandler`](#permissionauthorizationhandler) is the active half, as the doc
  comment states
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionRequirement.cs:5-9`).
- **Walkthrough**: a `sealed` class implementing `IAuthorizationRequirement`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionRequirement.cs:10`). Its
  constructor
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionRequirement.cs:14-18`) guards
  with `ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(permission)`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionRequirement.cs:16`) and
  stores the value into the get-only `Permission` property
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionRequirement.cs:21`), so a
  requirement can never carry an empty permission.
- **Why it's built this way**: keeping `Permission` immutable and non-empty means the handler can trust
  it without re-validating; the requirement is a value carrier with no behavior of its own.
- **Where it's used**: attached to a policy by [`PermissionPolicyProvider`](#permissionpolicyprovider)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:43`) and
  evaluated by [`PermissionAuthorizationHandler`](#permissionauthorizationhandler).

### FallbackAuthorizationHandler
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization.Fallback` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:35` · Level 1 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the `AuthorizationHandler<FallbackAuthorizationRequirement>` that decides whether an
  endpoint carrying no authorization metadata of its own should be allowed through: it succeeds for an
  authenticated caller, an exempt path, a request that matched no endpoint and names no web-root file,
  or an API-versioning rejection endpoint, and otherwise leaves the requirement unsatisfied.
- **Depends on**: [`FallbackAuthorizationRequirement`](#fallbackauthorizationrequirement),
  [`FallbackAuthorizationOptions`](#fallbackauthorizationoptions) (the exempt path prefixes, taken as
  `IOptions<FallbackAuthorizationOptions>` on the primary constructor,
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:35`);
  `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http`, `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization`.
- **Concept introduced, path-based exemption over endpoint routing's ambient resource.** `[Rubric §11,
  Security]` (assesses whether the fail-closed default still lets framework and static surfaces
  through without requiring `[AllowAnonymous]` on infrastructure that was never meant to declare
  authorization metadata) and `[Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]` (assesses whether the handler
  works without extra DI plumbing; it needs no `IHttpContextAccessor`).
- **Walkthrough**: `HandleRequirementAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:42-58`)
  null-guards both arguments and succeeds the requirement when any of
  `context.User.Identity?.IsAuthenticated == true`, `IsExemptPath(context.Resource)`,
  `IsUnmatchedRequest(context.Resource)` or `IsApiVersioningRejection(context.Resource)` holds
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:49-52`);
  otherwise it returns without calling `context.Succeed`, leaving the requirement unmet.
  `IsUnmatchedRequest`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:79-96`)
  returns `false` for a non-HTTP resource or any request that matched an endpoint
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:81-84`);
  for an unmatched request it consults the `IWebHostEnvironment.WebRootFileProvider` and passes only when
  neither a file nor a directory exists at the path (or no web root is available)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:88-95`).
  Nothing sits behind such a request, and challenging it would turn an unknown URL into a sign-in
  redirect instead of letting the host's not-found re-execute render the 404; a request for an existing
  web-root file keeps the gate because `UseStaticFiles` would still serve it.
  `IsApiVersioningRejection`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:67-74`)
  recognizes Asp.Versioning's client-error endpoints (no metadata, request delegate declared in the
  `Asp.Versioning.Routing` namespace, constant at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:39`),
  so an anonymous caller with a bad api-version gets the 400 version error rather than a 401
  (rationale comment at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:60-66`).
  `IsExemptPath` has one body per framework line, chosen by `#if NET11_0_OR_GREATER`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:98-127`).
  On .NET 11 it switches on the resource: an `HttpContext` is used as is, a SignalR
  `HubInvocationContext` yields the connection's own `HttpContext` through
  `invocation.Context.GetHttpContext()`, and anything else is not exempt
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:106-116`).
  The comment above it
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:99-105`)
  gives the reason: .NET 11 SignalR authorizes a hub method whenever the method carries any attribute
  (a compiler `NullableContextAttribute` is enough), so the fallback policy also runs per invocation;
  Blazor's circuit hub hits this on `ConnectCircuit`, and without the branch a signed-out visitor's
  reconnect after a dropped connection was refused. An invocation is therefore decided by the path the
  connection itself was admitted on. On .NET 10, which never ran the fallback for a hub invocation, the
  `#else` body keeps the plain `HttpContext` pattern match and returns `false` for anything else
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:118-126`).
  Both bodies end in `IsExemptRequestPath`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:129-132`),
  which checks the path against the non-empty entries of `options.Value.ExemptPathPrefixes` with
  `StartsWithSegments(prefix, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`.
  The comment above `IsUnmatchedRequest`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/Fallback/FallbackAuthorizationHandler.cs:76-78`)
  explains why no `IHttpContextAccessor` is needed: under endpoint routing the authorization resource
  IS the `HttpContext`, and a non-HTTP resource (a SignalR hub invocation) is never an unmatched request,
  so it falls through to the exempt-path and authenticated-user rules.
- **Why it's built this way**: reading the resource directly off `AuthorizationHandlerContext` instead
  of injecting `IHttpContextAccessor` keeps the handler stateless and singleton-safe; never calling
  `context.Fail()` follows the same ASP.NET Core convention as
  [`PermissionAuthorizationHandler`](#permissionauthorizationhandler), abstaining rather than vetoing.
  The hub-invocation branch is version-specific code written the dual-framework way (ADR-141): only
  under `#if NET11_0_OR_GREATER`, with the unchanged .NET 10 body as the `#else`.
- **Where it's used**: registered as an `IAuthorizationHandler` singleton and wired as ASP.NET Core's
  `AuthorizationOptions.FallbackPolicy` handler by
  [`AuthorizationExtensions.AddAuthorizationPolicies`](#authorizationextensions) whenever
  `FallbackAuthorizationOptions.Enabled` is true.

### HasPermissionAttribute
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/HasPermissionAttribute.cs:13` · Level 1 · class (sealed attribute)

- **What it is**: an `[Authorize]`-derived attribute that requires the authenticated principal to hold
  a named permission, applied to a controller or an action.
- **Depends on**: [`PermissionPolicy`](#permissionpolicy) (to build the policy name);
  `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.AuthorizeAttribute` (framework base).
- **Concept introduced, capability-based endpoint authorization.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses
  whether endpoints depend on *capabilities* rather than hard-coded role names) and `[Rubric §7,
  Microservices Readiness]` (assesses whether a module can be lifted out on its own; permissions travel
  as claims or through a per-module registry, so an extracted service authorizes without embedding the
  issuer's role taxonomy). The doc comment
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/HasPermissionAttribute.cs:5-11`)
  states the intent directly: prefer `[HasPermission("sessions:manage")]` over role-based
  `[Authorize(Policy = ...)]` so an endpoint declares the *capability* it needs, with the mapping from
  roles to that capability living in one registry ([`IPermissionRegistry`](#ipermissionregistry)).
- **Walkthrough**: `sealed class HasPermissionAttribute : AuthorizeAttribute`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/HasPermissionAttribute.cs:13`) with
  `[AttributeUsage(... AllowMultiple = true, Inherited = true)]`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/HasPermissionAttribute.cs:12`) so
  several permission requirements can stack on one target and subclasses inherit them. The constructor
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/HasPermissionAttribute.cs:17-18`)
  chains to the base with `PermissionPolicy.NameFor(permission)`: setting the inherited `Policy` to
  `"perm:<permission>"` is what routes the check through
  [`PermissionPolicyProvider`](#permissionpolicyprovider). It also stores the bare `permission` on the
  get-only `Permission` property
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/HasPermissionAttribute.cs:21`).
- **Why it's built this way**: deriving from `AuthorizeAttribute` (rather than inventing a filter)
  means the standard MVC authorization pipeline picks it up for free, and encoding the permission into
  the inherited `Policy` string is what removes the per-permission registration step.
- **Where it's used**: on controllers and actions across both apps; its policy name is resolved by
  [`PermissionPolicyProvider`](#permissionpolicyprovider) and satisfied by
  [`PermissionAuthorizationHandler`](#permissionauthorizationhandler) against the grants each module
  declares through [`AuthorizationExtensions.AddPermissions`](#authorizationextensions).

### PermissionAuthorizationHandler
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:14` · Level 1 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the `AuthorizationHandler<PermissionRequirement>` that decides whether the current
  principal satisfies a [`PermissionRequirement`](#permissionrequirement), either because it carries
  the permission as an explicit claim or because one of its roles grants it.
- **Depends on**: [`PermissionRequirement`](#permissionrequirement),
  [`IPermissionRegistry`](#ipermissionregistry) (the role-to-permission map, taken as a primary
  constructor parameter at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:14`),
  and the shared `ClaimsPrincipal` extension methods `HasPermissionClaim` / `GetRoleValues`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:31-32`).
- **Concept introduced, resolving a permission through claim-or-role.** `[Rubric §11, Security]`
  (assesses correctness of the grant decision; there are two independent grant paths, a direct
  permission claim and a role-derived one) and `[Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]` (assesses whether
  a service stands alone; the role lookup used by `GetRoleValues()` reads out of the token regardless of
  how the JWT middleware mapped the role claim type, so it survives inbound-claim mapping being on or
  off).
- **Walkthrough**: the decision lives in the `internal static` method `Holds(ClaimsPrincipal user,
  IPermissionRegistry? permissionRegistry, string permission)`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:29-32`),
  which its doc comment
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:17-28`)
  calls the one evaluation of "this principal holds this permission" every API-side check shares. It
  is `true` only for an authenticated principal (so an anonymous caller never holds anything) that
  *either* carries the permission as a claim (`user.HasPermissionClaim(permission)`, a direct grant)
  *or* holds a role the registry grants it to
  (`permissionRegistry?.HasPermission(user.GetRoleValues(), permission) == true`, a role-derived
  grant). The registry parameter is nullable: when the host registered none, the permission claim alone
  decides. `HandleRequirementAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:35`)
  null-guards both arguments
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:39-40`)
  and succeeds the requirement when `Holds(context.User, permissionRegistry, requirement.Permission)`
  is true
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:42-45`).
  The handler carries no role-gathering helper of its own: the three-claim-type role lookup (the
  standard `ClaimTypes.Role` URI plus the raw `"role"`/`"roles"` claims) lives once, on the shared
  `ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.GetRoleValues()` used by both this handler and
  [`ICurrentUserService.Roles`](#icurrentuserservice), so the two call sites cannot restate the
  predicate and drift.
- **Why it's built this way**: never calling `context.Fail()` (only `context.Succeed`) is the
  ASP.NET Core convention that lets multiple handlers vote independently: this handler abstains rather
  than vetoes when it cannot grant. Lifting the grant test into the static `Holds` lets every other
  API-side permission check reuse the exact predicate the authorization middleware applies instead of
  restating it.
- **Where it's used**: registered as an `IAuthorizationHandler` singleton by
  [`AuthorizationExtensions.AddAuthorizationPolicies`](#authorizationextensions)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:75-76`);
  invoked by the authorization middleware for every policy that carries a
  [`PermissionRequirement`](#permissionrequirement). `Holds` is called directly by
  [`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:56`),
  by `PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy` for its bypass permissions
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy.cs:188`),
  and by `UsersAdminControllerBase` when checking that the caller holds every permission of a role
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/UsersAdminControllerBase.cs:412`).

### PermissionPolicyProvider
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:13` · Level 1 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: an `IAuthorizationPolicyProvider` that lazily builds an `AuthorizationPolicy` for any
  policy name starting with the [`PermissionPolicy`](#permissionpolicy) prefix, attaching a
  [`PermissionRequirement`](#permissionrequirement) for the encoded permission, and delegates every
  other policy name to the default provider.
- **Depends on**: [`PermissionPolicy`](#permissionpolicy) (the prefix),
  [`PermissionRequirement`](#permissionrequirement); `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization`,
  `Microsoft.Extensions.Options`.
- **Concept introduced, on-demand policy materialization.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` and `[Rubric §15,
  Best Practices & Code Quality]` (assesses whether the design scales without repetitive registration; a system with
  an open-ended set of permissions cannot pre-register a named policy for each, so the policy is built
  from its own name at resolution time). The doc comment
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:6-12`)
  explains the design: `"perm:*"` names are materialized here, and every other name falls through to
  the default provider, so a policy the application registers itself is still resolved the usual way.
- **Walkthrough**: the constructor
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:19-20`)
  wraps a `DefaultAuthorizationPolicyProvider` built from the ambient `AuthorizationOptions` and keeps
  it in `_fallbackPolicyProvider`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:15`).
  `GetDefaultPolicyAsync` and `GetFallbackPolicyAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:23-28`)
  delegate straight to that fallback. `GetPolicyAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:31`) is
  the interesting one: it rejects a null or blank name outright
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:33`), and
  if the name does not start with `PermissionPolicy.Prefix` it defers to the fallback
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:35-38`);
  otherwise it slices the prefix off with the range expression
  `policyName[PermissionPolicy.Prefix.Length..]`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:40`) and
  builds a policy that requires an authenticated user plus a fresh `PermissionRequirement(permission)`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:41-44`).
  Note the `RequireAuthenticatedUser()` at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionPolicyProvider.cs:42`: it
  makes anonymous requests fail with a challenge before the handler ever runs, which is why the handler
  can treat "not authenticated" as a plain abstain.
- **Why it's built this way**: composing over `DefaultAuthorizationPolicyProvider` rather than
  reimplementing it means all pre-registered policies survive; only the `perm:` namespace is
  intercepted. That is what lets [`HasPermissionAttribute`](#haspermissionattribute) work for any
  permission string without a registration step.
- **Where it's used**: installed (via `Replace`) as the single `IAuthorizationPolicyProvider` by
  [`AuthorizationExtensions.AddAuthorizationPolicies`](#authorizationextensions)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:77-78`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: a policy object is built on every `GetPolicyAsync` call for a `perm:`
  name; no cache is present in this type, and whether ASP.NET Core caches the result upstream is not
  determinable from this source file.

### RefuseMachineClientsAttribute
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:34` · Level 4 · class (sealed attribute, `IAuthorizationFilter`)

- **What it is**: an MVC authorization filter, declared as an attribute on a controller or action,
  that answers 403 to a machine client (ADR-140) on an endpoint where a person takes part, and leaves
  every other caller alone.
- **Depends on**: [`AuthClaimTypes`](#authclaimtypes) (the `TokenUse` claim type and the
  `TokenUseMachine` value), [`Error`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error) (`Error.Forbidden`),
  [`ErrorHttpMapping`](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#errorhttpmapping) (the standard `errors`
  extension) and, when registered, [`IErrorLocalizer`](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#ierrorlocalizer);
  `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Filters.IAuthorizationFilter` and
  `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Infrastructure.ProblemDetailsFactory`.
- **Concept introduced, refusing a caller kind rather than a missing grant.** `[Rubric §11, Security]`
  (assesses whether endpoints meant for people cannot be driven by a service credential). The remarks
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:20-32`)
  state the gap it closes: a machine client holds what its backing role holds, so an endpoint that asks
  only for a signed-in caller (casting a vote, saving a bookmark, checking in) is open to every machine
  client whatever its role. The attribute states on the endpoint that the caller must be a person;
  whether the caller is signed in, and what it may do, stays with `[Authorize]` and the permission
  attributes such as [`HasPermissionAttribute`](#haspermissionattribute)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:13-19`).
- **Walkthrough**: `[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class | AttributeTargets.Method, AllowMultiple =
  false, Inherited = true)]`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:33`).
  The public constant `ErrorCode = "MachineClients.EndpointRefused"`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:37`)
  is the code the 403 carries. `OnAuthorization`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:40-50`)
  null-guards the context and returns without effect unless the user carries the claim
  `AuthClaimTypes.TokenUse` with the value `AuthClaimTypes.TokenUseMachine`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:44-47`);
  for a machine token it sets `context.Result`, which short-circuits the action
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:49`).
  The private `Refusal`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:57-77`)
  builds the problem body the way the rest of the API does: through the registered
  `ProblemDetailsFactory` when there is one, otherwise a plain `ProblemDetails`, both with status 403,
  title "Not available to machine clients" and a fixed detail
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:59-70`).
  It adds the `errors` extension from `ErrorHttpMapping.BuildErrorsExtension` over one
  `Error.Forbidden(ErrorCode, detail, nameof(RefuseMachineClientsAttribute))`, localized when an
  `IErrorLocalizer` is registered
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:72-74`),
  and returns an `ObjectResult` with status 403
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:76`).
- **Why it's built this way**: an `IAuthorizationFilter` runs before model binding and the action, so a
  refused machine token never reaches the handler, and it is independent of the policy pipeline, so it
  composes with any `[Authorize]` or permission attribute without changing what they grant. The remarks
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:27-31`)
  fix the scope: on a controller it covers every action, permission-gated ones included, so it goes on
  single actions when a program must still call the others; it adds nothing to the API description.
- **Where it's used**: declared on `TwoFactorControllerBase`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/TwoFactor/TwoFactorControllerBase.cs:59`).
  In MMCA.ADC the architecture fitness test `MachineClientParticipationTests` requires it at class level
  on every Engagement participation controller, matched by its full type name
  (`MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Api/MachineClientParticipationTests.cs:29-30`).

### ResultHandlerWrapper
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:222` · Level 5 · class (private sealed, nested in `AuthorizationExtensions`)

- **What it is**: the private helper [`AuthorizationExtensions`](#authorizationextensions) uses to
  replace the registered `IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler` with a
  [`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler`](#multifactorrefusalresulthandler) wrapped around it.
- **Depends on**: [`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler`](#multifactorrefusalresulthandler) and the
  `ServiceDescriptor` it replaces (primary constructor parameter `original`,
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:222`);
  `ActivatorUtilities`, `ILogger<T>` and `NullLogger<T>`.
- **Concept introduced, decorating a framework service by descriptor.** `[Rubric §15, Best Practices &
  Code Quality]` (assesses whether framework extension is done without losing the host's own
  registration). The doc comment
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:216-221`)
  states both jobs: build the originally registered result handler the way its descriptor says, and
  serve, through its own type, as the marker that a descriptor has already been wrapped.
- **Walkthrough**: `Create(IServiceProvider provider)`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:224-234`)
  builds the inner handler from the original descriptor in order: its `ImplementationInstance`, else
  the result of its `ImplementationFactory`, else `ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance` over its
  `ImplementationType`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:226-228`).
  It resolves an `ILogger<MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler>`, falling back to

  and returns `new MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler(inner, logger)`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:233`).
- **Why it's built this way**: `WrapResultHandler` registers the bound method `wrapper.Create` as the
  replacement factory, so `ImplementationFactory.Target` is the wrapper instance; checking
  `Target is ResultHandlerWrapper`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:179`) is how a
  second `AddAuthorizationPolicies` call recognizes an already-wrapped slot and avoids wrapping twice.
  Honoring all three descriptor shapes keeps whatever result handler the host (or the framework
  default) registered as the inner handler.
- **Where it's used**: only inside `AuthorizationExtensions.WrapResultHandler`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:184-188`);

### AuthorizationExtensions
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:19` · Level 6 · class (static, extension block)

- **What it is**: the DI wiring for the whole authorization model: one overload set that turns on
  ASP.NET Core authorization, installs the permission mechanism (handler, on-demand provider, registry),
  the role-level second-factor requirement and the framework's fallback policy, and one method each
  module uses to declare its role-to-permission grants.
- **Depends on**: [`PermissionAuthorizationHandler`](#permissionauthorizationhandler),
  [`PermissionPolicyProvider`](#permissionpolicyprovider), [`IPermissionRegistry`](#ipermissionregistry),
  [`IPermissionCatalog`](#ipermissioncatalog), [`PermissionRegistryBuilder`](#permissionregistrybuilder),
  [`FallbackAuthorizationOptions`](#fallbackauthorizationoptions),
  [`FallbackAuthorizationHandler`](#fallbackauthorizationhandler),
  [`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler),
  [`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings`](#multifactorauthorizationsettings),
  [`MultiFactorBearerWithholding`](#multifactorbearerwithholding),
  [`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler`](#multifactorrefusalresulthandler) and its own nested
  [`ResultHandlerWrapper`](#resulthandlerwrapper);
  `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` plus its `Extensions` namespace for `TryAddEnumerable`.
- **Concept introduced, `extension(T)` DI members and lazy registry accumulation.** `[Rubric §6,
  CQRS & Event-Driven Design]` (assesses whether a concern is configured once for every host rather than
  re-wired per application) and `[Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]` (assesses per-module
  self-sufficiency: each module contributes only the permissions it owns, so an extracted module
  carries its own grants). The `extension(IServiceCollection services)` block
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:21`) is the
  C# `extension(T)` DI idiom taught in the [primer](00-primer.md#c-extensiont-types-read-this-once):
  it adds `AddAuthorizationPolicies` and `AddPermissions` directly onto `IServiceCollection`. The
  doc comment on the no-argument overload
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:23-28`)
  states the permission model plainly: an endpoint states the capability it needs and the registry maps
  roles to capabilities, so no policy name has to be pre-registered per role. The parameterized
  overload's doc comment
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:33-66`)
  states the fallback half: an endpoint declaring NO authorization metadata now requires an
  authenticated caller instead of publishing anonymously by omission, exempt paths are seeded from
  [`FallbackAuthorizationOptions.DefaultExemptPathPrefixes`](#fallbackauthorizationoptions), the opt-out
  is `AddAuthorizationPolicies(options => options.Enabled = false)`, and two surfaces need a decision
  before adopting it in an existing host: a YARP gateway's proxied routes need
  `"AuthorizationPolicy": "anonymous"` per public route (or the opt-out), and a routable Blazor page is
  gated by `AuthorizeRouteView`, which reads attributes and ignores this policy entirely, so a page
  still declares `[Authorize]`/`[AllowAnonymous]` for itself. The same comment also notes that a request
  matching no endpoint and naming no web-root file is not gated, so it reaches the 404 (and a host's
  not-found re-execute) instead of a sign-in challenge
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:45-46`).
- **Walkthrough**
  - `AddAuthorizationPolicies()`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:30-31`):
    a one-line forward to `AddAuthorizationPolicies(configureFallback: null)`, so the fallback policy
    is enabled with its default exempt list unless a host opts out.
  - `AddAuthorizationPolicies(Action<FallbackAuthorizationOptions>? configureFallback)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:67`):
    calls `services.AddAuthorization()`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:69`) to
    bring in the framework's authorization services, then wires the permission mechanism:
    `TryAddEnumerable` adds [`PermissionAuthorizationHandler`](#permissionauthorizationhandler) as a
    singleton `IAuthorizationHandler`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:75-76`),
    `Replace` installs [`PermissionPolicyProvider`](#permissionpolicyprovider) as the transient
    `IAuthorizationPolicyProvider`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:77-78`),
    and `EnsurePermissionRegistry(services)` guarantees a registry exists
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:79`).
    Next it calls `AddMultiFactorRoleRequirement(services)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:81-84`),
    the role-level second factor driven by `Authorization:MultiFactor:RequiredForRoles`, which the
    comment there notes is inert while that list is empty. It
    then binds [`FallbackAuthorizationOptions`](#fallbackauthorizationoptions), applies
    `configureFallback` when supplied, registers
    [`FallbackAuthorizationHandler`](#fallbackauthorizationhandler) as a singleton
    `IAuthorizationHandler`, and configures `AuthorizationOptions.FallbackPolicy` through the options
    pipeline (`Configure<IOptions<FallbackAuthorizationOptions>>`) rather than inline, so the `Enabled`
    flag is read after every `AddAuthorizationPolicies`/`Configure` call the host makes
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:86-103`):
    a `FallbackAuthorizationRequirement`-carrying policy when `Enabled` is true, `null` (no fallback
    policy) when it is false.
  - `AddPermissions(Action<PermissionRegistryBuilder> configure)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:115`): the
    per-module entry point for declaring grants. It guards the callback
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:117`),
    fetches the shared builder via `EnsurePermissionRegistry`, and invokes `configure(builder)` so the
    module's grants accumulate
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:119-120`).
    The doc comment
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:108-114`)
    notes it is safe to call once per module because grants union into a single registry; the union
    itself happens in [`PermissionRegistryBuilder.Grant`](#permissionregistrybuilder)
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/PermissionRegistryBuilder.cs:32-39`).
  - `AddMultiFactorRoleRequirement(IServiceCollection)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:129-155`):
    idempotent, because the comment above it
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:126-128`)
    notes `AddAuthorizationPolicies` runs more than once in a Blazor web host. Only when no
    non-keyed `IAuthorizationHandler` descriptor already names
    [`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler)
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:131-135`)
    does it add that handler as a singleton and bind
    [`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings`](#multifactorauthorizationsettings) from
    `MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings.SectionName`, reading `IConfiguration` with `GetService` so a host
    without configuration binds nothing and the rule stays off
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:137-146`);
    binding once keeps the role list from being appended to twice, and the settings take no
    validation because every value, the empty default included, is valid. It then `TryAddEnumerable`s
    [`MultiFactorBearerWithholding`](#multifactorbearerwithholding) as an
    `IPostConfigureOptions<JwtBearerOptions>`, which withholds a listed role from a bearer principal
    without a second factor on every JWT bearer scheme
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:149-152`),
    and finally calls `WrapResultHandler`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:154`).
  - `WrapResultHandler(IServiceCollection)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:161-189`):
    walks the collection backwards for the last non-keyed `IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler`
    descriptor
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:163-171`)
    and returns if none is found; the comment
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:157-160`)
    notes `services.AddAuthorization()` has already `TryAdd`ed the framework default, so there is
    always one. A descriptor whose factory target is already a
    [`ResultHandlerWrapper`](#resulthandlerwrapper) is left alone
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:178-182`);
    otherwise the slot is replaced in place by a descriptor whose factory is `wrapper.Create`, keeping
    the original lifetime
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:184-188`),
    so a 403 from the multi-factor rule is answered through
    [`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler`](#multifactorrefusalresulthandler) with a coded body.
  - `EnsurePermissionRegistry(IServiceCollection)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:194`): the
    idempotent core. If a [`PermissionRegistryBuilder`](#permissionregistrybuilder) is already
    registered as a singleton instance it returns that existing one
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:196-200`);
    otherwise it creates one, registers it, and registers the built `PermissionRegistry` as a singleton
    factory
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:202-204`).
    Both [`IPermissionRegistry`](#ipermissionregistry) and `IPermissionCatalog` are then registered as
    singleton factories that resolve that same concrete `PermissionRegistry`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:210-211`);
    the inline comment
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:206-209`)
    states why: both contracts must forward to the ONE built instance so what an administration screen
    enumerates and what an authorization check answers from can never disagree, and calling
    `builder.Build()` a second time to satisfy the second contract would build two. Because the registry
    is built on first *resolve*, every module's `AddPermissions` call has already contributed by the
    time any request evaluates a permission, which is the point the comment at
    `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:191-193`
    makes.
- **Why it's built this way**: `TryAddEnumerable` lets the permission handler (and, separately, the
  fallback handler) coexist with any other authorization handlers a host registers; `Replace` guarantees
  exactly one policy provider (the permission-aware one); and the lazy `builder.Build()` factory is what
  makes module registration order irrelevant, since all grants are collected before the first `Build()`.
  Resolving `IPermissionRegistry` and `IPermissionCatalog` from the same singleton factory output (rather
  than each calling `builder.Build()`) is what keeps the read side and the enforcement side of the
  permission model looking at one object.
- **Where it's used**: `AddAuthorizationPolicies()` is called at the end of both framework
  authentication-wiring helpers, so a host that wires authentication through either gets the
  authorization model without an explicit call: `AddForwardedJwtBearerCore`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:77`,
  the call at `WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:117`) and `AddCommonAuthentication`
  (`WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:134`, the call at `WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:160`).
  The Blazor web host also calls the parameterized overload with its own fallback configuration
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Hosting/BlazorWebHostExtensions.cs:130`), which
  is why the multi-factor registration has to be idempotent.
  `AddPermissions(...)` is called by each module that owns permissions: in MMCA.ADC by Conference
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/DependencyInjection.cs:43`), Engagement
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/DependencyInjection.cs:58`), Identity
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.API/DependencyInjection.cs:44`) and Notification
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Notification/MMCA.ADC.Notification.API/DependencyInjection.cs:38`), and in
  MMCA.Store by Catalog
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Catalog/MMCA.Store.Catalog.API/DependencyInjection.cs:41`), Sales
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.API/DependencyInjection.cs:40`) and Identity
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.API/DependencyInjection.cs:42`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: a host that never calls either method has no `IPermissionRegistry`
  registered at all. That case is covered elsewhere in this group by
  [`UnconfiguredPermissionRegistry`](#unconfiguredpermissionregistry), whose diagnostic message names
  these two methods as the fix
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/UnconfiguredPermissionRegistry.cs:68`).

### OwnershipHelper
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:11` · Level 9 · class (static)

- **What it is**: static helpers a controller calls to enforce ownership: to scope a query to the
  current user's own data (a specification that filters by owner id, or `null` when the caller holds
  the privileged bypass role), to refuse a scoped read whose owner claim cannot be resolved, and to
  check that the caller owns one specific record.
- **Depends on**: [`ICurrentUserService`](#icurrentuserservice) (Application layer, imported at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:1`), plus
  [`Result`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and [`Error`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error)
  for the two gate methods. The specification it hands back is typically a
  [`Specification<TEntity, TIdentifierType>`](group-03-querying-specifications.md#specificationtentity-tidentifiertype),
  though the helper itself never says so (see caveats).
- **Concept introduced, ownership scoping at the query level, as distinct from the filter's gate.**
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses row-level data isolation: a non-admin caller can only read their
  own rows) and `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` (assesses separation of responsibility: the helper *produces* a
  specification, the repository *applies* it). Where [`OwnerOrAdminFilter`](#owneroradminfilter)
  *blocks* a request that names someone else's id, this helper *narrows the result set* so a list
  endpoint returns only the caller's rows without them passing any id at all.
  [ADR-033](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/033-resource-ownership-authorization.html) calls these
  the two enforcement points of one ownership axis: reject-one for single-resource routes, filter-many
  for collection routes.
- **Walkthrough**
  - `IsAdmin(ICurrentUserService, string bypassRole)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:24`): delegates
    to `currentUserService.IsInRole(bypassRole)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:27`), so it
    checks every role the caller holds, the same check a controller makes inline. `Role` is only the
    first role claim, so comparing against it alone would have treated a caller holding the bypass role
    second as non-privileged
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:18-22`).
    `bypassRole` has no default argument: every caller supplies its own, normally sourced from
    [`OwnerOrAdminFilterOptions.BypassRole`](#owneroradminfilteroptions), so the framework itself
    declares no role names
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:14-17`).
    [`OwnerOrAdminFilter`](#owneroradminfilter) reuses this same method so the gate and the scoping
    agree on who bypasses.
  - `GetOwnershipSpecification<TSpec, TId>(...)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:41`): the general
    form. It returns `null` for a bypass-role caller
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:52-55`, no scoping
    needed); otherwise it reads the owner id from the named claim via
    `currentUserService.GetClaimValue<TId>(claimType)` and, when present, calls the supplied
    `specFactory(id.Value)` to build the scoping specification
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:57-58`). Like
    `IsAdmin`, `bypassRole` is a required parameter with no default
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:45`). The
    `where TId : struct, IParsable<TId>` constraint
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:47`) is what lets
    the claim string be parsed into a strongly-typed id.
  - `GetOwnershipSpecification<TSpec>(...)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:71`): the
    convenience overload that fixes `TId` to `int` and the claim to `"customer_id"`, but still takes
    `bypassRole` as a required parameter and forwards it
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:74`).
  - `RequireResolvableOwner<TId>(currentUserService, claimType, bypassRole, source, target)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:97`): the
    fail-closed gate to call before a read scoped through `GetOwnershipSpecification`. It returns
    `Result.Success()` when the caller passes `IsAdmin` or carries a parsable owner claim, and
    otherwise a `Forbidden` failure
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:107-109`). The
    doc comment frames a missing claim as an authorization answer (403), never an unscoped read and
    never a 500
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:79-84`).
  - `ValidateOwnershipAsync<TId>(..., isOwnedBy, source, target, cancellationToken)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:139`): the
    single-record gate. A bypass-role caller passes without a lookup
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:152-155`); an
    unresolvable owner claim is refused with the same `Forbidden` failure and the lookup never runs
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:157-160`);
    otherwise the private `CheckOwnershipAsync`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:165`) awaits the
    caller-supplied `isOwnedBy(ownerId, cancellationToken)` predicate (typically an `ExistsAsync`
    query) and answers `Error.NotFound` with the given source and target when it is false.
  - `AccessDenied(source, target)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:180`): the one
    private factory both gates share, `Error.Forbidden("Error.Forbidden", "Access denied.", source,
    target)`.
- **Why it's built this way**: returning `null` for bypass-role callers (rather than a "match
  everything" specification) lets the caller skip filtering entirely on the privileged path; producing a
  specification rather than running the query keeps the helper in the API layer while the actual
  filtering runs in the query pipeline. Every method takes `bypassRole` as a required parameter and
  checks it through the same `IsAdmin`, so the scope and both gates agree on who is privileged, and,
  like [`OwnerOrAdminFilterOptions.BypassRole`](#owneroradminfilteroptions), the framework names no
  default role anywhere in the ownership axis. `ValidateOwnershipAsync` answers a non-owner with 404
  rather than 403 so the existence of another owner's record cannot be probed for
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:119-120`).
- **Where it's used**: MMCA.Store's `ShoppingCartsController` wraps `GetOwnershipSpecification`
  and `RequireResolvableOwner` in private helpers
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.API/Controllers/ShoppingCartsController.cs:65-67,79-84`),
  and `OrdersController` does the same
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.API/Controllers/OrdersController.cs:66-68,80-85`),
  also routing its mutating endpoints through `ValidateOwnershipAsync`
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.API/Controllers/OrdersController.cs:386-390`).
  In MMCA.ADC, `EventQuestionAnswersController` and `SessionQuestionAnswersController` scope by user
  id with `GetOwnershipSpecification` and gate with `RequireResolvableOwner`
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Events/EventQuestionAnswersController.cs:112,140`,
  `MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Sessions/SessionQuestionAnswersController.cs:112,140`).
  `IsAdmin` also decides the export override `AllowUnscopedExport` on all four controllers (for
  example
  `MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.API/Controllers/OrdersController.cs:249`) and is
  the bypass check inside [`OwnerOrAdminFilter`](#owneroradminfilter)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:43`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: two gaps are worth knowing. `TSpec` is an open generic with only a
  `class` constraint
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:46`), so the helper
  does not itself require the returned type to be a specification: that contract is the caller's. And
  `GetOwnershipSpecification` also returns `null` for a non-admin caller whose claim is missing or
  unparseable
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnershipHelper.cs:58`), which means
  no scoping. It does not distinguish that case from the bypass role; `RequireResolvableOwner` does,
  but only if the caller invokes it before the read, which nothing in the helper enforces.

### OwnerOrAdminFilter
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:31` · Level 10 · class (sealed action filter)

- **What it is**: an MVC async action filter that lets a request proceed only if the caller holds the
  bypass role or owns the resource named by the request, returning 403 Forbidden otherwise.
- **Depends on**: [`OwnershipHelper`](#ownershiphelper) (for the `IsAdmin` check),
  [`OwnerOrAdminFilterOptions`](#owneroradminfilteroptions) (the vocabulary),
  [`AllowMissingOwnerAttribute`](#allowmissingownerattribute) (the opt-out it honors),
  [`ICurrentUserService`](#icurrentuserservice) (claims); `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Filters`,
  `Microsoft.Extensions.Options`, `System.Globalization`.
- **Concept introduced, per-request ownership enforcement as a filter, and deny-by-default.**
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses whether a resource-level access gate runs before the action body
  and whether it fails closed) and `[Rubric §17, DevOps & Deployment]` (assesses whether the rule is
  expressed once and attached, rather than re-coded in each action). This is the *gate* counterpart to
  [`OwnershipHelper`](#ownershiphelper)'s *query scoping*: the helper narrows a list, this filter blocks
  an attempt to read or mutate a specific id the caller does not own
  ([ADR-033](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/033-resource-ownership-authorization.html), cited at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:15`). The
  deny-by-default half is the more important lesson, and the class doc comment spells it out
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:16-23`): a gate
  that treats "nothing to compare" as "nothing to enforce" silently stops guarding every action whose
  parameter is optional, non-integer, or carried inside a bound model.
- **Walkthrough**: `OnActionExecutionAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:36`) null-guards
  its arguments and reads the current `settings = options.Value`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:38-41`), then
  walks four decisions in order:
  1. **Bypass role**: if `OwnershipHelper.IsAdmin(currentUserService, settings.BypassRole)` it calls
     `next()` and returns
     (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:43-47`).
  2. **Missing owner claim**: it reads the caller's owner id with
     `currentUserService.GetClaimValue<int>(settings.OwnerClaimType)`
     (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:49`) and
     short-circuits to `ForbidResult` when the claim is absent
     (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:51-55`).
  3. **Unresolvable owner parameter**: if `TryGetOwnerParameter` cannot produce an int, the request is
     denied unless the endpoint carries
     [`AllowMissingOwnerAttribute`](#allowmissingownerattribute), in which case it falls through to
     `next()`
     (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:57-71`). Note
     the ordering: the opt-out excuses only a *missing* parameter, and it is checked after the claim
     check, so an `[AllowMissingOwner]` action still requires a valid owner claim.
  4. **Mismatch**: a resolved parameter that does not equal the claim value yields `ForbidResult`
     (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:73-77`); only
     an exact match reaches `await next()`
     (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:79`).

  Two private helpers back that flow. `HasAllowMissingOwner`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:84-85`) reads
  `context.ActionDescriptor.EndpointMetadata.OfType<AllowMissingOwnerAttribute>()`, which is how one
  lookup covers the attribute whether it sits on the action or on its declaring controller: MVC has
  already composed both into the metadata (comment at `OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:82-83`).
  `TryGetOwnerParameter`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:93-111`) resolves
  the id from the route values first
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:95-100`) and,
  failing that, from the model-bound action arguments
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:102-107`),
  reporting failure by setting `value = 0` and returning `false`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:109-110`). Both
  parses pass `NumberStyles.Integer` and `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` explicitly
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:97,104`); the
  comment above the method states the convention
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:90-92`): an
  owner id off the wire is not a number the request's ambient culture formatted, so the host's
  `CurrentCulture` must not decide which strings are ids.
- **Why it's built this way**: denying on an unresolvable parameter, with an explicit attribute as the
  only escape, converts a silent failure mode into a visible one: the action either compares an owner id
  or documents the guard that replaces the comparison
  ([ADR-033](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/033-resource-ownership-authorization.html)'s
  deny-by-default decision and the audit table that came with it). Reading the vocabulary from injected
  options keeps a single filter reusable across hosts, and checking the route before the bound arguments
  means a conventional `/{id}` route costs one dictionary lookup.
- **Where it's used**: registered scoped by `AddAPI`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/DependencyInjection.cs:88`, next to
  `IdempotencyFilter` at `DependencyInjection.cs:87`, because both depend on scoped services) and
  applied as `[ServiceFilter(typeof(OwnerOrAdminFilter))]`, per the remarks at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:25-30`. MMCA.Store
  applies it at controller level on `ShoppingCartsController`
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.API/Controllers/ShoppingCartsController.cs:49`) and
  `CustomersController`
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.API/Controllers/CustomersController.cs:34`),
  which covers every action on those controllers, so adoption there was an audit of the whole controller
  and the actions with no owner parameter carry
  [`AllowMissingOwnerAttribute`](#allowmissingownerattribute). MMCA.ADC instead applies it per action, on
  two `BookmarksController` endpoints
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/Controllers/BookmarksController.cs:91,147`),
  against the Engagement vocabulary configured at
  `MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/DependencyInjection.cs:45-56`.
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: the owner id is parsed as `int` only
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:97,104`), and the
  claim is read as `GetClaimValue<int>` (`OwnerOrAdminFilter.cs:49`), so a host whose owner id is a
  `Guid` or a string cannot use this filter as-is. It also assumes the owner parameter *is* the owning
  id, which holds for a cart or a customer profile but not for a resource with its own id and a
  foreign-key owner
  ([ADR-033](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/033-resource-ownership-authorization.html) lists orders
  as that case, handled with a specification or an explicit per-id check instead).

### MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization.MultiFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings.cs:28` · Level 0 · class

- **What it is**: the options class for the role-level second-factor rule: the list of roles that confer nothing on a bearer session that did not sign in with a second factor. Empty by default, which switches the rule off (`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings.cs:3-7`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; it is a plain bound options type.
- **Concept introduced, role-level step-up by withholding.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether authentication strength and authorization are enforced at the boundary rather than trusted to callers. Here a host names the powerful roles (for example `Admin`), and a session without the `mfa` claim loses those roles and the permission claims that came with them at token validation, so every later role and permission check sees an account without the role (`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings.cs:10-17`). Plain `[Authorize]` endpoints (sign-out, profile, the two-factor endpoints) stay reachable so the account can enroll (`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings.cs:14-15`). The moving parts are this settings class, [`MultiFactorRoleWithholding`](#multifactorrolewithholding) (the claim surgery), [`MultiFactorBearerWithholding`](#multifactorbearerwithholding) (where it runs), [`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler) (the coded refusal reason) and [`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler`](#multifactorrefusalresulthandler) (the coded `403` body).
- **Walkthrough**: `SectionName` is the constant `"Authorization:MultiFactor"` (`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings.cs:31`); `RequiredForRoles` is a get-only `IList<string>` initialized to an empty collection (`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings.cs:34`), so binding appends into it. The remarks give the JSON shape and the environment-variable form `Authorization__MultiFactor__RequiredForRoles__0=Admin`, and state that blank entries are ignored and roles match case-insensitively (`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings.cs:22-25`).
- **Why it's built this way**: each service binds its own section, so every service that hosts permission endpoints for a listed role must set the list itself (`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings.cs:22-23`). It is bound in [`AuthorizationExtensions`](#authorizationextensions) through `AddOptions<MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings>().Configure<IServiceProvider>(...)` with `GetService<IConfiguration>()`, deliberately with no `ValidateDataAnnotations` or `ValidateOnStart`, because every value, the empty default included, is valid (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:140-146`). That is a conscious exception to the fail-fast contract of [ADR-070](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.html); the permission model it layers onto is [ADR-020](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/020-permission-based-authorization.html).
- **Where it's used**: read per request by [`MultiFactorRoleWithholding`](#multifactorrolewithholding) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:45`) and injected into [`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler) (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:35`). [`UsersAdminControllerBase<TUserDto>`](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#usersadmincontrollerbasetuserdto) reads the same list to refuse giving a listed role to an account that has not enrolled a second factor when a two-factor store is registered (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/UsersAdminControllerBase.cs:451`; documented at `MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings.cs:17-19`).

### MultiFactorRoleWithholding
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization.MultiFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:30` · Level 1 · class (static, internal)

- **What it is**: the static helper that removes every listed role, and the permission claims that came with it, from a validated principal whose session has no second factor, and records what it removed as marker claims (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:9-14`).
- **Depends on**: [`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings`](#multifactorauthorizationsettings), [`IPermissionRegistry`](#ipermissionregistry), [`AuthClaimTypes`](#authclaimtypes), [`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions`](#claimsprincipalextensions) (`GetRoleValues`, `HasMultiFactor`); externals `System.Security.Claims` and `Microsoft.Extensions.Options`.
- **Concept**: the withholding half of the rule introduced at [`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings`](#multifactorauthorizationsettings). `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses least privilege at the boundary): the request's principal is changed, never the token, so every reader of the principal (role checks, permission checks, the current-user service, the ambient origin of scheduled work) sees the reduced account, while the subject, tenant, session and unlisted roles stay intact (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:17-21`).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `RoleClaimTypes` holds the three role spellings `ClaimTypes.Role`, `"role"`, `"roles"` that `GetRoleValues` reads (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:33`).
  - `Apply(ClaimsPrincipal?, IServiceProvider?)` (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:42`) returns at once when the principal is null or the request services yield no non-empty `RequiredForRoles` (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:44-48`), then delegates with the resolved `IPermissionRegistry`, which may be null (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:50`).
  - `Apply(principal, requiredForRoles, permissionRegistry)` (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:60`) builds a case-insensitive set of non-blank role names (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:65-67`) and returns when it is empty or the principal is not subject to the rule (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:68-71`).
  - It removes every listed role claim from every identity (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:73`) and stops if none was present (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:74-77`).
  - It then removes every permission claim except those the remaining roles still grant through the registry; with no remaining role or no registry, every permission claim goes (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:81-84`). The comment explains why: the token carries one permission claim per granted permission, so leaving them would keep the role's power in place (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:79-80`).
  - It adds one `MultiFactorWithheldRole` marker per distinct withheld role and one `MultiFactorWithheldPermission` marker per distinct withheld permission to the primary `ClaimsIdentity` (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:86-90`).
  - `IsSubjectToTheRule` requires an authenticated principal that is not a machine client (`token_use` = machine) and carries no second factor (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:94-97`). `IsRoleClaim` matches the three spellings plus the identity's own `RoleClaimType`, which is what `ClaimsPrincipal.IsInRole` reads (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:101-103`). `RemoveClaims` copies the matches before removing them, because an identity's claim list cannot change while it is enumerated (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:114-125`).
- **Why it's built this way**: removing the role and its permission claims, rather than adding a separate check to each endpoint, means every existing role and permission check refuses the caller with no change to that check. The markers let [`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler) tell "refused because withheld" from "never had it". It is idempotent: a second run finds no listed role left (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:26-27`). Permission model: [ADR-020](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/020-permission-based-authorization.html).
- **Where it's used**: called from [`MultiFactorBearerWithholding`](#multifactorbearerwithholding) on every JWT bearer `OnTokenValidated` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:35`), and exercised directly by `MultiFactorRoleRequirementTests` and `MultiFactorTestPrincipals` under `MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Authorization/MultiFactor/`.
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: markers are added only when `principal.Identity` is a `ClaimsIdentity` (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:86`), while the removals cover every identity of the principal (`MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:117`).

### MultiFactorBearerWithholding
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization.MultiFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:19` · Level 2 · class (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: an `IPostConfigureOptions<JwtBearerOptions>` that chains [`MultiFactorRoleWithholding`](#multifactorrolewithholding) onto the `OnTokenValidated` event of every JWT bearer scheme, after whatever handler is already there (`MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:6-11`).
- **Depends on**: [`MultiFactorRoleWithholding`](#multifactorrolewithholding); externals `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer` and `Microsoft.Extensions.Options`.
- **Concept**: the placement of the withholding introduced at [`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings`](#multifactorauthorizationsettings). `[Rubric §2, Design Patterns]` (assesses whether patterns solve a real problem idiomatically): a post-configure step is the options-pipeline way to decorate a value after every configure delegate has run, so it wraps event handlers the framework or host assigned in `AddJwtBearer`, such as the hub access-token events (`MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:13-14`).
- **Walkthrough**: `PostConfigure` (`MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:22`) guards the options, creates `Events` if absent (`MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:26`), captures the existing `OnTokenValidated` delegate (`MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:27`), and installs a new one that awaits the previous delegate first (`MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:28-33`) and then calls `MultiFactorRoleWithholding.Apply(context.Principal, context.HttpContext.RequestServices)` (`MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:35`).
- **Why it's built this way**: changing the identity inside `OnTokenValidated` happens before the authentication ticket is built, so every later reader of the request sees the same principal (`MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:9-10`). The role list is read per request, so with an empty list the call returns before any work (`MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:15-16`). It is registered with `TryAddEnumerable`, which keys on the implementation type, so repeated `AddAuthorizationPolicies` calls add it once (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:149-152`).
- **Where it's used**: registered by [`AuthorizationExtensions`](#authorizationextensions) (`AuthorizationExtensions.cs:151-152`); referenced from the doc comment of [`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler) (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:16`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: a non-bearer scheme (a cookie session) is not touched (`MultiFactorBearerWithholding.cs:16-17`); [`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler) is the backstop for a principal this path did not reach.

### MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization.MultiFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:33` · Level 2 · class (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: an `AuthorizationHandler<PermissionRequirement>` that fails a permission requirement with the coded reason `AuthErrorCodes.MultiFactorRequired` when the permission was withheld along with a listed role, or when a listed role is still held without a second factor. It never succeeds a requirement (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:9-13`).
- **Depends on**: [`PermissionRequirement`](#permissionrequirement), [`PermissionAuthorizationHandler`](#permissionauthorizationhandler) (`Holds`), [`IPermissionRegistry`](#ipermissionregistry), [`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings`](#multifactorauthorizationsettings), [`AuthClaimTypes`](#authclaimtypes), [`AuthErrorCodes`](#autherrorcodes), [`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions`](#claimsprincipalextensions); external `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization`.
- **Concept**: the refusal half of the rule introduced at [`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings`](#multifactorauthorizationsettings). `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses defense in depth): the withholding already makes the plain permission check refuse; this handler only codes the refusal, and also catches a principal the withholding did not reach, so the rule never depends on one path alone (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:71-73`).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - The primary constructor takes the registry and the bound settings (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:33-35`).
  - `HandleRequirementAsync` (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:38`) returns at once when `RequiredForRoles` is empty (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:45-48`) or the user is not authenticated (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:50-54`).
  - It asks `PermissionAuthorizationHandler.Holds` whether the user holds the permission (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:56`). If it does, it fails only when the user still carries a listed role without a second factor; if it does not, it fails only when the permission was withheld (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:57-60`). The failure carries an `AuthorizationFailureReason` whose handler is `this` and whose message is `AuthErrorCodes.MultiFactorRequired` (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:59`).
  - `WasWithheld` requires a withheld-role marker and either a matching withheld-permission marker or a registry grant of the permission to a withheld role (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:66-69`).
  - `HoldsThroughAnUnwithheldListedRole` requires no second factor, not a machine client, and any non-blank listed role held (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:74-77`).
- **Why it's built this way**: a caller whose withheld role would not have granted the permission keeps the plain `403` and never learns about the step-up, matching the CQRS authorization gate (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:25-26`); a principal with no marker gets exactly the answer the permission check gives (`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:26-28`). Never succeeding means it cannot widen access. Permission model: [ADR-020](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/020-permission-based-authorization.html).
- **Where it's used**: registered as a singleton `IAuthorizationHandler` by [`AuthorizationExtensions`](#authorizationextensions), with an explicit already-registered check (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:131-138`). [`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler`](#multifactorrefusalresulthandler) recognizes its failure reasons by handler type (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:46`). Covered by `MultiFactorRoleRequirementTests` and `MultiFactorPermissionBackstopTests` under `MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Authorization/MultiFactor/`.

### MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler
> MMCA.Common.API · `MMCA.Common.API.Authorization.MultiFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:25` · Level 4 · class (internal, sealed, partial)

- **What it is**: a decorator over the host's `IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler` that turns a refusal raised by [`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler) into a coded `403` Problem Details body (`Authorization.MultiFactorRequired` in the `errors` extension) instead of the default body-less forbid; every other result goes to the wrapped handler unchanged (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:14-19`).
- **Depends on**: [`MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler), [`PermissionRequirement`](#permissionrequirement), [`AuthErrorCodes`](#autherrorcodes), [`Error`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error), [`IErrorLocalizer`](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#ierrorlocalizer), [`ErrorHttpMapping`](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#errorhttpmapping); externals `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.Policy`, `ProblemDetails`/`IProblemDetailsService`, `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging`.
- **Concept**: the response half of the rule introduced at [`MultiFactorAuthorizationSettings`](#multifactorauthorizationsettings). `[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]` (assesses consistent, machine-readable error contracts): a client gets a stable error code it can act on (prompt for enrollment or a second sign-in) in the same `errors` extension shape the rest of the API uses.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - Constants: the `application/problem+json` content type, the title `"Second factor required"` and the user-facing message (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:29-32`).
  - `HandleAsync` (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:35`) forwards to the inner handler unless the result is `Forbidden`, at least one failure reason came from `MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler`, and the request is not gRPC (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:45-51`). Otherwise it takes the first `PermissionRequirement`'s permission name (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:53`), logs it (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:54`) and writes the refusal (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:56`).
  - `IsGrpc` checks for an `application/grpc` content-type prefix (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:59-60`).
  - `WriteRefusalAsync` builds `Error.Forbidden(AuthErrorCodes.MultiFactorRequired, Message, "HasPermission")` (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:66`), a `ProblemDetails` with the RFC 9110 section 15.5.4 type, status `403` and a detail localized through `IErrorLocalizer` when one is registered (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:68-74`), and the `errors` extension from `ErrorHttpMapping.BuildErrorsExtension` (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:75`). It sets status `403` and `Cache-Control: no-store` (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:78-79`), prefers `IProblemDetailsService.TryWriteAsync` (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:81-89`) and falls back to `WriteAsJsonAsync` with the problem content type (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:91-92`).
  - `MultiFactorRefused` is a source-generated `[LoggerMessage]` at Information that logs the permission name only, no user id and no address (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:95-97`).
- **Why it's built this way**: wrapping, rather than replacing, keeps whatever result handler the host registered in charge of every other outcome. A gRPC request keeps the default forbid so a JSON body cannot break its framing (`MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:21`). `[Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]`: the refusal is logged with no personal data.
