  - `RetentionDays` (`:72`, `[Range(0, 3650)]`, default 30) is measured from the instant a session died (its revocation, or its expiry when never revoked), so a live session is never a sweep candidate. The comment (`:59-66`) states the constraint that makes the number security-relevant: retention **bounds reuse detection**, because BR-206 catches a replayed refresh token by landing on its revoked row, and a swept row turns that replay into an unknown token that fails alone instead of revoking the family. Thirty days sits well past the seven-day refresh-token lifetime for exactly that reason. `0` keeps every row forever (`:67-69`).
  - `CleanupIntervalHours` (`:80`, `[Range(1, 168)]`, default 6) is how often the sweep runs, ignored when `RetentionDays` is `0`, and matches the outbox sweep cadence because the deadline is measured in days (`:74-77`).
  - `ReuseGraceSeconds` (`:99`, `[Range(0, 300)]`, default 10) is how long after a session was rotated a second presentation of its token counts as a **rotation race** rather than reuse (`:82-97`). Two tabs, or one browser served by two replicas, can present the same refresh token a moment apart; the later request is answered `409 Conflict` (`Auth.RefreshSuperseded`) with nothing revoked, and the client retries with the winner's token. The default matches the cookie refresher's rotation grace. The comment is explicit that this is a **security trade-off**: a stolen-token replay arriving inside the window gets a 409 instead of the BR-206 family revocation. Only a row revoked as `Rotated` qualifies: a row already flagged as reuse fails that request alone, without revoking the family a second time, however recent (`:92-94`), and `0` treats every rotated token that comes back as reuse.
  - `LostResponseRecoveryMinutes` (`:123`, `[Range(0, 1440)]`, default `0`, which is off) is how long after a rotation a client that never received the rotation's response can still recover its session by presenting the old token again (`:101-121`). The case is a mobile client whose refresh succeeded on the server while the response was lost (the app suspended mid-request, or the network dropped): it presents the old pair minutes later and BR-206 would revoke every session the user holds. With a window set, that presentation is recovered instead when, and only when, the presented row was revoked as `Rotated` inside the window **and** its successor is still live, meaning nobody ever presented the successor; the successor is then rotated in its place through the normal rotation claim (`:106-112`). The comment names this a security trade-off as well (`:114-120`): a thief replaying inside the window while the legitimate client is idle is handed a session, and the legitimate client's next refresh presents a successor that was rotated away, which is reuse, so the whole family, thief included, is revoked. Detection is delayed by one refresh, never lost, and a successor that was already used is never recovered.
- **Why it's built this way**: the same `AddOptions(...).Bind(...).ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart()` treatment as every other settings class in the framework (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:169-172`) means an out-of-range cap, a negative retention window or a recovery window past a day fails the host at startup, not at the first login. Defaulting `Enabled` to `false` is the safe direction for a multi-service host: a service that never opts in never grows a table it does not own. Defaulting `LostResponseRecoveryMinutes` to `0` keeps the strict BR-206 answer unless a host with mobile clients chooses the trade-off.
- **Where it's used**: bound at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:169-172`; injected as `IOptions<RefreshSessionSettings>` into [AuthSessionIssuer](#authsessionissuer) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:57`, read for the reuse grace at `:601`, the lost-response recovery window at `:624` and the cap at `:707`), into [EFRefreshSessionStore](group-07-persistence-ef-core.md#efrefreshsessionstore) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFRefreshSessionStore.cs:38`, which routes by `DataSourceName` at `:357`), and into [RefreshSessionCleanupService](group-07-persistence-ef-core.md#refreshsessioncleanupservice) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/RefreshSessionCleanupService.cs:51`, snapshotted at `:55`). The design-time context helper supplies an instance so `dotnet ef` can build a model that includes the table (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/DbContexts/Design/DesignTimeDbContextHelper.cs:174-175`). The app Identity services do not take it: the issuer owns it, so ADC's `AuthenticationService` has no reference to it.

### UnconfiguredPermissionRegistry
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/UnconfiguredPermissionRegistry.cs:20` · Level 1 · class (internal sealed partial)

- **What it is**: the fallback [IPermissionRegistry](#ipermissionregistry) (and, since it also implements [IPermissionCatalog](#ipermissioncatalog), the fallback catalog) for a host that wired the CQRS pipeline without declaring any role-to-permission grants. It grants nothing, so a permission-gated command or query is **denied** rather than allowed, and it logs one warning naming the call that would fix it (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/UnconfiguredPermissionRegistry.cs:6-11`).
- **Depends on**: [IPermissionRegistry](#ipermissionregistry) and [IPermissionCatalog](#ipermissioncatalog) (`:20`), [IRequiresPermission](group-05-cqrs-pipeline.md#irequirespermission) by reference in the doc comment (`:9`), and `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging` for the source-generated log message (`:1`).
- **Concept introduced: failing closed, and only where it costs nothing.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses the direction a misconfiguration fails in: a registry that answered "no permission model, therefore allow" would silently open every gated request, so this one denies, and now that it doubles as the fallback [IPermissionCatalog](#ipermissioncatalog) it renders an **empty** catalog rather than throwing, so a role-administration screen on an unconfigured host reads as "this host grants nothing yet" instead of failing (`:225-228`). `[Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]` assesses whether an operator can tell why: the log message spells out the remedy verbatim (`:264-267`, naming `AddAuthorizationPolicies()` / `AddPermissions(...)` and the required ordering before `AddApplicationDecorators()`). The second half of the doc comment (`:12-17`) is the more interesting teaching point and is an availability story rather than a security one: the two authorization decorators are registered **unconditionally** and take an `IPermissionRegistry` constructor dependency, so without any registration the whole pipeline fails to activate and a small app with no Identity module answers 500 on **every** read, not only the gated ones. This type turns a total activation failure into a correct, noisy denial on the subset of requests that actually declare a permission.
- **Walkthrough**: two fields, two catalog properties, and three methods.
  - `private static readonly HashSet<string> None = []` (`:221`) is the single empty grant set every permission call returns, and `private int _warned` (`:223`) is the one-time-warning latch.
  - `IReadOnlyList<string> Roles => []` (`:229`) and `IReadOnlyList<string> Permissions => []` (`:232`) are the [IPermissionCatalog](#ipermissioncatalog) members: both always empty, so an unconfigured host's role editor renders no roles and no permissions to pick from rather than erroring.
  - `GetPermissions(string role)` (`:235-239`) warns then returns `None`.
  - `HasPermission(IEnumerable<string> roles, string permission)` (`:242-249`) argument-guards both parameters (`:244-245`) before warning and returning `false`, so a caller bug still surfaces as an `ArgumentException` rather than being swallowed by the stub.
  - `WarnOnce()` (`:256-262`) uses `Interlocked.Exchange(ref _warned, 1) == 0` (`:258`) so concurrent requests produce exactly one log line. The comment (`:251-255`) explains why the warning is deferred to the first permission check instead of emitted at startup: a host with no permission-gated request is **correctly** configured and simply never needs a registry, so warning at boot would cry wolf. Reading the catalog properties never triggers the warning, only `GetPermissions`/`HasPermission` do.
  - `LogNoPermissionsConfigured` (`:264-267`) is a `[LoggerMessage]` source-generated `Warning`, which is why the class is `partial`.
- **Why it's built this way**: it is registered with `TryAddSingleton` from inside `AddApplicationDecorators()` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:141`), and the surrounding comment (`:119-123`) states both halves of the rule: `TryAdd` so a host that already declared its grants (via `AddAuthorizationPolicies()` or `AddPermissions(...)`, both of which run before this call) keeps its own registry and never constructs this type, and *here* rather than in `AddApplication()` so the registration lands exactly where the decorators that need it are wired. Adding [IPermissionCatalog](#ipermissioncatalog) to the same fallback type, rather than a second stub class, means the one `TryAddSingleton` call keeps both ports covered from the same no-op instance.
- **Where it's used**: reached through the [IPermissionRegistry](#ipermissionregistry) dependency of the authorization command and query decorators in the CQRS pipeline (see [group 05](group-05-cqrs-pipeline.md)), and through the [IPermissionCatalog](#ipermissioncatalog) dependency of [IRoleAdministrationService](#iroleadministrationservice)'s `GetCatalogAsync` on a host that never configured a registry.
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: `internal`, so it is not part of the framework's public API and cannot be referenced or asserted against from a consumer's code.

### ILoginProtectionService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ILoginProtectionService.cs:10` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the application-layer contract for **brute-force and rate-limit protection** on authentication endpoints: lockout checks, failed-attempt increments, successful-login resets, and registration rate-limiting per IP address.
- **Depends on**: [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) from `MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ILoginProtectionService.cs:1`).
- **Concept introduced: rate limiting as a first-class application concern.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses brute-force protection on auth flows, and `[Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]` assesses whether such a policy is extracted to a port so the application layer can reason about it without coupling to a specific store (the doc comment at `:7-8` names both a distributed and an in-memory cache as valid backers). Returning [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) from `CheckLockoutAsync` (`:18`) and `CheckRegistrationRateLimitAsync` (`:42`) makes "account is locked out" a normal control-flow branch rather than a thrown exception.
- **Walkthrough**: five async methods in two scopes.
  - **Email-scoped (failed-login lockout):** `CheckLockoutAsync` (`:18`) returns a failure result when the email is currently locked; `IncrementFailedAttemptsAsync` (`:26`) records a failure and, per the doc comment (`:20-22`), applies **exponential-backoff lockout** once the maximum is exceeded; `ResetFailedAttemptsAsync` (`:33`) clears the counter after a successful login.
  - **IP-scoped (registration flood):** `CheckRegistrationRateLimitAsync` (`:42`) and `IncrementRegistrationCountAsync` (`:49`) throttle account creation per client IP. Both accept a nullable `ipAddress` and **skip** the check when it is null, so a host that cannot resolve the caller IP degrades to no limit rather than blocking everyone; `CheckRegistrationRateLimitAsync` returns `Result.Success()` in that case (doc comment, `:36-37`).

  All five take a `CancellationToken` with a `default` argument, per convention.
- **Why it's built this way**: keeping the protection policy behind an interface lets the shared authentication workflow compose it in while the concrete cache mechanics stay in the implementation; the null-IP skip keeps the limiter from becoming an availability hazard ([ADR-029](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/029-authentication-brute-force-protection.html)).
- **Where it's used**: injected into [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser) (constructor parameter at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:77`), which calls all five across its login and registration flows: `CheckLockoutAsync` (`:131`), `IncrementFailedAttemptsAsync` on both the unknown-email and wrong-password branches (`:146`, `:161`), `ResetFailedAttemptsAsync` on success (`:178`), `CheckRegistrationRateLimitAsync` (`:197`) and `IncrementRegistrationCountAsync` (`:256`). The concrete, cache-backed [LoginProtectionService](#loginprotectionservice) (tuned by [LoginProtectionSettings](#loginprotectionsettings), bound at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:155-158`) implements it, and the framework registers that pairing at `:135`.

### IPasswordResetTokenService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IPasswordResetTokenService.cs:10` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the two-method port behind the forgot-password workflow: issue a single-use reset token for an email address, and validate-then-consume a token presented back by the user. Implementations keep the token material outside the database, hashed at rest, and enforce both the per-email request throttle and the per-token validation-attempt cap (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IPasswordResetTokenService.cs:5-9`).
- **Depends on**: [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and its generic form from `MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions` (`:1`), plus the `UserIdentifierType` alias. Its Infrastructure adapter is [PasswordResetTokenService](#passwordresettokenservice), backed by [ICacheService](group-09-caching.md#icacheservice) and tuned by [PasswordResetSettings](#passwordresetsettings).
- **Concept introduced: a single-use credential without a schema change.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses how a secondary credential is minted, stored, and retired; `[Rubric §8, Data Architecture]` assesses whether short-lived state earns a place in the durable store. A reset token is not durable data: it is valid for minutes and must stop working the instant it is redeemed. Putting it in columns on the user row costs a migration in every consumer and needs a sweeper to reap expired rows, because expiry is not something a table enforces; a self-contained signed payload needs no store but then cannot be single-use, since a signed token that has not expired stays valid however many times it is presented. This port takes the third path and hides the choice: the handlers see two `Result`-returning methods, and the cache substrate is entirely the implementation's business ([ADR-091](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/091-cache-backed-password-reset.html)).

  The second teaching point is in the return shapes. `ValidateAndConsumeAsync` is documented to collapse **unknown, expired, mismatched, and attempt-capped** into one generic failure (`:32-35`), so the redeem endpoint cannot be used to distinguish a wrong token from an expired one from an address that was never issued a token. The issue path is throttled rather than refused loudly, for the same anti-enumeration reason the forgot-password handler answers success to every input.
- **Walkthrough**: two members.
  - `Task<Result<string>> IssueAsync(string email, UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:23`) returns the **raw** token to email, or a failure when the per-email request throttle has been exceeded. The doc comment (`:12-15`) states the replace semantics: issuing overwrites any token already outstanding for that address, so requesting a new link immediately stops the older one from working. The `userId` parameter is what the token resolves back to at redeem time, which is why the redeem call never has to trust an identifier supplied by the caller.
  - `Task<Result<UserIdentifierType>> ValidateAndConsumeAsync(string email, string token, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:36`) validates the presented token against the outstanding record and **consumes it on success**, so a token never redeems twice (`:25-28`), returning the account the token belongs to.
- **Why it's built this way**: taking `email` on both methods, rather than treating the token as self-describing, is what lets the implementation key its records by address and enforce the per-address throttle and the one-active-token rule at the same key. Returning `Result<UserIdentifierType>` rather than a boolean means the redeem handler gets the account identity from the token store itself. See [PasswordResetTokenService](#passwordresettokenservice) for the mechanics the port hides: a 32-byte random token (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/PasswordResetTokenService.cs:39`), only its digest stored, an attempt counter, and an address normalized through [Email](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#email) before it becomes a cache key (`:34-45`) so `User@x.com` and `user@x.com` cannot hold independent tokens for one account.
- **Where it's used**: injected into the shared [ForgotPasswordHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>](group-14-module-system-composition.md#forgotpasswordhandlerbasetuser-tcommand) (constructor parameter at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ForgotPassword/ForgotPasswordHandlerBase.cs:39`, called at `:72`, where a throttled issue is logged and still answered as success) and into [ResetPasswordHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>](group-14-module-system-composition.md#resetpasswordhandlerbasetuser-tcommand) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ResetPassword/ResetPasswordHandlerBase.cs:45`, redeemed at `:61-62`). Both apps' sealed subclasses take the same dependency, for example ADC's [ForgotPasswordHandler](group-24-identity-module.md#forgotpasswordhandler) and [ResetPasswordHandler](group-24-identity-module.md#resetpasswordhandler). The framework registers the concrete as scoped at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:165`.

### AuthSignInMetrics
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:1099` · Level 3 · class (internal static)

- **What it is**: the OpenTelemetry instrument for password sign-in outcomes: one `MMCA.Common.Auth` meter carrying one counter, `mmca.auth.signin`, tagged by a low-cardinality `outcome`. It is declared in the same file as [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser), after the log companion (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:1092-1099`).
- **Depends on**: `System.Diagnostics.Metrics` for `Meter` and `Counter<long>` (BCL, `AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:2`), [Error](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error) and [TwoFactorErrors](#twofactorerrors) (its `TwoFactorRequiredCode`) for classifying a second-factor failure. Nothing else.
- **Concept introduced: an outcome tag, never an identity, on a security metric.** `[Rubric §13, Observability]` assesses whether the system exposes the signals an operator needs, and `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether telemetry leaks personal data. The doc comment (`:1092-1098`) sets the rule in one line: tags carry only the low-cardinality outcome, never an address, a user id or a client IP. Seven fixed values keep the series count bounded however many accounts exist, and a rise in `invalid_credentials` or `locked_out` is visible without the metric pipeline ever holding who was attempted. The same comment records a packaging consequence: a host exports the meter by registering its name, the Aspire service defaults already do, and the name is duplicated there as a literal because MMCA.Common.Aspire has no reference to Application (`:1093-1096`).
- **Walkthrough**: eleven internal members.
  - `MeterName = "MMCA.Common.Auth"` (`:1102`).
  - Seven outcome constants (`:1105-1123`): `Success` ("success", a token pair was issued), `InvalidCredentials` ("invalid_credentials": unknown address, wrong password, no password credential, or a request that failed validation), `LockedOut` ("locked_out"), `SecondFactorRequired` ("second_factor_required": the password verified and no code was supplied), `SecondFactorFailed` ("second_factor_failed"), `EmailNotConfirmed` ("email_not_confirmed") and `Rejected` ("rejected": the app gate or the issuance refused the account).
  - A private `Meter` built from `MeterName` (`:1125`) and the `SignIns` counter (`:1128`), created as `mmca.auth.signin` with unit `{attempt}`, one count per `LoginAsync` call.
  - `ForSecondFactorFailure(IEnumerable<Error> errors)` (`:1140-1141`) maps a failed challenge to `second_factor_required` when any error carries `TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorRequiredCode` (no code supplied) and to `second_factor_failed` for anything else, a wrong code, a replay, or a redemption that could not be persisted.
  - `Record(string outcome)` (`:1145-1146`) adds 1 to the counter with the single `outcome` tag.
- **Why it's built this way**: a static class with a static meter matches how .NET metrics are meant to be created (one instrument per process, recorded from anywhere), and keeping it `internal` beside the workflow means the outcome vocabulary changes in the same file as the branches that emit it. Counting a validation failure as `invalid_credentials` rather than adding an eighth value keeps the tag set small and matches what the caller is told.
- **Where it's used**: only by [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser)'s `LoginAsync`, which records `Success` once the tokens are issued (`AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:293`) and routes every failure through the private `SignInFailed` helper (`:976-984`), which calls `Record` (`:981`) and then writes the matching Warning through [AuthenticationServiceLog](#authenticationservicelog). The second-factor branch picks its tag through `ForSecondFactorFailure` (`:253`). No usage outside the defining file; the background is [ADR-041](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/041-observability-and-telemetry.html).

### AuthenticationServiceLog
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:1051` · Level 5 · class (internal static partial)

- **What it is**: the source-generated log-message companion of [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser), declared in the same file after the base closes. It carries two messages, `PasswordRehashRejected` and `SignInFailed`, and the `EmailLogHash` helper that makes an address safe to put in the second (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:1051-1090`).
- **Depends on**: `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging` for `ILogger`, `LogLevel` and the `[LoggerMessage]` generator (`AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:6`), `System.Security.Cryptography` and `System.Text` for the SHA-256 digest (`:4-5`), the [Email](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#email) value object for normalizing the address, and the solution-wide `UserIdentifierType` alias for the user-id parameter (`:1059`).
- **Concept: a non-generic log companion beside a generic base, and an address that never reaches a log.** `[Rubric §13, Observability]` assesses structured, allocation-free logging with stable message templates, and `[Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]` covers keeping a public type's shape free of incidental requirements. The `[LoggerMessage]` source generator needs a `partial` method on a `partial` type. Putting it on the public abstract base would force that base to be `partial` and make the generated method generic over `TUser`; the doc comment (`:1047-1050`) names the alternative taken: "a separate non-generic companion so the public base does not have to be partial". The class is `internal`, so it is not part of the framework's public surface. `[Rubric §11, Security]` applies to the sign-in line: a failed sign-in is logged with a 12-hex-character (48-bit) prefix of the SHA-256 of the normalized address, never the address, and the comment (`:1065-1071`) gives both halves of the reasoning: it is the same digest the login-protection counters key on, so the two log streams correlate, and a 48-bit prefix matches too many addresses to name one.
- **Walkthrough**: three members and one private constant.
  - `EmailLogHashLength = 12` (`:1054`), private, the number of hex characters a log line carries.
  - `PasswordRehashRejected(ILogger logger, UserIdentifierType userId, string errorCodes)` (`:1059`) logs at `LogLevel.Warning` (`:1057`) with the template "Password rehash for user {UserId} was refused by the aggregate ({ErrorCodes}); the sign-in is unaffected and the stored hash is unchanged" (`:1058`). The template states the consequence for an operator reading it: the sign-in already succeeded and nothing was written.
  - `SignInFailed(ILogger logger, string outcome, string emailHash)` (`:1062-1063`) logs at `Warning` with "Password sign-in failed ({Outcome}) for address hash {EmailHash}", where `Outcome` is one of the [AuthSignInMetrics](#authsigninmetrics) tag values.
  - `EmailLogHash(string? email)` (`:1074-1089`) normalizes a blank address to the empty string (`:1077-1080`), otherwise takes `Email.Create(email)`'s normalized value and falls back to `Trim().ToLowerInvariant()` for a malformed address (`:1084`, under a scoped CA1308 suppression that names the RFC 5321 lowercase rule it matches, `:1083`), and returns the first 12 uppercase hex characters of the SHA-256 digest (`:1088`).
- **Why it's built this way**: a refused rehash is a domain answer (the aggregate's `RehashPassword` returned a failure), not an exception, so it never reaches the best-effort wrapper's own failure log and metric; that message is what makes the branch visible. Logging the error codes joined with `", "` rather than the error messages keeps the line free of any user-facing text. A failed sign-in needs a per-address handle for an investigation (the same address failing repeatedly) without writing personal data, which is what the truncated digest gives. The background is [ADR-133](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/133-versioned-password-hash-work-factor.html) (the stored hash carries its work factor and is upgraded on sign-in), [ADR-096](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/096-best-effort-side-effects.html) (best-effort side effects never fail the primary operation) and [ADR-041](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/041-observability-and-telemetry.html).
- **Where it's used**: `PasswordRehashRejected` is called once, from the private `RehashPasswordIfNeededAsync` of [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser) when `IPasswordRehashableUser.RehashPassword` fails (`AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:1023-1030`). `SignInFailed` and `EmailLogHash` are called together from the base's private `SignInFailed` helper (`:982`), which every failing branch of `LoginAsync` returns through. Both use the base's overridable `Logger` property as the sink, which defaults to `NullLogger.Instance` (`:153`), so the lines are emitted only by an app subclass that overrides `Logger` with an injected logger. No usage outside the defining file.

### SoftDeletedUserCache
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUserCache.cs:19` · Level 5 · class (static)

- **What it is**: the shared cache contract for the **soft-deleted user marker** (BR-133), which now means "deleted or locked": the key shape, the marker lifetime, and the helpers that write and clear it. The API middleware reads the marker on every authenticated request and answers 401 while it is set; the module that soft-deletes a user, an administrator's lock (`UserAdministrationServiceBase`) and a machine-client revocation write it, and an unlock clears it (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUserCache.cs:6-12`).
- **Depends on**: [ICacheService](group-09-caching.md#icacheservice) from `MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces` (`:2`), `CrossServiceCacheKeys` for the unqualified key prefix, the `UserIdentifierType` alias, and `System.Globalization.CultureInfo` (BCL, `:1`).
- **Concept introduced: revoking a stateless credential without a per-request lookup.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether a revoked principal actually loses access, and `[Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]` assesses whether such a concern is factored so both ends share one definition. A JWT is a bearer credential: signature validation never asks "is this account still active?", so soft-deleting or locking a user leaves an already-issued access token passing validation until it expires ([ADR-047](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/047-soft-deleted-user-session-revocation.html)). The textbook fixes (a deny-list, or an account-status query on every request) reintroduce exactly the per-request state that stateless JWT was chosen to avoid. This type is the middle path: a short-lived cache marker written at deletion or lock time and read cheaply on the hot path.

  The `remarks` (`:13-18`) explain why the constants live in the **Application** layer rather than next to the middleware that reads them: a downstream application deleting an account has to write the exact same key the middleware reads, and a private constant in the presentation layer is unreachable from an application-layer command handler. Same reasoning as [IdempotencyHeaders](#idempotencyheaders), applied one layer up.
- **Walkthrough**: six static members, no state.
  - A private `DefaultClockSkew` of 5 minutes (`:22`), the JWT bearer library's default, which the framework never overrides.
  - `MarkerDuration => TimeSpan.FromMinutes(20)` (`:41`). The remarks (`:27-40`) justify the number rather than leaving it magic: the marker must outlive **every access token issued before the delete or lock**. A host that does not run Identity registers no validator query, and the Identity host's query checks deletion only, so the marker is the only thing that rejects a deleted user's token on the first and a locked user's on any host. A token is accepted until its expiry **plus** the bearer clock skew, so the marker lasts the default 15-minute access-token lifetime (the BR-205 default on [ITokenService](#itokenservice)) plus the 5-minute skew. It is a constant because the static helper cannot reach the JWT settings; a host with a longer lifetime or skew writes a longer marker through `MarkerDurationFor`. Only positive markers are written.
  - `MarkerDurationFor(TimeSpan accessTokenLifetime, TimeSpan? clockSkew = null)` (`:51-55`) returns the lifetime plus the skew (the 5-minute default when null), never less than `MarkerDuration` (`:53-54`).
  - `KeyFor(UserIdentifierType userId)` (`:73-74`) builds `{CrossServiceCacheKeys.Prefix}user:deleted:{userId}` through `string.Create(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, ...)`. The remarks (`:62-66`) name the bug the invariant culture prevents: an identifier renders differently under some cultures (digit shapes, group separators), so a culture-sensitive key would be written under one request's culture and missed under another, silently letting a deleted user keep making requests. The second paragraph (`:67-71`) explains the prefix: the Identity service writes the marker and every other service's middleware reads it, so the key must not be qualified with each host's own namespace, or a service that does not host Identity would never see a lock.
  - `MarkDeletedAsync(ICacheService cache, UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:84-92`) null-guards the cache (`:89`) and writes `true` under `KeyFor(userId)` for `MarkerDuration` (`:91`). It returns the task without awaiting, so there is no extra async state machine for a one-call passthrough.
  - `MarkDeletedForAsync(cache, userId, TimeSpan duration, ...)` (`:103-112`) is the same write with an explicit lifetime, for a host whose access tokens outlive `MarkerDuration`.
  - `ClearMarkerAsync(cache, userId, ...)` (`:129-137`) removes the marker through `ICacheService.RemoveAsync` (`:136`), so a token issued after an unlock is accepted at once. The remarks (`:122-128`) explain why that is enough on every replica: another replica may still hold a local copy, but the middleware never reads one, it reads the marker from the shared store.
- **Why it's built this way**: publishing the key shape and the TTL as framework API is what keeps the writers and the reader honest, and it is a precondition for the module boundary in [ADR-047](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/047-soft-deleted-user-session-revocation.html): Identity owns the delete and the lock, every service hosts the middleware, and the only thing they share is a cache entry rather than a database. `[Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]` applies directly: an extracted service can enforce the revocation without a reference to the Identity database.
- **Where it's used**: read by [SoftDeletedUserMiddleware](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#softdeletedusermiddleware), which builds the key (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/SoftDeletedUserMiddleware.cs:85`) and, when it caches a deleted answer itself, sizes it with `MarkerDurationFor(tokens.AccessTokenLifetime, ...)` or falls back to `MarkerDuration` when no [ITokenService](#itokenservice) is registered (`:183-189`). Written through [SoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter](#softdeletedusermarkerwriter), the default [ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter](#isoftdeletedusermarkerwriter), which writes for `MarkerDurationFor(tokenService.AccessTokenLifetime)` and clears through `ClearMarkerAsync` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUsers/SoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:17-25`). The shared delete workflow calls that writer (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandlerBase.cs:214`) and swallows any non-cancellation fault (`:216`) so a failed marker cannot turn a successful erasure into an error the caller would retry. [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice) writes the marker for a revoked client's service account with a lifetime computed from its own token lifetime (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:231-234`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: the marker is best effort on both ends by design. The middleware fails **open** on a cache fault (`SoftDeletedUserMiddleware.cs:98`), and the writers log and continue. The exposure that leaves is bounded by the access-token lifetime, which is the trade-off ADR-047 accepts explicitly.

### AuthenticationValidators
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationValidators.cs:26` · Level 5 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: a tiny **parameter object** that bundles the three FluentValidation validators the authentication workflow needs (login, registration, refresh), the optional Terms of Service version registration requires, and, when the host registered one, the sign-in second-factor challenge, into one injectable dependency.
- **Depends on**: FluentValidation's `IValidator<T>` (NuGet, `:1`) over the request DTOs [LoginRequest](#loginrequest), [RegisterRequest](#registerrequest), and [RefreshTokenRequest](#refreshtokenrequest) (all in `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth`), `IOptions<LegalAcceptanceOptions>` and `LegalAcceptancePolicy` from `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Legal` for the terms check, and [ITwoFactorAuthenticator](#itwofactorauthenticator) for the optional challenge.
- **Concept introduced: the parameter object as a constructor-arity guardrail.** `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` assesses whether a class stays a single, cohesive responsibility rather than sprawling into a god class, and `[Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]` assesses whether cross-cutting dependencies are grouped so a class can grow without exploding its constructor. The doc comment (`:6-11`) states the exact motive: collapsing three closely-related dependencies into one keeps the app's `AuthenticationService` **below the application-service constructor-arity ceiling** (a god-class analyzer guardrail) without giving up per-request validation. Because the request DTOs already live in `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth`, the bundle is app-agnostic, which is why it could be hoisted out of the apps into the framework. The same move is now used twice more: the terms options and the second-factor authenticator ride in here so adopting either feature adds no constructor argument to the app's subclass. The pressure is real rather than theoretical: ADC's subclass already carries a long primary constructor (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/AuthenticationService.cs:52-70`, the bundle at `:57`).
- **Walkthrough**: two constructors and five get-only members.
  - The primary constructor (`:26-30`) takes the three `IValidator<T>` instances plus an optional `IOptions<LegalAcceptanceOptions>? legalAcceptance = null`.
  - A second public constructor (`:45-51`) takes the same four arguments, `legalAcceptance` without a default, plus a required `ITwoFactorAuthenticator twoFactor`, chains to the primary and sets `TwoFactor`. Its doc comment (`:32-44`) gives the selection rule: the container picks it only when an `ITwoFactorAuthenticator` is registered (by `AddTwoFactorAuthentication(configuration)`), so a host that has not adopted two-factor resolves the primary constructor and is unchanged. The class-level `RS0027` suppression (`:25`) records why the shipped constructor keeps its optional parameter: removing the default would break every three-argument call, and the longer overload has no optional parameter, so positional calls bind unambiguously.
  - `Login` (`:54`), `Register` (`:57`) and `Refresh` (`:60`) surface the validators by name.
  - `CurrentTermsVersion` (`:66`) returns `LegalAcceptancePolicy.ResolveCurrentVersion(legalAcceptance?.Value)`: the Terms of Service version registration requires, or `null` when acceptance is not configured.
  - `TwoFactor` (`:73`) is the sign-in challenge, or `null` when the host registered none. Its doc comment (`:68-72`) fixes precedence: `AuthenticationServiceBase` uses it only when its own `twoFactor` constructor argument is null, so an explicit argument wins.
  Beyond the one resolver call the type has no logic.
- **Why it's built this way**: a `sealed` grouping type with get-only properties is the cheapest way to fold cohesive dependencies into one constructor slot, so the workflow base can validate each request shape, and challenge a second factor, without pushing its constructor or the app's over the arity limit; DI resolves the underlying services and composes them into this one object, choosing the constructor by what is registered. Two of the three validators ([LoginRequestValidator](#loginrequestvalidator), [RefreshTokenRequestValidator](#refreshtokenrequestvalidator)) come from the framework assembly, while `IValidator<RegisterRequest>` is satisfied by the app's own `RegisterRequestValidator`, so the bundle is the point where framework and app validation meet.
- **Where it's used**: injected into [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser) (constructor parameter at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:78`), whose `LoginAsync`, `RegisterAsync`, and `RefreshTokenAsync` call `validators.Login` (`:170`), `validators.Register` (`:307`), and `validators.Refresh` (`:407`) respectively before doing any work, which re-exposes `CurrentTermsVersion` as a protected property (`:141`) that `RegisterAsync` tests (`:316`), and whose `ChallengeSecondFactorAsync` resolves `twoFactor ?? validators.TwoFactor` (`:862`). It is registered by each app's Identity module rather than by the framework, since one of its dependencies is app-owned: `MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:42` and `MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:46`, both `TryAddScoped<AuthenticationValidators>()`. `AddTwoFactorAuthentication` registers the authenticator the longer constructor picks up (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:63`, with the by-type registration precondition stated at `:38-40`), and the terms options are bound by the opt-in `AddLegalAcceptance(configuration)` (`DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:140-146`).

### IAuthenticationService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IAuthenticationService.cs:12` · Level 5 · interface

- **What it is**: the application-layer contract for the Identity module's authentication workflows: login, registration, token refresh, per-device and global session revocation, session and sign-in history listing, external (OAuth) login, and the two credential-proved sign-ins (a redeemed sign-in link and a verified passkey).
- **Depends on**: [LoginRequest](#loginrequest), [RefreshTokenRequest](#refreshtokenrequest), [RegisterRequest](#registerrequest), [AuthenticationResponse](#authenticationresponse), [RegistrationOutcome](#registrationoutcome), [RefreshSessionSummaryResponse](#refreshsessionsummaryresponse), [SignInSummaryResponse](#signinsummaryresponse), [SignInLinkErrors](#signinlinkerrors) and [PasskeyErrors](#passkeyerrors) (the defaults' failures), [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result), [Error](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error), and the `UserIdentifierType` alias.
- **Concept introduced: default interface methods for optional capabilities.** `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` (interface segregation and dependency inversion): four members ship a **default implementation** in the interface itself, so an implementation that has not adopted a capability inherits a safe answer and need not override anything. `ExternalLoginAsync` (`:150-158`) returns a not-supported [Error](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error) (`"Auth.ExternalLoginNotSupported"`, `:158`) ([ADR-036](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/036-external-oauth-login.html)); `SignInVerifiedEmailOwnerAsync` (`:174-180`) and `SignInWithPasskeyAsync` (`:197-203`) reject through `SignInLinkErrors.NotSupported` and `PasskeyErrors.NotSupported`, so an implementation that has not adopted sign-in links ([ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html)) or passkeys ([ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html)) keeps compiling and never opens a session through that path; and `HasSignInMethodBesidesPasskeysAsync` (`:217-220`) answers `false`, which the remarks (`:213-216`) justify as the recoverable direction: refusing to delete the last passkey can be undone, a locked-out account cannot. `[Rubric §11, Security]`: every sign-in member returns `Result<AuthenticationResponse>`, so auth outcomes flow as values and no exception leaks credential detail to the caller.

  The second concept the signatures teach is that a session is a **device**, not a user. `LoginAsync`, `RegisterAsync` and `RefreshTokenAsync` all take optional `ipAddress` and `userAgent` (`:25-26`, `:41-42`, `:56-57`) recorded on the session row, and the doc comments state the invariant each time: signing in opens a session for the calling device and leaves the user's other devices signed in (`:15-16`), and refreshing rotates the presenting device's session only (`:46-47`).
- **Walkthrough**: twelve methods, all async, all ending in a `CancellationToken`.
  - `LoginAsync(LoginRequest, string? ipAddress = null, string? userAgent = null, ...)` returns `Result<AuthenticationResponse>` (`:23-27`).
  - `RegisterAsync(RegisterRequest, string? ipAddress = null, string? userAgent = null, ...)` (`:39-43`); the `ipAddress` does double duty, feeding [ILoginProtectionService](#iloginprotectionservice)'s registration rate limit and the new session row (`:35`). The summary (`:30-32`) adds one outcome to the contract: when the host requires a confirmed address and the new account is unconfirmed, the result is a **success** carrying `RegistrationOutcome.ConfirmationPending` and no session is opened.
  - `RefreshTokenAsync(RefreshTokenRequest, string? ipAddress = null, string? userAgent = null, ...)` (`:54-58`) exchanges an expired access token plus a valid refresh token for a rotated pair, recording the caller's IP and user agent on the rotated session.
  - `RevokeTokenAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, string? refreshToken = null, ...)` (`:69-72`) signs **one device** out. The documented fallback is the interesting part (`:61-63`): passing no token, or one that does not belong to this user, revokes every session the user holds, which the comment calls the safe reading of "log me out" from a caller that cannot produce its refresh token.
  - `RevokeAllSessionsAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, ...)` (`:81-83`) signs every device out: a password change, an admin lockout, or an explicit "sign out everywhere".
  - `GetSessionsAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, Guid? currentSessionId = null, ...)` (`:98-101`) lists live sessions newest first with the caller's own device marked. `currentSessionId` is the caller token's `sid` claim and is used only to set `RefreshSessionSummaryResponse.IsCurrent`; passing `null` marks no row (`:91-94`).
  - `GetSignInsAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, Guid? currentSessionId = null, ...)` (`:115-118`) lists the user's sign-in **history**: one row per sign-in however often its refresh token rotated, ended sign-ins included with how they ended, newest first, capped at the newest 50, over what the session store retains (`RefreshSessions:RetentionDays`, 30 by default) (`:104-106`). `currentSessionId` sets `SignInSummaryResponse.IsCurrent` the same way.
  - `RevokeSessionByIdAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, Guid sessionId, ...)` (`:134-137`) revokes one named device. The remarks (`:124-128`) fix two behaviors as contract: an unknown id and another account's id both return `NotFound` and are indistinguishable, so a caller cannot probe for another user's sessions; and revoking an **already-revoked** session changes nothing and also returns `NotFound` with the code `Auth.SessionAlreadyRevoked` (`:126-128`), so a device list can tell the user the device was already signed out instead of claiming this request signed it out.
  - `ExternalLoginAsync(loginProvider, providerKey, email, firstName, lastName, ...)` (`:150-158`), the default-implemented OAuth path.
  - `SignInVerifiedEmailOwnerAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, string? ipAddress = null, string? userAgent = null, ...)` (`:174-180`) opens a session for an account whose owner has just redeemed a single-use sign-in link; the caller has already spent the token, and this member applies the same account gates a password sign-in does and mints the pair (`:161-163`).
  - `SignInWithPasskeyAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, ...)` (`:197-203`) does the same after a verified passkey assertion, and the resulting access token carries `mfa=passkey` (`:183-186`).
  - `HasSignInMethodBesidesPasskeysAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, ...)` (`:217-220`) asks whether the account still has a password or an external login, before its last passkey is deleted (`:206-208`).

  The doc comment (`:6-9`) also records a scope decision: **password change is not on this interface**. It is dispatched directly through its own command handler at the controller layer.
- **Why it's built this way**: concentrating the token-issuing and session-management workflows behind one port keeps the Identity controllers thin and lets the protection and rate-limit policy ([ILoginProtectionService](#iloginprotectionservice)) compose in; the defaulted members keep the contract stable across hosts that do and do not enable social login, sign-in links or passkeys, and route every credential-proved sign-in through the same account gates and issuance. Encoding the anti-probing and idempotent-revoke rules in `remarks` rather than leaving them to an implementation makes them testable expectations of every implementer.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser) (which realises every member except the default `ExternalLoginAsync`) and, through it, by each app's sealed [AuthenticationService](group-24-identity-module.md#authenticationservice); consumed by the API controller bases (`AuthControllerBase`, `OAuthControllerBase`, `TwoFactorControllerBase`), by `RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase` for the sign-in link redemption, and by the passkey sign-in flow.

### RefreshSessionSignIn
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/RefreshSessionSignIn.cs:19` · Level 5 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: one sign-in as the session store aggregates it: its identifier, the instant its earliest retained session was issued, and its newest session (the **head**), which carries the last activity, the device and how the sign-in ended (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/RefreshSessionSignIn.cs:5-9`).
- **Depends on**: [RefreshSession](#refreshsession) from `MMCA.Common.Domain.Auth` (`:1`). Nothing else.
- **Concept introduced: a sign-in is a rotation chain, not a row.** `[Rubric §8, Data Architecture]` assesses whether read shapes match what the data means, and `[Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]` assesses whether a read stays bounded as data grows. Every refresh rotates a session into a new row, so a user who stayed signed in for a month owns hundreds of rows for one sign-in. This record is the unit a sign-in history needs: one entry per chain, its start, and only its newest row. `SignInId` is the chain's shared `RefreshSession.SignInId`, or, for a row written before that column existed, the row's own `Id` (`:10-13`), so older data still lists. `Head` is read-only: a store may return it untracked, so a mutation on it is never persisted (`:15-18`).
- **Walkthrough**: a positional `sealed record` with three members (`:19`): `Guid SignInId`, `DateTime StartedAt` (the UTC issue instant of the earliest retained session, `:14`) and `RefreshSession Head`. Value equality and immutability come from the record; there is no behavior.
- **Why it's built this way**: aggregating in the store, and handing back this small projection, is what lets [IRefreshSessionStore](#irefreshsessionstore)'s `GetRecentSignInsAsync` bound its read by the number of sign-ins requested rather than by the user's total row count, so a sign-in that rotated a thousand times costs one entry. Carrying the whole head rather than a flattened DTO leaves the response shaping (device, end reason, current marker) to the application layer.
- **Where it's used**: returned by `IRefreshSessionStore.GetRecentSignInsAsync` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IRefreshSessionStore.cs:80-83`); produced by [EFRefreshSessionStore](group-07-persistence-ef-core.md#efrefreshsessionstore) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFRefreshSessionStore.cs:96`) and by the test double [InMemoryRefreshSessionStore](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#inmemoryrefreshsessionstore); consumed by [SignInHistory](#signinhistory) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/SignInHistory.cs:45`), which sits behind the issuer's `ListSignInsAsync` that [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser)'s `GetSignInsAsync` calls. Background: [ADR-097](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.html).

### IRefreshSessionStore
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IRefreshSessionStore.cs:21` · Level 6 · interface

- **What it is**: persistence for [RefreshSession](#refreshsession) rows, one hashed refresh session per signed-in device (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IRefreshSessionStore.cs:5-6`). Sessions are added, looked up by token hash or by id, listed per user (live, unrevoked, all, or aggregated into sign-ins), counted per user, rotated, and saved.
- **Depends on**: [RefreshSession](#refreshsession) from `MMCA.Common.Domain.Auth` (`:1`), [RefreshSessionSignIn](#refreshsessionsignin) for the sign-in aggregate, and the `UserIdentifierType` alias. The shipped implementation is [EFRefreshSessionStore](group-07-persistence-ef-core.md#efrefreshsessionstore); the test double is [InMemoryRefreshSessionStore](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#inmemoryrefreshsessionstore) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/InMemoryRefreshSessionStore.cs:27`).
- **Concept introduced: a repository whose contract is deliberately missing an `Update`.** `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` assesses interface segregation, and `[Rubric §8, Data Architecture]` assesses whether the persistence contract expresses the aggregate's rules. The doc comment (`:8-14`) explains the shape: sessions are mutated only through `RefreshSession.Revoke` on instances **this store returned**, so an implementation that tracks its entities persists a revocation with no update method at all, and `TryRotateAsync` is the one exception because rotation is a claim, not a mutation. The requirement that makes that safe is stated as a contract obligation, not left implicit: implementations must return **tracked** instances from every lookup **except** `FindByIdUntrackedAsync`, which is untracked by design and for reading only, because a no-tracking read anywhere else would accept revocations and rotations and drop them silently at save time (`:15-19`). This is the same trap called out for composed EF queries elsewhere in the framework, promoted here to interface documentation.

  The second concept is **lookup by hash, never by token** (`:8`, `:37`). The store never sees plaintext: callers hash first with `RefreshSession.HashToken` and search on the digest, which is what lets the table hold only digests. `[Rubric §11, Security]` applies directly.
- **Walkthrough**: eleven members.
  - `AddAsync(RefreshSession session, ...)` (`:26`) stages an insert.
  - `FindByTokenHashAsync(string tokenHash, ...)` (`:37`) finds by digest **including revoked and expired rows**, and the comment (`:29-32`) marks that as load-bearing: a rotated token that comes back is found on its revoked row, which is the BR-206 reuse signal, so a store that filtered revoked rows out would report a replay as "unknown token" and never revoke the family.
  - `GetUnrevokedByUserAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, ...)` (`:45-47`) returns the user's un-revoked sessions oldest first, expired ones included since they still occupy a row, which is what makes both family revocation and cap eviction deterministic (`:40-41`).
  - `GetAllByUserAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, ...)` (`:59-61`) returns **every** session row the user holds, revoked and expired included, oldest first, as tracked instances. Account erasure needs the whole set: a revoked row still carries the IP address and user agent captured at issue time, so anonymizing only the un-revoked rows would leave the rest behind (`:50-54`).
  - `GetRecentSignInsAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, int maxSignIns, ...)` (`:80-83`) returns the user's newest `maxSignIns` sign-ins as [RefreshSessionSignIn](#refreshsessionsignin) entries, newest first by `StartedAt`, **aggregated in the store**: one entry per `RefreshSession.SignInId` with its earliest issue instant and only its newest row (`:64-68`). A row with no `SignInId` (written before the column existed) is its own sign-in unless it was rotated away, in which case its successor stands for it (`:68-69`). Two obligations follow (`:71-73`): the returned heads are for reading only (the shipped EF store reads them untracked), and an implementation must bound what it reads by `maxSignIns`, never by the user's total row count.
  - `GetUserIdsWithLiveSessionsAsync(DateTime now, ...)` (`:93-95`) returns each user holding at least one **live** session at `now` exactly once, where live means not revoked and `ExpiresAt` strictly after `now` (`RefreshSession.IsActiveAt`), evaluated as one query in the store (`:86-88`).
  - `CountLiveSessionsByUserAsync(IReadOnlyCollection<UserIdentifierType> userIds, DateTime now, ...)` (`:106-109`) counts live sessions for many users in one grouped query, never one per user; a requested user with no live session is absent from the result and duplicates count once (`:98-102`). The EF store implements the two live-session reads at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFRefreshSessionStore.cs:221` and `:236`.
  - `FindByIdAsync(Guid id, UserIdentifierType userId, ...)` (`:121-124`) takes the owner as part of the **query** rather than as a check the caller performs afterwards. The comment (`:112-115`) gives the reason: a session id is a value a client hands back, so scoping the query to the owner is what makes another account's id indistinguishable from a nonexistent one. That is an authorization decision encoded in a signature.
  - `FindByIdUntrackedAsync(Guid id, ...)` (`:141-142`) re-reads a session as the database holds it **now**, bypassing any tracked copy, revoked and expired rows included (`:127-136`). The rotation loser needs it: its tracked instance was read before the winner's conditional update and still shows the row live, so only a fresh read can say when and why the row was revoked. The instance is for reading only, so a mutation on it is never persisted. The default returns `null`, which the caller treats as "cannot tell" and answers with the conservative BR-206 family revocation; the shipped EF store overrides it with a no-tracking query (`EFRefreshSessionStore.cs:277`).
  - `SaveChangesAsync(...)` (`:147`) persists staged inserts and revocations.
  - `TryRotateAsync(RefreshSession presented, RefreshSession successor, DateTime revokedAt, ...)` (`:177`) is the one exception to the no-update rule, and it ships a **default interface implementation**. It argument-guards both sessions (`:183-184`), revokes the presented session as `RefreshSession.ReasonRotated` linked to the successor's hash (`:186`), then stages and saves the successor (`:191-192`). The `bool` return is the whole point (`:154-160`): two requests presenting the same still-live token both read an un-revoked row, so a check-then-act rotation would mint two successors from one token and the presented row could never fire reuse detection again. Returning `false` tells the caller it lost the claim. The caller then re-reads the row through `FindByIdUntrackedAsync` to tell a sibling rotation inside the reuse grace (a 409 with nothing revoked) or a sign-out or cap eviction (that request fails alone) from a genuine replay (the family is revoked). The default body is atomic only per instance, which is all an in-memory or test store can offer; the shipped EF store replaces it with a conditional `ExecuteUpdateAsync` the database arbitrates (`EFRefreshSessionStore.cs:304`, the update at `:322`).
- **Why it's built this way**: hashed-at-rest, per-device session rows are what turn refresh-token rotation into something a user can inspect and revoke per device, and what let reuse detection revoke a whole family ([ADR-050](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/050-jwt-refresh-token-rotation.html), BR-205/206). Keeping the contract in Application means the workflow that uses it is independent of EF, so an extracted Identity service can bring its own store. Making rotation a *claim* rather than a mutation is the difference between a race that mints two live tokens and a race one side of which is answered as a replay. Pushing the sign-in aggregation into the store keeps a history page's cost proportional to the page, not to how often the user's tokens rotated.
- **Where it's used**: registered as scoped against the EF implementation at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:173`, scoped, like the unit of work it shares a `DbContext` with, so a login and its session insert commit together. Consumed by [AuthSessionIssuer](#authsessionissuer), not by `AuthenticationServiceBase` (injected at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:56`) for the owner-scoped lookups behind targeted revocation (`:298`, `:338`), the unrevoked-session reads behind sign-out and family revocation (`:242`, `:683`), cap eviction (`:708`), the insert of a new session (`:491`) and the successor lookup of a lost-response recovery (`:634`). The sign-in aggregate is read by [SignInHistory](#signinhistory) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/SignInHistory.cs:45`), the all-sessions read behind account erasure by [RefreshSessionRevocation](#refreshsessionrevocation) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/RefreshSessionRevocation.cs:81`), and the live-session reads by [UserSessionsAdministrationService](#usersessionsadministrationservice) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserSessionsAdministrationService.cs:80`, `:99`).

### RefreshSessionRevocation
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/RefreshSessionRevocation.cs:21` · Level 6 · class (public static)

- **What it is**: a shared static helper with two steps. `RevokeAllAsync` (public) revokes every un-revoked refresh session a user holds; `RevokeAndAnonymizeAllAsync` (internal) is the account-erasure step. Used wherever a credential-rotation path needs to make sure a stale token cannot keep authenticating after the event that should have invalidated it.
- **Depends on**: [IRefreshSessionStore](#irefreshsessionstore) (nullable: a host that never registered one, because refresh sessions are opt-in, is a no-op), [RefreshSession](#refreshsession) (`.Revoke`, `RefreshSession.ReasonSignedOut`), and the BCL `TimeProvider`.
- **Concept introduced: a credential-rotation event is a call site, not a feature flag.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether changing a credential actually invalidates the sessions issued under the old one. Because refresh sessions are opt-in ([RefreshSessionSettings](#refreshsessionsettings)`.Enabled`), a change-password or reset-password handler cannot assume a store exists; the doc comment states this directly (`:23-26`), and `refreshSessions is null` (`:37-40`) is checked first so the call degrades to a no-op rather than throwing, meaning the same handler code runs unchanged on a host that never enabled the feature.
- **Walkthrough**: one static method, `RevokeAllAsync(IRefreshSessionStore? refreshSessions, TimeProvider? timeProvider, UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken)` (`:31-35`). It returns immediately on a null store (`:37-40`) or an empty session list (`:44-47`), otherwise stamps `now` from the supplied `timeProvider` or `TimeProvider.System` (`:42`), calls `session.Revoke(now, RefreshSession.ReasonSignedOut)` on every un-revoked session in a loop (`:49-52`), and saves once (`:54`).

  `RevokeAndAnonymizeAllAsync` (`:69-90`) is the erasure variant. It reads **every** session through `IRefreshSessionStore.GetAllByUserAsync`, revokes the un-revoked ones as `RefreshSession.ReasonAccountDeleted`, and calls `Anonymize()` on every row, revoked ones too, since each still carries the IP address and user agent captured at issue time (`:57-64`, `:81-89`). It saves nothing: the store returns tracked rows, so the caller's own unit-of-work save persists the changes together with the erasure. It is used by `DeleteUserHandlerBase` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandlerBase.cs:178`).
- **Why it's built this way**: a static class with no instance state keeps the helper a one-line call from any handler that needs it (`RevokeAllAsync` is public so an app-side `IUserAdministrationService` can run the same step after locking an account or changing its role instead of re-implementing it, class doc `:16-19`), and centralizing the null-store check here means every caller gets the same opt-in-safe behavior instead of re-deriving it.
- **Where it's used**: the documented mechanism behind [IUserAdministrationService<TUserDto>](#iuseradministrationservicetuserdto)'s `SetLockedAsync` obligation (see that type); also `ChangePasswordHandlerBase` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ChangePassword/ChangePasswordHandlerBase.cs`) and `ResetPasswordHandlerBase` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ResetPassword/ResetPasswordHandlerBase.cs`).

It realises [IAuthenticationService](#iauthenticationservice) and leaves the genuinely app-specific decisions to a small set of `abstract` and `virtual` hooks a sealed subclass overrides (class doc comment, `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:29-48`).

response DTOs. The base itself takes no session store, no session settings, no clock and no logger (`:74-81`): the first three belong to the issuer, and the logger is an overridable property instead.
- **Concept introduced: the Template Method that de-duplicates a whole vertical slice.** `[Rubric §2, Design Patterns]` assesses idiomatic pattern use: this is a textbook **Template Method**, the invariant sequence of an operation living in the base while the variable steps are deferred to subclass hooks, and the class doc comment lists the hooks with what each app supplies (`:35-46`). `[Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]` (DRY across services) and `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` also apply: a fix to the lockout order or the rotation logic is written once for every app. `[Rubric §11, Security]`: the base encodes the security posture directly, validate first, an [ILoginProtectionService](#iloginprotectionservice) lockout and rate-limit gate ([ADR-029](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/029-authentication-brute-force-protection.html)), an untracked-then-tracked dual fetch ([ADR-004](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/004-authentication-dual-fetch.html)), an opt-in upgrade of an outdated password hash on sign-in ([ADR-133](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/133-versioned-password-hash-work-factor.html)), a refusal of every interactive sign-in for a machine client's service account ([ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html)), and, through [IAuthSessionIssuer](#iauthsessionissuer), refresh-token rotation with **reuse detection** ([ADR-050](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/050-jwt-refresh-token-rotation.html), BR-205/206). `[Rubric §13, Observability]`: every password sign-in is counted by outcome and every failure logged without the address. `[Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]`: the workflow depends only on ports, so it runs unchanged whether the Identity module is in-monolith or its own service.

  **The division of labour is the other concept to absorb before reading the code** (`:49-54`): this class decides **who** is signed in, and [IAuthSessionIssuer](#iauthsessionissuer) decides **what they are handed**. Once a caller is proved, the multi-device refresh sessions (hashed at rest), BR-205 rotation with BR-206 reuse detection, the per-user session cap, and the `sid` and `mfa` claims on the minted access token are the issuer's job, so this workflow never touches a [RefreshSession](#refreshsession) row. Every session-shaped member below is a single delegation to the issuer; the reuse, replay, expiry and cap rules are taught on [AuthSessionIssuer](#authsessionissuer).
- **Walkthrough** (members in teaching order):
  - **Constructor, arming fields and protected accessors** (`:74-153`): a primary constructor takes the five required collaborators plus the two optional ones; when `twoFactor` is null the challenge falls back to `AuthenticationValidators.TwoFactor`, and an explicit argument wins (parameter doc, `:62-68`). A private constant `PasswordRehashOperation = "password-rehash"` (`:85`) is the best-effort operation name and metric tag for the sign-in rehash. Two private fields arm the minted token for one request: `_multiFactorMethod` (`:97`), the second-factor method that satisfied this request (a plain field because the service is scoped and one request issues one token pair, remarks `:93-96`), and `_authenticatedAt` (`:105`), the sign-in instant (`auth_time`) a presented token carried, armed only by `RefreshTokenAsync` so the rotated token keeps it unchanged; a sign-in leaves it null and the issuer stamps the instant of the session it opens (`:99-104`). Protected read-only properties re-expose `UnitOfWork` (`:108`), `TokenService` (`:120`), which returns `sessionIssuer.TokenService`, the issuer's stamping instance, so minting through it is what puts `sid` on the token (remarks, `:112-118`), and a `Repository` resolved lazily as `unitOfWork.GetRepository<TUser, UserIdentifierType>()` (`:123-124`). A protected `CurrentTermsVersion` (`:141`) forwards `validators.CurrentTermsVersion`, so adopting Terms of Service acceptance adds no constructor dependency here or in the app's subclass; when it is non-null, `RegisterAsync` has already refused a request whose `AcceptedTerms` is false before `CreateUser` runs, so a `CreateUser` override stamps that version on the new user (doc comment `:126-140`). A `protected virtual ILogger Logger` (`:153`) defaults to `NullLogger.Instance`; its doc comment (`:143-152`) says it is the sink for both the failed sign-in Warnings and the rehash line, that an app wanting them overrides it with its own injected logger, and that it is a virtual property rather than a constructor argument so the constructor stays within the framework's dependency ceiling. Token lifetimes and the session cap are not members of this class: they are configuration read by the issuer.
  - **`LoginAsync`** (`:164-298`): every call is counted once on the `MMCA.Common.Auth` meter by outcome, and every outcome but `success` writes one Warning carrying the outcome and a truncated hash of the normalized address (remarks, `:156-163`). Each failing branch returns through the private `SignInFailed(outcome, request.Email, failure)` helper (`:976-984`), which records the [AuthSignInMetrics](#authsigninmetrics) outcome and logs through [AuthenticationServiceLog](#authenticationservicelog) before handing the failure back unchanged. The sequence: validate the request (a failure counts as `invalid_credentials`, `:170-177`), check lockout (ADR-029 and BR-212, `locked_out`, `:180-187`), normalize the raw email into an [Email](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#email) value object (`:191`) so the EF predicate compares same-typed converted values (an invalid address yields a null value object that simply matches no user). **Step 1** is an *untracked* fetch via the `FindUntrackedByEmailAsync` hook (`:195`) to verify credentials without change-tracker overhead. The gate is `CanSignInWithPassword(untracked)` (`:201`, private helper at `:941-942`): the account must exist, must not be a machine client's service account (ADR-140), and must carry stored password material (`HasStoredCredential`, `:935`, through `PasswordCredential.IsStored`); an external-OAuth account (ADR-036) carries none. All three refusals answer the identical generic 401 after the identical `BurnPasswordVerificationCost(request.Password)` call (`:203`) and `IncrementFailedAttemptsAsync` (`:204`), so none of them can be told apart, by status or by timing, from an unknown address (comment, `:197-200`). `passwordHasher.VerifyPassword` runs next (`:212`) and fails the same way on a wrong password. Only after the password check does the app gate (`ValidateLoginCandidateAsync`, `:226`, outcome `rejected`) run, deliberately: reaching it proves the caller owns the account, so its distinct status message (for example a deactivated-account rejection) is told to the account's owner rather than to anyone sweeping addresses, and running it first would make account state readable with no credential at all and skip the failed-attempt counter (comment, `:222-225`). Two more gates follow the same rule, for the same reason: `CheckEmailConfirmed(untracked)` (`:239`, outcome `email_not_confirmed`, hook at `:832-842`), off unless the host both supplied `EmailConfirmationSettings.RequireConfirmedEmail` and the app's `User` implements [IEmailConfirmableUser](#iemailconfirmableuser), and `ChallengeSecondFactorCountingFailuresAsync(untracked.Id, request, cancellationToken)` (`:248-249`, private helper at `:876-889`, outcome chosen by `AuthSignInMetrics.ForSecondFactorFailure`).
