The culture seed exists because the confirmation email is composed later, outside this request, in the recipient's **stored** culture ([ADR-027](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/027-multi-locale-i18n.html)); it applies only to a `User` that implements [IUserPreferences](#iuserpreferences) and has no culture yet, and stores nothing for the invariant culture, the pseudo-locale or a culture that resolves to the default (doc comments, `:764-770`, `:781-787`). Next, registration opens **no session** exactly when sign-in would refuse the new account: if `CheckEmailConfirmed(tokenUser)` fails, the result is a success carrying `RegistrationOutcome.ConfirmationPending` (`:387-393`), and because the same virtual gate decides both, a subclass override moves them together. Otherwise the session is opened last (`:397`): it carries the user id, which a store-generated key only has once the insert has run.

    The save is wrapped in a deliberately **broad** `catch (Exception)` (`:355`) whose comment (`:358-371`) is the teaching material. The email lookup above is a check-then-act: two concurrent registrations for the same address both pass it, and the loser only fails on the insert, against the unique index every consumer puts on `Email` (ADC unfiltered, Store filtered on `IsDeleted`). Without the catch, that race surfaces as a generic 500 instead of the 409 a serialized pair would have produced. The catch cannot name `DbUpdateException`, because Application has no EF Core dependency by layer rule, so the **re-check is what narrows it** (`:372-377`): if the address exists now, the concurrent registration is the cause and the caller gets the same conflict the serial path returns through the shared `EmailAlreadyExistsFailure()` helper; anything else rethrows untouched and still reaches the exception middleware. The re-check passes `CancellationToken.None` on purpose: it has to run even when the caller's token is what aborted the save, or a cancelled save could never be classified.
  - **`RefreshTokenAsync`** (`:401-473`): validate (`:407`), pull claims from the *expired* JWT via `TokenService.GetPrincipalFromExpiredToken` (`:415`, the issuer's instance; signature still checked, only lifetime skipped), read the identifier with `principal.GetUserId()` (`:425`, rides the standard `sub` claim, also accepts the `NameIdentifier` form the bearer handler maps it to, and parses through `IParsable` so the identifier alias can change shape without editing this file), load the tracked user (`:432`, a missing user answered by `CreateRefreshUserMissingError`, `:435`), run the refresh app gate (`:439`), and hand the presented refresh token to `sessionIssuer.RotateAsync` (`:460-466`) together with a mint callback over `CreateAccessTokenForSession`. The issuer resolves the session behind the token (reuse detection included), rotates it, and answers with a token pair whose access token carries the **successor's** `sid`. Two claims ride the rotation, both read off the presented access token, whose signature was already validated, and both armed in one `try`/`finally` around the successor mint and cleared together (`:468-472`): the step-up the user already performed, `_multiFactorMethod = principal.FindMultiFactorMethod()` (`:450`; dropping it would quietly demote a signed-in session every access-token lifetime and make every `IRequiresMfa` use case unreachable without a fresh sign-in, comment `:445-449`), and the sign-in instant, `_authenticatedAt = principal.FindAuthTime()` (`:455`), carried **unchanged** because a refresh is not a sign-in, so a stolen refresh token cannot make its session look recently signed in; a token with no `auth_time` rotates into one with none (comment, `:452-454`, ADR-139).
  - **`RevokeTokenAsync`** (`:476-490`): load the user (a `NotFound` when absent), then delegate to `sessionIssuer.SignOutAsync(userId, refreshToken, ...)` (`:487`). Only a **live session belonging to this user** identifies the device to sign out; when the token is absent or identifies no live session of this user, the issuer revokes every live session instead, rather than reporting success for a revocation that reached nothing.
  - **`RevokeAllSessionsAsync`** (`:493-506`): the unconditional form of the same thing, through `sessionIssuer.SignOutEverywhereAsync` (`:503`).
  - **`GetSessionsAsync`** (`:510-518`) and **`GetSignInsAsync`** (`:522-530`): no user lookup, so each is one call to the issuer, `sessionIssuer.ListActiveAsync` (`:515`) for live devices and `sessionIssuer.ListSignInsAsync` (`:527`) for the sign-in history, wrapped in a success (remarks, `:509`, `:521`).
  - **`RevokeSessionByIdAsync`** (`:538-542`): an expression-bodied delegation to `sessionIssuer.RevokeSessionAsync`. Ownership is checked by the issuer's store query, so another account's id and a nonexistent id produce the same `NotFound` (remarks, `:533-537`); an already-revoked session writes nothing and returns `NotFound` with `Auth.SessionAlreadyRevoked`, matching the interface contract (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IAuthenticationService.cs:126-128`).
  - **`SignInVerifiedEmailOwnerAsync`** (`:558-586`): the sign-in-link path. A missing account or a service account reads as an invalid link (`:564-570`), the app gate runs (`:572`), and the second factor is challenged with **no code** (`:578`): any outcome other than `NotEnrolled` is refused with `SignInLinkErrors.SecondFactorRequired` (`:579-583`), because the link proves only mailbox access and honoring it would let that alone bypass an enrolled factor (remarks, `:553-555`). The email-confirmation gate is skipped on purpose: redeeming the link is the proof that gate asks for (`:549-550`). It then mints through `IssueTokensCoreAsync` (`:585`).
  - **`SignInWithPasskeyAsync`** (`:604-633`): the passkey path. A missing account or a service account answers `PasskeyErrors.AssertionFailed` (`:610-616`), the app gate runs (`:618`), and with **no second-factor challenge** `_multiFactorMethod` is armed to `AuthClaimTypes.MultiFactorMethodPasskey` around the issuance (`:624-632`): a passkey is possession of the authenticator plus its own user verification, so it satisfies the second factor itself, and `RefreshTokenAsync` carries `mfa=passkey` across rotations like `otp` (remarks, `:597-601`).
  - **`HasSignInMethodBesidesPasskeysAsync`** (`:641-653`): a vanished account answers `false` (`:646-649`); otherwise a non-empty stored password hash counts, and so does the virtual `HasExternalLoginAsync` (`:651-652`, hook at `:664-665`, default `false`).
  - **`IssueTokensAsync`** (`:694-716`): the protected open-and-respond an app-level sign-in that proves no factor (external login) mints through. It null-guards the user (`:700`) and, for anyone but a service account, runs the second-factor challenge with no code first, refusing an enrolled account with `TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorRequired` and opening no session (`:701-713`; doc `:680-686`). It ends in the private **`IssueTokensCoreAsync`** (`:728-746`), the core every framework sign-in (password, registration, sign-in link, passkey) calls directly once it has settled the factor itself. The core refuses a service account with the generic `Auth.InvalidCredentials` 401 (`:734-738`), which makes it the backstop behind every path-specific refusal (doc `:672-678`), and otherwise delegates to `sessionIssuer.IssueAsync(user.Id, sessionId => CreateAccessTokenForSession(user, sessionId), ...)` (`:740-745`): the access token is a callback because it carries the session's id, which exists only once the issuer has opened the session.
  - **The private mechanics** are login-side only. `ChallengeSecondFactorCountingFailuresAsync` (`:876-889`) is the counting wrapper described under `LoginAsync`. `MultiFactorMethodFor` (`:897-906`) maps an unrecognized outcome to `null`, so an enum that grew cannot silently mint an `mfa` claim. `HasStoredCredential` (`:935`) delegates to `PasswordCredential.IsStored`, and `CanSignInWithPassword` (`:941-942`) adds the existence and service-account checks. `BurnPasswordVerificationCost` (`:958-966`) skips a blank password and otherwise calls the hasher's own `passwordHasher.BurnVerificationCost(password)` (`:965`), so a branch that never reaches the real check still pays the key-derivation cost. The remarks (`:949-957`) explain both choices: the burn costs what verifying the most expensive record the hasher can have stored costs (for the shipped hasher, the larger of its current and legacy work factors), so an unknown address costs the same as an account still on an older record, and it does not verify against fixed decoy material because a hasher that rejects wrong-sized material before deriving anything (the shipped one does) would answer a decoy instantly and silently reopen the timing gap. `SignInFailed` (`:976-984`) is the record-and-log helper above.

    `RehashPasswordIfNeededAsync` (`:1004-1035`) is the work-factor upgrade. It returns at once unless the issuance succeeded and the app's `User` opts in by implementing [IPasswordRehashableUser](#ipasswordrehashableuser) (`:1006-1009`). Otherwise it runs inside `BestEffort.ExecuteAsync(PasswordRehashOperation, Logger, ..., CancellationToken.None)` (`:1011-1034`): when `passwordHasher.NeedsRehash(rehashable.PasswordHash)` reports the stored hash is current it does nothing (`:1016-1019`); otherwise it hashes the verified plaintext and hands the new material to `rehashable.RehashPassword(hash, salt)` (`:1021-1022`), logs [AuthenticationServiceLog](#authenticationservicelog)`.PasswordRehashRejected` with the joined error codes and returns if the aggregate refuses (`:1023-1030`), and saves through the unit of work on its own (`:1032`). The remarks (`:992-1000`) give the ordering its reason: it runs **after** the tokens are issued and saves separately, so the session save never carries the user row, and a refused invariant, a concurrency conflict or a dropped connection cannot fail a sign-in that has already succeeded; any non-domain failure is logged and counted by the best-effort wrapper, and the record is simply upgraded on a later sign-in. `CancellationToken.None` is deliberate: the sign-in is complete, and an abandoned request must not surface as a cancellation from this step. `EmailAlreadyExistsFailure()` (`:1042-1044`) is the 409 shared by the up-front check and the race recovery so the two paths are indistinguishable to a caller. Session resolution, rotation, family revocation and the cap are private to [AuthSessionIssuer](#authsessionissuer).
  - **The hooks**: four are `abstract`, so a subclass must supply them. `FindUntrackedByEmailAsync` (`:753`) and `EmailExistsAsync` (`:759`) are deliberately written against the app's concrete `User` so EF translates the predicate against the app's own mapped columns, and the second explicitly leaves the app to decide whether soft-deleted accounts count (`ignoreQueryFilters: true` blocks re-registration of an erased address); `CreateUser` (`:762`) runs the app's domain factory; `CreateAccessToken` (`:801`) mints the app's claim set (for example `speaker_id` versus `customer_id`). Eight `virtual` methods can be overridden, besides the `Logger` property above: `CreateAccessTokenForSession` (`:821-822`) calls `sessionIssuer.MintForSession(sessionId, _multiFactorMethod, _authenticatedAt, () => CreateAccessToken(user))`, so the issuer arms its stamping token service for the duration of the app hook and `sid` (plus `mfa` when this request verified a second factor, and `auth_time`, carried over unchanged on a refresh) is appended to whatever claim set the app passes, which is what keeps the claims additive with no change to `CreateAccessToken`'s signature (remarks, `:807-817`); `CheckEmailConfirmed` (`:832-842`) is the email-confirmation gate, used by both sign-in and registration; `ChallengeSecondFactorAsync` (`:858-864`) runs the second-factor challenge through `twoFactor ?? validators.TwoFactor` (`:862`) and, with neither, answers `TwoFactorOutcome.NotEnrolled` with no extra query, which is what keeps the feature free for an app that has not adopted it; `HasExternalLoginAsync` (`:664-665`) reports an external login for the last-passkey check; `ValidateLoginCandidateAsync` (`:909`) and `ValidateRefreshCandidateAsync` (`:913`) add extra gates such as a deactivated-account check (the first also guards the sign-in-link and passkey paths); `OnUserRegisteredAsync` (`:920`) runs the post-commit side-effect; and `CreateRefreshUserMissingError` (`:928-929`) defaults the vanished-user case to 401 (a token for a missing user is indistinguishable from an invalid one) while letting an app return 404 where its public contract already promises it.
- **Why it's built this way**: the untracked-then-tracked dual fetch keeps the common credential-verification path off the change tracker (cheaper, and soft-deleted accounts fall out via EF query filters returning the generic 401) while still giving a tracked instance to mint from ([ADR-004](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/004-authentication-dual-fetch.html)). Per-device session rows with hashed tokens, rotation, family revocation on reuse, and a per-user cap are the BR-205/206 model ([ADR-050](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/050-jwt-refresh-token-rotation.html)), and keeping them behind [IAuthSessionIssuer](#iauthsessionissuer) gives the sign-in decision and the session mechanics one owner each (`:49-54`). Routing every sign-in path, password or not, through one issuance core is what lets a single check refuse a service account everywhere ([ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html)) and lets the sign-in-link and passkey paths ([ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html), [ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html)) reuse the app gate and the session mint unchanged. Password material flows through [IAuthUser](#iauthuser)'s `PasswordHash` and `PasswordSalt` ([ADR-032](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/032-password-hashing.html)). A successful sign-in is the only moment the verified plaintext is in hand, which is why the hash upgrade lives here, opt-in per app through [IPasswordRehashableUser](#ipasswordrehashableuser) ([ADR-133](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/133-versioned-password-hash-work-factor.html)), and why it is best-effort rather than part of the sign-in's success ([ADR-096](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/096-best-effort-side-effects.html)). The whole workflow depends only on abstractions, so it is identical whether the module runs in-process or as an extracted service.
- **Where it's used**: subclassed by each app's sealed [AuthenticationService](group-24-identity-module.md#authenticationservice), for example `MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/AuthenticationService.cs:52`, which binds `TUser = User`, adds the Attendee default role (BR-45) and the `speaker_id` claim (BR-209, claims builder documented at `:559`), passes the injected [AuthenticationValidators](#authenticationvalidators) and [IAuthSessionIssuer](#iauthsessionissuer) through to the base (`:57-58`), re-lists `IAuthenticationService` (`:70`) so it can re-implement `RegisterAsync` and `ExternalLoginAsync` outright (`:76`), and overrides `HasExternalLoginAsync` (`:190`). ADC's `User` opts into the sign-in rehash by implementing `IPasswordRehashableUser` (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Domain/Users/User.cs:39`). MMCA.Store supplies its own subclass with a `customer_id` claim. Consumed by the Identity API controllers via the [IAuthenticationService](#iauthenticationservice) port.
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: `ExternalLoginAsync` is intentionally **not** overridden here: the base inherits the interface's default not-supported failure, and OAuth account linking stays in the app subclass because it is coupled to the app's `User` factory surface (doc comment, `:47-48`). ADC's subclass does not override `Logger`, so in ADC both the failed sign-in Warnings and a refused rehash go to the `NullLogger` and leave no log line; the `mmca.auth.signin` counter still records every attempt, and a thrown rehash failure is still counted on the `MMCA.Common.BestEffort` meter (doc comment, `:151-152`).

### EmailConfirmationSettings
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.EmailConfirmation` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/EmailConfirmation/EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:10` · Level 0 · class

- **What it is**: the options class bound to the `Authentication:EmailConfirmation` configuration section (`EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:28`), controlling token lifetime, throttling, and whether an unconfirmed address blocks sign-in.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations` (`[Range]`) and `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis` (`[SuppressMessage]`) validate the bound values.
- **Concept introduced**: the config-bound settings-class shape (a `SectionName` constant plus `init`-only, range-validated properties with sane defaults) is the same one the sibling `PasswordResetSettings` uses elsewhere in this group; see it there for the general pattern rather than re-teaching it here. `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses whether authentication-adjacent behavior is safely configurable): every numeric knob here is range-constrained (`EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:43,50,54,58`), so a bad value in configuration fails validation instead of silently disabling throttling.
- **Walkthrough**: `ConfirmationUrl` (`EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:40`) defaults to empty rather than being `[Required]`, deliberately, per its own doc comment (`EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:30-34`): an unconfigured host still boots and degrades to a token-only, paste-in-by-hand flow. `TokenLifetimeMinutes` (line 44) defaults to 1440 (one day). `MaxValidationAttempts` (line 51) caps wrong-token guesses at 5 before the record is discarded. `MaxRequestsPerEmail` (line 55) and `RequestWindowMinutes` (line 59) throttle re-issuance per address. `RequireConfirmedEmail` (line 70) defaults to `false`.
- **Why it's built this way**: the `RequireConfirmedEmail` default is called out as load-bearing in its own remarks (`EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:49-54`): turning it on locks out every account whose address was never confirmed, so a host backfills existing rows as confirmed before flipping it, and with it off the whole feature is additive. This is the opt-in shape recorded in [ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html).
- **Where it's used**: read by `AuthenticationServiceBase` and `EmailConfirmationTokenService` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs`, `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/EmailConfirmationTokenService.cs`) and registered in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`; ADC binds it via `MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/AuthenticationServiceSettings.cs` and consumes it in `SendEmailConfirmationHandler`.

### LegalAcceptanceOptions
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Legal` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Legal/LegalAcceptanceOptions.cs:12` · Level 0 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the options class for terms-of-service acceptance, bound from the `Legal` section (`SectionName`, `LegalAcceptanceOptions.cs:15`). Its one setting, `CurrentTermsVersion` (`:21`), is the terms version every user must have accepted (for example `2026-10-01`); changing it asks every signed-in user to accept again, and null or whitespace turns the feature off.
- **Depends on**: nothing; it is a plain options bag.
- **Concept**: a feature switch carried by configuration rather than a flag. "Not configured" is a legal state that disables the feature, and [LegalAcceptancePolicy](#legalacceptancepolicy)`.ResolveCurrentVersion` is the single place that turns the raw value into a trimmed version or null.
- **Why it's built this way**: an opt-in host (ADR-116) that never sets the section changes nothing, so the registration only binds the section (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:145-146`, inside `AddLegalAcceptance` at `:104`). Related: [ADR-070](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.html), [ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html).
- **Where it's used**: injected as `IOptions<LegalAcceptanceOptions>` by [LegalAcceptanceControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#legalacceptancecontrollerbase) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Legal/LegalAcceptanceControllerBase.cs:48`, read at `:54`) and, optionally, by [AuthenticationValidators](#authenticationvalidators) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationValidators.cs:30,66`), which exposes `CurrentTermsVersion` to the registration check.

### MachineClientSettings
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientSettings.cs:19` · Level 0 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the options class for machine clients (OAuth client credentials), bound from the `MachineClients` section (`SectionName`, `MachineClientSettings.cs:22`) by `AddMachineClients(configuration)` and validated at startup.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party at runtime; its doc comment points at [IServiceAccountProvisioner](#iserviceaccountprovisioner), which an enabled host must register.
- **Concept introduced**: the config-bound settings shape is the one [EmailConfirmationSettings](#emailconfirmationsettings) already shows; what is new here is a lifetime cap derived from another mechanism's window. `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses whether credentials and their revocation are bounded): `MaxAccessTokenMinutes` is 15 (`:33`) because revocation works by the soft-deleted marker for the service account, which lives 20 minutes, and a token must lapse within that window minus the bearer handler's 5-minute clock skew (doc comment `:27-32`).
- **Walkthrough**: `MinAccessTokenMinutes` is 1 (`:25`). `Enabled` (`:36`) defaults to `false`; while it is false the token endpoint and every administration endpoint answer 404 and the `MachineClients` table is in no model, so a host that never opts in sees no route and no migration (remarks `:8-13`). `AccessTokenMinutes` (`:42`) defaults to `MaxAccessTokenMinutes`; nothing renews the token, a program asks again. `DataSourceName` (`:48`) names the logical data source that owns the `MachineClients` table (the Identity database) and defaults to `"Default"`.
- **Why it's built this way**: off by default so the feature is additive, and turning it on needs consumer code (an [IServiceAccountProvisioner](#iserviceaccountprovisioner) over the app's own `User` aggregate, remarks `:14-17`). `MachineClientSettingsValidator` enforces both at startup: the 1 to 15 range (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientSettingsValidator.cs:23-27`) and, when enabled, a registered provisioner (`:37-40`). Recorded in [ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html); the fail-at-startup shape is [ADR-070](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.html).
- **Where it's used**: bound in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.MachineClients.cs:41-45` (inside `AddMachineClients`, `:37`); read by [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice), by [EFMachineClientStore](group-07-persistence-ef-core.md#efmachineclientstore) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/MachineClients/EFMachineClientStore.cs:32`), and by `ApplicationDbContext` and `DesignTimeDbContextHelper` to decide whether the table is in the model.

### ServiceAccount
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/ServiceAccount.cs:13` · Level 0 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: the facts a machine token is minted from, for one service account: user id (the token's `sub`), name, email and role (`ServiceAccount.cs:13-17`), the same standard claims a person's token carries.
- **Depends on**: the `UserIdentifierType` alias and [PiiAttribute](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#piiattribute) on `Name` and `Email` (`:15-16`).

### EmailConfirmationErrors
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.EmailConfirmation` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/EmailConfirmation/EmailConfirmationErrors.cs:9` · Level 2 · class

- **What it is**: the static `Error`-factory class for the email-confirmation flow: one factory for a sign-in refused because the address is unconfirmed, one for every failing token redemption.
- **Depends on**: `Error` (the Result-pattern error type taught in the primer).
- **Concept**: the same named-code-plus-factory-method convention used by every `*Errors` class in this codebase (see [AuthErrorCodes](#autherrorcodes) for the general shape); no new concept here.
- **Walkthrough**: `EmailNotConfirmedCode` (`EmailConfirmationErrors.cs:12`) and `InvalidTokenCode` (line 15) are the two error codes. `EmailNotConfirmed(source)` (lines 25-28) returns `Error.Unauthorized`, distinct from `Auth.InvalidCredentials` so a UI can offer to resend the link. `InvalidToken(source)` (lines 33-36) is the single rejection every failing redemption (unknown, expired, mismatched, or attempt-capped token) collapses to.
- **Why it's built this way**: the doc comment on `EmailNotConfirmed` (lines 474-478) explains it is reachable only after the password has already been proved, so the message can safely tell the account owner what is wrong rather than help an address sweeper enumerate valid accounts; `InvalidToken` collapsing every failure mode to one message denies an attacker any signal about which reason a redemption failed for.
- **Where it's used**: raised by `ConfirmEmailHandlerBase.cs` (2 sites) and `AuthenticationServiceBase.cs`, and by `EmailConfirmationTokenService.cs`; asserted against in `EmailConfirmationHandlerBaseTests.cs`, `EmailConfirmationTokenServiceTests.cs`, and ADC's `ConfirmEmailHandlerTests.cs`.

### LegalAcceptanceErrors
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Legal` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Legal/LegalAcceptanceErrors.cs:11` · Level 2 · class (static)

- **What it is**: the two validation errors of terms acceptance, as factory methods plus their code constants.
- **Depends on**: `Error` (the primer's Result/Error pattern), [AuthErrorCodes](#autherrorcodes) (`TermsNotAcceptedCode` aliases `AuthErrorCodes.TermsNotAccepted`, `LegalAcceptanceErrors.cs:14`) and [LegalAcceptanceErrorCodes](#legalacceptanceerrorcodes) (`VersionNotCurrentCode`, `:17`).
- **Concept**: error factories with stable codes, mirroring [EmailConfirmationErrors](#emailconfirmationerrors); no new concept.
- **Walkthrough**: `TermsNotAccepted(source)` (`:22`) is the registration refusal when a terms version is configured and the box was not ticked ("You must accept the Terms of Service to register."). `VersionNotCurrent(source)` (`:33`) refuses an acceptance of any version other than the configured one, including any acceptance while none is configured. Both build `Error.Validation` with the caller-supplied source.
- **Why it's built this way**: the shared code constants let a client switch on a stable string without referencing the Application layer.
- **Where it's used**: `TermsNotAccepted` is returned by `AuthenticationServiceBase.RegisterAsync` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:318`); `VersionNotCurrent` by [LegalAcceptancePolicy](#legalacceptancepolicy)`.EnsureAcceptsCurrentVersion` (`LegalAcceptancePolicy.cs:36`).

### MachineClientErrors
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientErrors.cs:6` · Level 2 · class (static)

- **What it is**: the error factories of the machine-client flow, plus the code constants the token endpoint switches on.
- **Depends on**: [Error](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error) (the primer's Result/Error pattern).
- **Concept**: error factories with stable codes, mirroring [EmailConfirmationErrors](#emailconfirmationerrors); no new concept. `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses whether failures leak information): one code covers every authentication failure.
- **Walkthrough**: four public codes: `InvalidClientCode` (`MachineClientErrors.cs:9`), `UnsupportedGrantTypeCode` (`:12`), `InvalidRequestCode` (`:15`), `RoleNotAllowedCode` (`:18`). `InvalidClient(source)` (`:27`) is `Error.Unauthorized` for an unknown id, wrong secret, revoked or expired client, missing or non-service account, or a forbidden role, all deliberately indistinguishable (doc comment `:20-24`). `UnsupportedGrantType` (`:33`) and `InvalidRequest` (`:39`) are `Error.Validation` for a grant type other than `client_credentials` and a missing one. `RoleNotAllowed` (`:49`) refuses a role granting `users:view-as`, `users:manage`, `roles:manage` or `clients:manage`. `RoleRequired` (`:55`) and `NotFound` (`:61`, `Error.NotFoundError`) use inline codes with no public constant.
- **Why it's built this way**: the constants let the API map a refusal onto the RFC 6749 body without string literals: `MachineTokenControllerBase.TokenError` answers 400 for the two grant-type codes and 401 `invalid_client` for everything else (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/MachineClients/MachineTokenControllerBase.cs:115-123`).
- **Where it's used**: raised by [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice) and read by [MachineTokenControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#machinetokencontrollerbase).

### IEmailConfirmationTokenService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.EmailConfirmation` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/EmailConfirmation/IEmailConfirmationTokenService.cs:15` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the token-lifecycle abstraction for email confirmation: issue a token for an address, validate and consume one presented back.
- **Depends on**: `UserIdentifierType` (the module's identifier-type alias), `Result<T>`.
- **Concept**: an issue/validate-and-consume token contract, mirroring the shape `IPasswordResetTokenService` uses elsewhere in this group; no new concept.
- **Walkthrough**: `IssueAsync(email, userId, cancellationToken)` (`IEmailConfirmationTokenService.cs:28`) replaces any token already outstanding for that address, so there is one active token per address, and fails only when the per-address request throttle ([EmailConfirmationSettings](#emailconfirmationsettings).`MaxRequestsPerEmail`/`RequestWindowMinutes`) has been exceeded. `ValidateAndConsumeAsync(email, token, cancellationToken)` (line 41) validates against the outstanding token and consumes it on success so it never redeems twice, collapsing unknown/expired/mismatched/attempt-capped failures to the single [EmailConfirmationErrors](#emailconfirmationerrors).`InvalidToken` error.
- **Why it's built this way**: consuming on success is what makes redemption single-use; collapsing every failure reason to one error, per its own doc comment (lines 603-606), denies an attacker signal about why a guess failed.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by `EmailConfirmationTokenService` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/EmailConfirmationTokenService.cs`), consumed by `SendEmailConfirmationHandlerBase.cs` and `ConfirmEmailHandlerBase.cs`, and by ADC's `SendEmailConfirmationHandler.cs`/`ConfirmEmailHandler.cs`; registered in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`.

### ILegalAcceptanceService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Legal` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Legal/ILegalAcceptanceService.cs:21` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the per-user storage contract behind terms acceptance: read the signed-in user's standing, and record that they accepted a version.
- **Depends on**: [LegalAcceptanceDTO](#legalacceptancedto), `Result<T>`, and the `UserIdentifierType` alias.
- **Concept**: a deliberately thin consumer boundary. The controller base validates the request first (`ILegalAcceptanceService.cs:14`, via [LegalAcceptancePolicy](#legalacceptancepolicy)`.EnsureAcceptsCurrentVersion`) and re-derives every answer afterwards (`:17`, via `Normalize`), so an implementation only has to load and save the accepted version and instant.
- **Walkthrough**: `GetForCurrentUserAsync(currentUserId, currentVersion, ct)` (`:26`) reads the caller's standing, or a failure such as NotFound. `AcceptForCurrentUserAsync(currentUserId, version, ct)` (`:39`) records the acceptance stamped with the implementation's own clock and returns the standing afterwards.
- **Why it's built this way**: Common ships no implementation and `AddLegalAcceptance` deliberately registers none (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:129`), because where the accepted version lives is the consumer's `User` aggregate (see `ILegalAcceptingUser` in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/ILegalAcceptingUser.cs`). Recorded in [ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html).
- **Where it's used**: consumed by [LegalAcceptanceControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#legalacceptancecontrollerbase) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Legal/LegalAcceptanceControllerBase.cs:46`); ADC implements it as `LegalAcceptanceService` (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/LegalAcceptanceService.cs`), registers it in that module's `DependencyInjection.cs`, and subclasses the controller base as `LegalAcceptanceController`.

### IMachineClientService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/IMachineClientService.cs:11` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the machine-client contract: the OAuth client credentials grant, and administration of the clients behind it.
- **Depends on**: `Result<T>`, the response and request records in `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.MachineClients` ([MachineTokenResponse](#machinetokenresponse), [MachineClientResponse](#machineclientresponse), [MachineClientSecretResponse](#machineclientsecretresponse), [CreateMachineClientRequest](#createmachineclientrequest)).
- **Concept**: a service a program (not a person) authenticates against with an id and a secret, receiving a short-lived bearer token and no refresh token or session. The feature switch lives on the interface itself, so a controller can resolve it per action and answer 404 while it is off.
- **Walkthrough**: `IsEnabled` (`IMachineClientService.cs:14`) mirrors `MachineClients:Enabled`. `IssueTokenAsync(grantType, clientId, clientSecret, ct)` (`:28`) runs the grant and fails with `MachineClients.InvalidClient`, `UnsupportedGrantType` or `InvalidRequest`. `ListAsync` (`:37`) lists every client, revoked ones included. `CreateAsync(request, ct)` (`:46`) provisions the service account, stores the client and returns the primary secret once. `RotateAsync` (`:52`) issues a secondary secret, returned once; both work until `PromoteAsync` (`:58`) makes it primary and the old one stops at once. `RevokeAsync` (`:67`) stops the secrets and writes the soft-deleted marker so tokens already held are rejected.
- **Why it's built this way**: two secrets with an explicit promote let a caller rotate without downtime. See [ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html).
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice), registered by `AddMachineClients` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.MachineClients.cs:49`), resolved per request by [MachineTokenControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#machinetokencontrollerbase) (`MachineTokenControllerBase.cs:57`) and [MachineClientsControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#machineclientscontrollerbase) (`MachineClientsControllerBase.cs:42-43`), and checked by [CloudAdapterTripwire](group-14-module-system-composition.md#cloudadaptertripwire).

### IServiceAccountProvisioner
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/IServiceAccountProvisioner.cs:15` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the consumer-implemented contract that creates and reads the service-account users behind machine clients.
- **Depends on**: [ServiceAccount](#serviceaccount), `Result<T>`, the `UserIdentifierType` alias.
- **Concept**: the consumer-supplied-store shape of ADR-116 (compare [ILegalAcceptanceService](#ilegalacceptanceservice)): Common has no user entity, so the app implements this over its own `User` aggregate. A service account is a user whose [IAuthUser](#iauthuser)`.IsServiceAccount` is true: no password, no external login, never a person; the framework refuses it on every interactive sign-in path and as a view-as target (remarks `IServiceAccountProvisioner.cs:10-14`).
- **Walkthrough**: `CreateAsync(name, role, ct)` (`:24`) creates a passwordless service-account user with the role and returns its id, or the app's own refusal (an unknown role, say). `FindAsync(userId, ct)` (`:33`) returns the account, or null when it does not exist, is deleted or locked, or is not a service account, so a token is never minted for a person.
- **Why it's built this way**: an enabled host without a registration fails at startup naming it (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientSettingsValidator.cs:37-40`). Related: [ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html), [ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html).
- **Where it's used**: called by [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice) at create and on every mint; ADC implements it as `ServiceAccountProvisioner` (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/Administration/ServiceAccountProvisioner.cs:25`), registered at `MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:57`.

### LegalAcceptancePolicy
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Legal` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Legal/LegalAcceptancePolicy.cs:10` · Level 3 · class (static)

- **What it is**: the pure rules of terms acceptance, kept out of the controller and the consumer's service so they cannot drift.
- **Depends on**: [LegalAcceptanceOptions](#legalacceptanceoptions), [LegalAcceptanceErrors](#legalacceptanceerrors), [LegalAcceptanceDTO](#legalacceptancedto), `Result`.
- **Concept**: server-authoritative version checking. `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether consent is recorded against what the user actually saw: the client says which version it showed, and the server refuses unless it equals the configured one.
- **Walkthrough**: `ResolveCurrentVersion(options)` (`LegalAcceptancePolicy.cs:18`) returns the trimmed configured version, or null for null options, null value or whitespace. `EnsureAcceptsCurrentVersion(currentVersion, suppliedVersion, source)` (`:36`) succeeds only when a version is configured and the trimmed supplied one matches it with an ordinal comparison; otherwise it fails with `LegalAcceptanceErrors.VersionNotCurrent`. `Normalize(currentVersion, standing)` (`:50`) re-derives the standing through `LegalAcceptanceDTO.Evaluate`, taking only the accepted version and instant from the consumer's answer, so the result never depends on a consumer filling `CurrentVersion` or `IsCurrent` correctly.
- **Why it's built this way**: the ordinal match means a client holding stale terms cannot record consent to the new ones, and the no-version-configured failure means there is nothing to accept when the feature is off.
- **Where it's used**: [LegalAcceptanceControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#legalacceptancecontrollerbase) (`LegalAcceptanceControllerBase.cs:54,83,110,125`), [AuthenticationValidators](#authenticationvalidators) (`AuthenticationValidators.cs:66`), and `LegalAcceptancePolicyTests.cs` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/Legal/`).

### IMachineClientStore
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/IMachineClientStore.cs:10` · Level 5 · interface

- **What it is**: persistence for [MachineClient](#machineclient) rows.
- **Depends on**: [MachineClient](#machineclient).
- **Concept**: a narrow store interface rather than the generic repository; no new concept. Every caller sits behind `MachineClients:Enabled`, so it never queries a table the model does not carry (doc comment `IMachineClientStore.cs:5-9`).
- **Walkthrough**: `ListAsync` (`:15`) returns every client, revoked ones included, oldest first. `FindAsync(clientId, ct)` (`:21`) returns a tracked instance, so `SaveAsync(client, ct)` (`:33`) persists changes made to it. `AddAsync` (`:27`) adds and saves a new client. `RecordUseAsync(client, usedOn, ct)` (`:44`) calls `MachineClient.RecordUse` and saves best effort: a concurrent issuance that saved first wins, because the last-used instant is informational and must never fail a token request.
- **Why it's built this way**: the best-effort `RecordUseAsync` keeps a concurrency conflict on a diagnostic column off the token path. See [ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html).
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [EFMachineClientStore](group-07-persistence-ef-core.md#efmachineclientstore) over the Identity database, registered with `TryAddScoped` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.MachineClients.cs:48`), and consumed by [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice).

### MachineClientService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:35` · Level 6 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the framework's [IMachineClientService](#imachineclientservice): it runs the client credentials grant and administers clients.
- **Depends on**: [IMachineClientStore](#imachineclientstore), [IServiceAccountProvisioner](#iserviceaccountprovisioner), [ITokenService](#itokenservice), [IPermissionRegistry](#ipermissionregistry), [ICacheService](group-09-caching.md#icacheservice), `IOptions<`[MachineClientSettings](#machineclientsettings)`>`, `TimeProvider` (primary constructor, `MachineClientService.cs:35-42`); plus [MachineClient](#machineclient), [MachineClientSecret](#machineclientsecret), [AdministrationPermissions](#administrationpermissions), [AuthClaimTypes](#authclaimtypes) and [SoftDeletedUserCache](#softdeletedusercache).
- **Concept introduced**: a machine token is minted by the raw `ITokenService`, not the session-stamping wrapper the sign-in workflow uses, so it carries no `sid`, `mfa` or `auth_time` and opens no refresh session; it carries the service account's standard claims and role permissions as a person's token does, plus `client_id` and `token_use=machine` (remarks `:16-21`). `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses least privilege and revocation): four permissions are refused on the backing role, checked at create and again at every mint, and revocation reuses the soft-deleted-user marker of [ADR-047](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/047-soft-deleted-user-session-revocation.html).
- **Walkthrough**: `ClientCredentialsGrantType` is `"client_credentials"` (`:45`). `ForbiddenPermissions` (`:52-58`) lists `ViewAsUsers`, `ManageUsers`, `ManageRoles` and `ManageClients`: role and client management are included because a client could otherwise grant its own role anything or mint further clients for itself (`:47-51`). `IssueTokenAsync` (`:66`) refuses a missing or foreign grant type, then collapses every other failure to one `InvalidClient` result: unparsable id or empty secret, unknown client or `Accepts` false (`:90`), and an account that is missing, mismatched or holds a forbidden role, re-read on every mint (`:97-98`). It then mints with `GenerateShortLivedAccessToken` at `AccessTokenMinutes` (`:103-115`), records the use (`:117`) and returns a `Bearer` response. `CreateAsync` (`:135`) requires a role, checks it against `ForbiddenPermissions` (`:146`) and validates the client row on a throwaway hash BEFORE provisioning the account (`:160`), so a refused create leaves no orphaned account. `RotateAsync` (`:173`) and `PromoteAsync` (`:193`) delegate to the entity and save. `RevokeAsync` (`:219`) saves the revoked row first (`:227-228`), then writes the marker for the service account with a duration from `SoftDeletedUserCache.MarkerDurationFor` over the longer of the machine and host access-token lifetimes (`:231-234`). `IsForbiddenRole` (`:250`) reads the role's permissions from the registry.
- **Why it's built this way**: saving before marking means no new token is minted once revocation starts, and the marker then makes every service's [SoftDeletedUserMiddleware](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#softdeletedusermiddleware) answer 401 to tokens the client already holds (remarks `:212-218`). The duration assumes the default bearer clock skew, since this layer cannot read the host's `JwtBearerOptions` (`:230`). See [ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html).
- **Where it's used**: registered by `AddMachineClients` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.MachineClients.cs:49`) and reached through the G12 controller bases; covered by `MachineClientServiceRevocationMarkerTests.cs` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/MachineClients/`) and ADC's `MachineClientControllersTests.cs`.

### IPermissionGrantCache
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Permissions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionGrantCache.cs:21` · Level 0 · interface

- **What it is**: the read side of the in-memory snapshot of stored (database-granted, as opposed to compiled-into-code) permissions, keyed by role.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party in its own signature; consumed alongside `IPermissionRegistry`.
- **Concept introduced**: the cache-in-front-of-a-store pattern used across this group for data that is read on every authorization check but changes rarely. `[Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]` (assesses whether hot paths avoid a database round trip): `GetPermissions` (`IPermissionGrantCache.cs:29`) is synchronous and reads the already-loaded snapshot, so it stays off the authorization hot path's I/O.
- **Walkthrough**: `GetPermissions(string role)` (line 99) returns the role's stored permissions, matched case-insensitively, empty when the role has none or the cache has not loaded yet. `RefreshAsync` (line 107) reloads the whole snapshot from the store; called at startup, on a configured interval, and explicitly by [IPermissionGrantCacheInvalidator](#ipermissiongrantcacheinvalidator) after a grant changes.
- **Why it's built this way**: separating the read interface from the invalidation interface ([IPermissionGrantCacheInvalidator](#ipermissiongrantcacheinvalidator)) lets [LayeredPermissionRegistry](#layeredpermissionregistry), which only needs to read, depend on a narrower contract than the administration path that needs to force a reload.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by `PermissionGrantCache` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/PermissionGrantCache.cs`), read by [LayeredPermissionRegistry](#layeredpermissionregistry) (`LayeredPermissionRegistry.cs`) and `StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService`, and registered in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`.

### IPermissionGrantCacheInvalidator
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Permissions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionGrantCache.cs:53` · Level 0 · interface

- **What it is**: the write-triggering half of the cache: forces a reload of one role's grants (or every role) after an administrative change.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party in its own signature.
- **Concept**: same cache-invalidation split introduced at [IPermissionGrantCache](#ipermissiongrantcache); no new concept here.
- **Walkthrough**: `InvalidateAsync(string? role = null, ...)` (`IPermissionGrantCache.cs:61`) invalidates the cached grants and reloads them; `null` means every role.
- **Why it's built this way**: kept on a separate, narrower interface from the read side so a caller that only grants or revokes (the administration surface) depends on exactly the capability it needs.
- **Where it's used**: implemented alongside `IPermissionGrantCache` by `PermissionGrantCache.cs`, called by `StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs` after a grant or revoke, and registered in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`.

### PasskeyAttestation
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyAttestation.cs:9` · Level 0 · record

- **What it is**: the verified result of a passkey registration: the credential id, the public key, the authenticator's starting signature counter and its transports.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; BCL `byte[]`, `IReadOnlyList<string>`.
- **Concept**: a library-neutral output record, so the WebAuthn library's own types never cross into the core layers (see [IPasskeyCeremony](#ipasskeyceremony)); no new concept.
- **Walkthrough**: a single positional record line (`PasskeyAttestation.cs:9`): `CredentialId`, `PublicKey`, `SignCount` (`uint`) and `Transports`.
- **Why it's built this way**: it carries exactly what [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice) needs to build a [PasskeyCredential](#passkeycredential) (`PasskeyService.cs:100-107`) and nothing of the verification library, which keeps `Fido2NetLib` confined to `MMCA.Common.Passkeys` ([ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html), decision 1).
- **Where it's used**: returned by [IPasskeyCeremony](#ipasskeyceremony)`.VerifyRegistrationAsync` and produced by [Fido2PasskeyCeremony](#fido2passkeyceremony) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/Fido2PasskeyCeremony.cs`).

### PasskeyChallenge
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyChallenge.cs:7` · Level 0 · record

- **What it is**: the server-side half of a passkey ceremony in flight: which ceremony it is, which account it was issued to (registration only), and the options JSON exactly as sent to the browser.
- **Depends on**: the `UserIdentifierType` alias (see [the primer](00-primer.md#4-c-build-and-code-style-conventions)).
- **Concept**: the stored challenge a completion must redeem; the single-use mechanics live in [PasskeyChallenges](#passkeychallenges).
- **Walkthrough**: the positional record `PasskeyChallenge(string Ceremony, UserIdentifierType? UserId, string OptionsJson)` (`PasskeyChallenge.cs:7`) plus two ceremony constants: `Register = "register"` (line 10) and `SignIn = "signin"` (line 13). `UserId` is `null` for a sign-in, because a discoverable sign-in names no account before the assertion.
- **Why it's built this way**: keeping the options verbatim lets the completion verify against what was actually issued, and recording the ceremony and account lets [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice) refuse a flow redeemed by the wrong ceremony or another account (`PasskeyService.cs:80-84`).
- **Where it's used**: built by [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice) (`PasskeyService.cs:66`, `:188`), serialized and redeemed by [PasskeyChallenges](#passkeychallenges).

### PasskeySettings
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeySettings.cs:19` · Level 0 · class

- **What it is**: the options class bound to the `Passkeys` section: the on/off switch, the WebAuthn relying party, the allowed browser origins, and the data source that owns the passkey table.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party.
- **Concept**: the same config-bound settings shape as [EmailConfirmationSettings](#emailconfirmationsettings); its validation is a separate validator, [PasskeySettingsValidator](#passkeysettingsvalidator), per the fail-fast configuration contract ([ADR-070](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.html)).
- **Walkthrough**: `SectionName` (`PasskeySettings.cs:22`) is `"Passkeys"`. `Enabled` (line 25) defaults to `false`. `RelyingPartyId` (line 31) is the registrable domain the passkeys belong to (`example.com` also covers `app.example.com`), required when enabled. `RelyingPartyName` (line 34) is the name the authenticator shows, required when enabled. `Origins` (line 40) lists the exact scheme, host and port the browser ceremonies may run on, at least one required when enabled. `DataSourceName` (line 46) defaults to `"Default"` and names the logical data source holding the `PasskeyCredentials` table (the Identity database).
- **Why it's built this way**: passkeys are an opt-in, so the default is off and a disabled host carries no relying-party configuration at all ([ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html), decision 2). `DataSourceName` follows the same gated-table shape as the permission grants ([PermissionGrantSettings](#permissiongrantsettings)): the table is mapped only on the named source.
- **Where it's used**: bound and validated by [PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions](#passkeysservicecollectionextensions) and [PasskeySettingsValidator](#passkeysettingsvalidator) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys`), read by [Fido2PasskeyCeremony](#fido2passkeyceremony), [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice) (`IsEnabled`), `EFPasskeyCredentialStore.cs`, `ApplicationDbContext.cs` and `DesignTimeDbContextHelper.cs` (under `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure`); pinned by `PasskeyModelGateTests.cs` and `AddPasskeysTests.cs`.

### PasskeyStepUp
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyStepUp.cs:17` · Level 0 · class

- **What it is**: the rule that decides whether a signed-in caller may register a passkey: their interactive sign-in must be at most ten minutes old.
- **Depends on**: BCL `ClaimsPrincipal`, `TimeSpan`, `DateTimeOffset`; the `FindAuthTime()` principal extension that reads the `auth_time` claim.
- **Concept introduced**: step-up by sign-in age. A sensitive action (planting a new sign-in method on the account) asks "how long ago did this person actually sign in", not "how fresh is this token". `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses how authentication and authorization resist account takeover): the check reads `auth_time`, which a refresh carries over unchanged, so a stolen refresh token can never keep itself fresh enough to register its own passkey.
- **Walkthrough**: `MaxSignInAge` (`PasskeyStepUp.cs:20`) is ten minutes. `IsSatisfiedBy(principal, now)` (lines 26-30) reads the sign-in instant with `principal.FindAuthTime()` (line 27); a principal with no `auth_time` never qualifies, and a sign-in stamped slightly in the future (clock skew between hosts, comment at line 29) counts as recent because only `now - signedInAt <= MaxSignInAge` is tested (line 30).
- **Why it's built this way**: per [ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html) decision 8, the alternatives ("a token under ten minutes old" or "a token carrying `mfa`") both ride every refresh, since a refresh resets `iat` and carries `mfa`; only `auth_time` measures the sign-in itself.
- **Where it's used**: checked by both registration actions of `PasskeysControllerBase.cs` and by `TwoFactorControllerBase.cs` (under `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers`); the refusal is [PasskeyErrors](#passkeyerrors)`.StepUpRequired`; pinned by `AuthTimeClaimTests.cs`.

### PasskeyStoredKey
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyStoredKey.cs:8` · Level 0 · record

- **What it is**: what an assertion is verified against: the stored public key, the last signature counter, and the owning account's WebAuthn user handle.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party.
- **Concept**: the input-side twin of [PasskeyAttestation](#passkeyattestation), keeping the ceremony contract free of the domain entity; no new concept.
- **Walkthrough**: one positional record line (`PasskeyStoredKey.cs:8`): `PublicKey`, `SignCount` (`uint`), `UserHandle`.
- **Why it's built this way**: [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice) builds it from a [PasskeyCredential](#passkeycredential) with the handle derived by `UserHandleFor` (`PasskeyService.cs:255`), so the verification library sees bytes, never the entity.
- **Where it's used**: passed to [IPasskeyCeremony](#ipasskeyceremony)`.VerifyAssertionAsync`, consumed by [Fido2PasskeyCeremony](#fido2passkeyceremony).

### PermissionGrantSettings
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Permissions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Permissions/PermissionGrantSettings.cs:9` · Level 0 · class

- **What it is**: the options class bound to `Authentication:PermissionGrants`, controlling how long a cached grant snapshot is served, which logical data source owns the grant table, and which role names the administration surface lists.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations` (`[Range]`, `[Required]`).
- **Concept**: the same config-bound settings shape as [EmailConfirmationSettings](#emailconfirmationsettings); no new concept.
- **Walkthrough**: `SectionName` (`PermissionGrantSettings.cs:12`) is `"Authentication:PermissionGrants"`. `CacheSeconds` (line 34) defaults to 30, is range-validated to 5-3600 (line 33), and its remarks (lines 17-32) spell out two things. First the trade-off (lines 18-26): this is the bound on how stale another replica may be after an edit, since invalidation is per process, and the stored grants are read by the token-minting Identity service, so any lag here is added on top of the access token's lifetime (15 minutes by default) before a revoke reaches every service. Second the failure behavior (lines 27-31): each cached entry lives three intervals, so the snapshot outlives the gap before the next reload and survives up to two failed reloads, after which it stops answering and stored grants fail closed. `DataSourceName` (line 42, `[Required]` at line 41) defaults to `"Default"`, naming the logical data source a modular host points at its Identity database. `KnownRoles` (line 54) defaults to an empty list, and its remarks (lines 48-53) explain why it must be configured: neither `IPermissionRegistry` (which answers questions about a role but does not list roles) nor the grant table (which only knows roles that already have a grant) can enumerate roles on its own; left empty, the surface still works but lists nothing until the first grant exists.
- **Why it's built this way**: the 30-second default keeps the revoke window close to the token lifetime itself, at the cost of one small query per Identity replica every 30 seconds and with no broker on the authorization path; raising it trades a longer revoke window for fewer database reads (`PermissionGrantSettings.cs:24-26`). The three-interval entry lifetime means a transient store outage costs nothing for two reload cycles, while a longer one degrades to denying stored grants (compiled permissions are unaffected, see [LayeredPermissionRegistry](#layeredpermissionregistry)) rather than serving an arbitrarily old snapshot.
- **Where it's used**: read by `PermissionGrantCache.cs`, `PermissionGrantRefreshService.cs`, `EFPermissionGrantStore.cs`, `StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs`, `ApplicationDbContext.cs`, and `DesignTimeDbContextHelper.cs` (all under `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure`); registered in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs`; pinned by `PermissionGrantModelGateTests.cs` and `PermissionGrantCacheTests.cs` in `MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests`.

### LayeredPermissionRegistry
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Permissions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Permissions/LayeredPermissionRegistry.cs:30` · Level 1 · class

- **What it is**: an `IPermissionRegistry` decorator that unions the compiled-into-code permission set with the stored (database-granted) set, so a role's effective permissions are "compiled OR granted", never a replacement of one by the other.
- **Depends on**: `IPermissionRegistry` (the inner, compiled registry), [IPermissionGrantCache](#ipermissiongrantcache) (the stored-grant cache).
- **Concept introduced**: the decorator pattern applied to a registry lookup. `[Rubric §2, Design Patterns]` (assesses whether a pattern is used idiomatically and solves a real problem): `LayeredPermissionRegistry` wraps `inner` without changing its contract, adding a second data source transparently to every caller of `IPermissionRegistry`.
- **Walkthrough**: the type is a primary-constructor class taking `inner` and `grants` (`LayeredPermissionRegistry.cs:30-32`). `GetPermissions(role)` (lines 35-52) reads both layers; when the stored set is empty it returns the compiled set as-is (no allocation), and only when both layers contribute does it materialize a `HashSet<string>` union, per the comment at lines 45-47: this call is a reporting path (administration surface, diagnostics), not the hot authorization path. `HasPermission(roles, permission)` (lines 55-66) is that hot path: it short-circuits on the compiled registry first (`inner.HasPermission`), and only falls through to a per-role stored-grant lookup (`grants.GetPermissions(role).Contains(permission)`) when the compiled check fails; the caller's `roles` sequence is materialized once (line 62) because both passes would otherwise enumerate it twice.
- **Why it's built this way**: separating the always-cheap compiled check from the stored-grant fallback keeps the common case (a permission granted in code) allocation-free and single-pass, per [ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html), which records the opt-in database-grant layer as additive on top of the existing compiled registry.
- **Where it's used**: registered as the `IPermissionRegistry` implementation in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs` (3 sites) when database grants are enabled; exercised directly in `MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/LayeredPermissionRegistryTests.cs`.

### PasskeyErrors
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyErrors.cs:10` · Level 2 · class

- **What it is**: the catalogue of passkey refusals, each a stable code constant plus a factory returning a typed [Error](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error).
- **Depends on**: [Error](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error).
- **Concept**: the same per-feature error catalogue as [TwoFactorErrors](#twofactorerrors) and [SignInLinkErrors](#signinlinkerrors); the error kind on each factory picks the HTTP status (see [the Result pattern in the primer](00-primer.md#2-architectural-styles-this-codebase-commits-to)).
- **Walkthrough**: seven code constants (`PasskeyErrors.cs:13-31`), all prefixed `Passkeys.`; `PasskeysNotSupportedCode` is named apart from the sign-in-link constant because the error-resource scan resolves codes by name (comment at line 12). The factories, each taking an optional `source`: `NotSupported` (line 36, `Error.Failure`), `ChallengeInvalid` (line 42, `Error.Validation`: unknown, expired, used, or the wrong ceremony or account), `RegistrationFailed` (line 48, `Error.Validation`), `AssertionFailed` (line 54, `Error.Unauthorized`), `StepUpRequired` (line 63, `Error.Forbidden`, pointing at [PasskeyStepUp](#passkeystepup)), `LastPasskey` (line 69, `Error.Conflict`) and `NotFound` (line 75, `Error.NotFoundError`).
- **Why it's built this way**: `AssertionFailed` is deliberately one vague message for every sign-in refusal (unknown credential, bad signature, counter); the specific reason goes only to a Warning log in [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice), so a caller cannot probe which credentials exist ([ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html), decision 7).
- **Where it's used**: [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice) (8 sites), [Fido2PasskeyCeremony](#fido2passkeyceremony), `PasskeysControllerBase.cs`, [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser) and [IAuthenticationService](#iauthenticationservice) (the not-supported default), and `PasskeysPanel.razor.cs` in `MMCA.Common.UI`.

### IPasskeyCeremony
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/IPasskeyCeremony.cs:19` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the core contract for the WebAuthn cryptography: build creation and request options, verify an attestation, read a credential id from an assertion, verify an assertion.
- **Depends on**: [PasskeyAttestation](#passkeyattestation), [PasskeyStoredKey](#passkeystoredkey), [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result); BCL `JsonElement`.
- **Concept introduced**: a library boundary held by a core interface. `[Rubric §32, Dependency & Supply-Chain]` (assesses how third-party code is contained and pinned): every member speaks JSON strings, `JsonElement` and byte arrays, so the `Fido2` package and its native dependencies live only in `MMCA.Common.Passkeys`, which a host opts into, and the core layers never load them.
- **Walkthrough**: `CreateRegistrationOptions(userHandle, userName, displayName, excludeCredentialIds)` (`IPasskeyCeremony.cs:27`) returns creation options as JSON, excluding the account's existing credentials so an authenticator is not enrolled twice. `VerifyRegistrationAsync(optionsJson, attestation, isCredentialIdUnique, ...)` (lines 35-39) verifies against the options as issued and calls back to ask whether the credential id is unused. `CreateSignInOptions()` (line 43) builds request options naming no credential (a discoverable sign-in). `ReadCredentialId(assertion)` (line 48) returns the id or `null` when malformed. `VerifyAssertionAsync(optionsJson, assertion, credential, ...)` (lines 60-64) checks the signature, user handle and counter, and returns the counter the authenticator reported.
- **Why it's built this way**: [ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html) decision 1 keeps the WebAuthn library in one package behind this contract, guarded at build time (`EnforcePasskeysBoundary`) and test time (`PasskeysIsolationTests.cs`). The uniqueness callback lets the store answer without the ceremony depending on persistence.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [Fido2PasskeyCeremony](#fido2passkeyceremony), registered by [PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions](#passkeysservicecollectionextensions), consumed by [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice); its absence while `Passkeys:Enabled` is true fails startup in `CloudAdapterTripwire.cs` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration`).

### IPasskeyService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/IPasskeyService.cs:12` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the application-facing passkey surface: begin and complete a registration, list, rename and delete an account's passkeys, and begin and complete a passkey sign-in.
- **Depends on**: [PasskeyOptionsResponse](#passkeyoptionsresponse), [PasskeyRegisterRequest](#passkeyregisterrequest), [PasskeyResponse](#passkeyresponse), [PasskeySignInRequest](#passkeysigninrequest), [AuthenticationResponse](#authenticationresponse), [IAuthenticationService](#iauthenticationservice), [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result).
- **Concept**: a two-step begin/complete ceremony, where begin stores a single-use challenge and complete must redeem it (see [PasskeyChallenges](#passkeychallenges)); no further new concept.
- **Walkthrough**: `IsEnabled` (`IPasskeyService.cs:15`) mirrors `Passkeys:Enabled`. `BeginRegistrationAsync(userId, userName, displayName, ...)` (lines 23-27) and `CompleteRegistrationAsync(userId, request, ...)` (lines 34-37) run registration for a signed-in account, which must be the one the flow was issued to. `ListAsync` (line 43) returns the passkeys oldest first; `RenameAsync` (lines 51-55) relabels one. `DeleteAsync` (line 65) removes one, the last only while the account still has a password or external login (remarks at lines 58-59, via [IAuthenticationService](#iauthenticationservice)`.HasSignInMethodBesidesPasskeysAsync`). `BeginSignInAsync` (line 70) starts an anonymous discoverable sign-in, and `CompleteSignInAsync(request, ipAddress, userAgent, ...)` (lines 81-85) verifies the assertion and mints the token pair through `IAuthenticationService.SignInWithPasskeyAsync`.
- **Why it's built this way**: the sign-in ends in the app's own authentication service, so a passkey sign-in produces the same token pair, refresh session and sign-in history as any other, stamped `mfa=passkey` ([ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html), decision 7).
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice), registered by [PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions](#passkeysservicecollectionextensions), called by `PasskeysControllerBase.cs` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Passkeys`); pinned by `AddPasskeysTests.cs` and `PasskeysIsolationTests.cs`.

### IPasskeyCredentialStore
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/IPasskeyCredentialStore.cs:10` · Level 4 · interface

- **What it is**: the persistence abstraction for stored passkeys: list an account's, find by row id or by WebAuthn credential id, add, update, remove.
- **Depends on**: [PasskeyCredential](#passkeycredential).
- **Concept**: the same narrow store-behind-an-interface shape as [IPermissionGrantStore](#ipermissiongrantstore); each write saves immediately rather than joining a unit of work.
- **Walkthrough**: `ListForUserAsync(userId, ...)` (`IPasskeyCredentialStore.cs:16`) returns oldest first. `FindAsync(userId, id, ...)` (line 23) scopes by account, so another account's row reads as missing. `FindByCredentialIdAsync(credentialId, ...)` (line 29) searches across all accounts, which is what sign-in and the registration uniqueness check need. `AddAsync` (line 35), `UpdateAsync` (line 41, for a rename or a recorded use) and `RemoveAsync` (line 47) each save.
- **Why it's built this way**: scoping `FindAsync` by account makes ownership a property of the query rather than a check every caller must remember. Removal is a hard delete: passkeys are flat bookkeeping with no soft-delete flag ([ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html), decision 4).
- **Where it's used**: implemented by `EFPasskeyCredentialStore` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFPasskeyCredentialStore.cs`), registered in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`, consumed by [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice); faked in `PasskeyTestHost.cs`.

### IPermissionGrantStore
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Permissions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionGrantStore.cs:16` · Level 4 · interface

- **What it is**: the persistence abstraction behind the stored-grant layer: read every grant, read one role's grants, grant a permission, revoke a permission.
- **Depends on**: `PermissionGrant` (the persisted grant row), `Result`.
- **Concept**: an idempotent grant/revoke pair, so a click repeated by an administration UI is not an error; no new concept beyond that idempotency guarantee.
- **Walkthrough**: `GetAllAsync(cancellationToken)` (`IPermissionGrantStore.cs:23`) reads every stored row, used to build the in-memory snapshot the authorization path reads. `GetPermissionsAsync(role, cancellationToken)` (line 31) reads one role's stored permissions for the administration surface. `GrantAsync(role, permission, grantedBy, cancellationToken)` (lines 42-46) grants a permission, succeeding and writing nothing when the role already has it stored (doc comment lines 33-36). `RevokeAsync(role, permission, cancellationToken)` (line 60) removes a stored grant, also idempotent; its remarks (lines 51-55) are explicit that this removes only the STORED grant, never a compiled-into-code one, which is exactly what keeps a data edit from disabling an endpoint the code guarantees.
- **Why it's built this way**: the "stored grant is additive, never subtractive over compiled permissions" rule enforced here is the same invariant [LayeredPermissionRegistry](#layeredpermissionregistry).`HasPermission` implements: the compiled check always wins first, and revoking a stored grant can never take away a compiled-in permission.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by `EFPermissionGrantStore` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFPermissionGrantStore.cs`), read by `PermissionGrantCache.cs` (2 sites) to build the [IPermissionGrantCache](#ipermissiongrantcache) snapshot, called by [IRoleAdministrationService](#iroleadministrationservice)'s implementation `StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs` (2 sites), and registered in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`.

### PasskeyChallenges
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyChallenges.cs:21` · Level 5 · class

- **What it is**: the single-use challenge store for passkey ceremonies, plus the per-account lock that serializes passkey deletions.
- **Depends on**: [ICacheService](group-09-caching.md#icacheservice), [IDistributedLock](group-05-cqrs-pipeline.md#idistributedlock), [PasskeyChallenge](#passkeychallenge); BCL `RandomNumberGenerator`, `JsonSerializer`.
- **Concept introduced**: read-and-burn under a distributed lock. A challenge must be redeemable exactly once across every replica, so redemption reads the shared store and removes the entry inside one lock, and a contended lock is itself treated as the replay. `[Rubric §11, Security]` (assesses replay and takeover resistance): a captured flow id cannot be redeemed twice, even by two requests racing on different replicas.
- **Walkthrough**: `Lifetime` (`PasskeyChallenges.cs:24`) is five minutes. Keys are `passkeys:challenge:` plus a flow id of `FlowIdLength` 32 (lines 26-27); the lock lease and wait are 10 and 5 seconds (lines 31-32), sized like the OAuth exchange-code lock. `IssueAsync` (lines 38-47) generates the flow id from 16 random bytes as lower-case hex (line 42) and stores the serialized challenge for `Lifetime` (lines 43-44). `RedeemAsync` (lines 56-83) rejects anything not exactly 32 lower-case hex characters (line 58), takes `lock:` plus the key (line 64) and returns `null` when contended (lines 65-69), reads with `GetFromSharedStoreAsync` rather than a local copy (line 74) so a flow burned on another replica misses, then removes the entry and deserializes it (lines 80-81). `LockAccountAsync(userId, ...)` (lines 92-94) takes `lock:passkeys:user:{userId}`, returning `null` past the wait.
- **Why it's built this way**: this is the OAuth exchange-code pattern applied to WebAuthn ([ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html) decision 5, building on [ADR-108](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/108-distributed-lock-primitive.html) for the lock and [ADR-077](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/077-hybridcache-substrate.html) for the cache). The account lock lives here because it uses the same lock primitive and timings.
- **Where it's used**: consumed by [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice) (3 sites), registered in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Caching.cs` and by [PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions](#passkeysservicecollectionextensions).

### PasskeyService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyService.cs:33` · Level 6 · class

- **What it is**: the implementation of [IPasskeyService](#ipasskeyservice): it orchestrates the challenge store, the WebAuthn ceremony, the credential store and the app's authentication service.
- **Depends on**: [PasskeySettings](#passkeysettings), [IPasskeyCeremony](#ipasskeyceremony), [IPasskeyCredentialStore](#ipasskeycredentialstore), [PasskeyChallenges](#passkeychallenges), [IAuthenticationService](#iauthenticationservice), [PasskeyCredential](#passkeycredential), [PasskeyErrors](#passkeyerrors); BCL `TimeProvider`, `ILogger<T>`.
- **Concept**: orchestration over the contracts introduced at [IPasskeyCeremony](#ipasskeyceremony) and [PasskeyChallenges](#passkeychallenges). `[Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]` (assesses whether failures are diagnosable): every refusal logs its specific reason at Warning through source-generated `LoggerMessage` methods (`PasskeyService.cs:277-281`) while the caller sees one generic error.
