- **Walkthrough**: a sealed partial primary-constructor class (`PasskeyService.cs:33-40`). `IsEnabled` (line 43) reads `Enabled`. `UserHandleFor(userId)` (lines 48-49) is the account id as UTF-8, opaque and free of personal data. `BeginRegistrationAsync` (lines 52-69) excludes the account's existing credential ids and issues a `Register` challenge. `CompleteRegistrationAsync` (lines 72-115) redeems the challenge and refuses it unless the ceremony is `Register` and the account matches (lines 80-84), verifies with a uniqueness callback over `FindByCredentialIdAsync` (lines 87-93), builds the entity with `PasskeyCredential.Create` (lines 100-107) and adds it (line 113). `ListAsync` (line 118) and `RenameAsync` (line 125) are thin. `DeleteAsync` (lines 153-179) takes the account lock (line 155), answering a `Passkeys.Busy` conflict when it cannot (line 158), and refuses `LastPasskey` when one passkey remains and the account has no other sign-in method (lines 170-173). `BeginSignInAsync` (line 182) issues a `SignIn` challenge with no account. `CompleteSignInAsync` (lines 194-218) redeems a `SignIn` challenge (line 203), verifies (line 209) and hands the user id to `SignInWithPasskeyAsync` (lines 215-216). The private `VerifyAssertionAsync` (line 236) reads the credential id (line 238), finds the credential across accounts (line 244), verifies against a [PasskeyStoredKey](#passkeystoredkey) (lines 251-257), then applies the counter rule itself with `credential.RecordUse` (line 266) before saving the use (line 273).
- **Why it's built this way**: the signature-counter check runs here as well as in the library so the cloned-key rule does not depend on the library's own check ([ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html), decision 6), and the count-then-delete inside the account lock stops two concurrent deletes of the last two passkeys from locking the user out (remarks at lines 148-152).
- **Where it's used**: registered as [IPasskeyService](#ipasskeyservice) by [PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions](#passkeysservicecollectionextensions); `UserHandleFor` is referenced from [IPasskeyCeremony](#ipasskeyceremony)'s documentation.

### ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SoftDeletedUsers` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUsers/ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:9` · Level 0 · interface

- **What it is**: the two-verb contract that writes and clears the soft-deleted user marker (ADR-047). Its summary (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUsers/ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:3-8`) records that the marker now means "deleted or locked": an account erasure and an administrator's lock both write it, for as long as an already-issued access token on this host can still be accepted, and an unlock clears it.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party beyond the `UserIdentifierType` alias; `Task` and `CancellationToken` from the BCL. The cache and the token settings the marker needs are deliberately absent from the contract.
- **Concept introduced: a narrow writer that hides how a revocation is stored and how long it lasts.** `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` assesses interface segregation and dependency inversion: whether a consumer depends only on what it uses. Writing the marker correctly needs two unrelated things (the shared cache it lives in, and the host's access-token lifetime that decides how long it must live), and the summary states the point of the abstraction directly: "neither workflow needs the cache nor the token settings itself" (`ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:6-7`). `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses session revocation: a JWT stays valid until its `exp`, so a deleted or locked account's already-issued tokens must be refused by something other than the token. The marker is that something, and the second verb matters as much as the first: without `ClearMarkerAsync`, a token issued after an unlock would be refused on every host until the marker expired (doc at `:19-22`).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `MarkDeletedAsync(userId, ct)` (`ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:17`): marks the user as deleted or locked, so requests bearing an already-issued token are rejected (`:11-13`).
  - `ClearMarkerAsync(userId, ct)` (`:26`): removes the user's marker from the shared store, so a token issued after an unlock is accepted at once on every host (`:19-22`).
- **Why it's built this way**: two workflows (account erasure and administrator lock/unlock) need the same marker with the same duration rule; putting the rule behind one writer keeps it in one place. The revocation model is recorded in [ADR-047](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/047-soft-deleted-user-session-revocation.html).
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [SoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter](#softdeletedusermarkerwriter) and registered as a scoped factory in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:52`. Injected into [UserAdministrationServiceBase<TUser, TUserDto>](#useradministrationservicebasetuser-tuserdto) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserAdministrationServiceBase.cs:56`, which writes the marker at `:264` and clears it at `:277`) and into [DeleteUserHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>](group-14-module-system-composition.md#deleteuserhandlerbasetuser-tcommand) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandlerBase.cs:98`, writing at `:214`). ADC passes it through its `UserAdministrationService` and `DeleteUserHandler` (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/`).

### IssuedSession
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:725` · Level 0 · record (private sealed, nested)

- **What it is**: the two-field result of opening or rotating a refresh session: the plaintext refresh token the client is handed, and the id of the session row it belongs to. It is a `private sealed record` nested inside [AuthSessionIssuer](#authsessionissuer) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:725`), not part of the framework's public surface.
- **Depends on**: nothing beyond the BCL (`string`, `Guid`). It is produced and consumed entirely inside its declaring class.
- **Concept introduced: the plaintext token exists in exactly one place, and it is a return value.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses how a bearer credential is stored. [RefreshSession](#refreshsession) rows keep only a digest (`RefreshSession.HashToken`, used at `AuthSessionIssuer.cs:200` and `:285` to *look up* by hash), so once a session is persisted the raw token cannot be recovered from the store at all. The type comment says exactly this (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:720-724`): the plaintext "exists nowhere else, since the store keeps only its hash". Modelling the hand-off as a small record rather than an out-parameter or a tuple is what keeps that fact readable: both methods that can produce a token return `Result<IssuedSession>`, so the compiler shows you the complete list of places raw token material is in flight. `[Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]` also applies: a positional record gives value equality and immutability for free, and `Guid SessionId` names what would otherwise be an anonymous second tuple element.
- **Walkthrough**: one positional declaration, `IssuedSession(string RefreshToken, Guid SessionId)` (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:725`). `RefreshToken` is what goes back to the caller in the [AuthenticationResponse](#authenticationresponse); `SessionId` is what the access token's `sid` claim carries, which is why the session must be opened before the token is minted (the comment at `AuthSessionIssuer.cs:97-98`).
- **Why it's built this way**: the pairing is load-bearing rather than incidental. A caller that received only the token could not stamp `sid`, and a caller that received only the id could not answer the client. Returning both together removes the ordering mistake where a token is minted for a session that does not exist yet.
- **Where it's used**: returned by `OpenSessionAsync` (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:469`, constructed at `:337`) and `RotateSessionAsync` (`:350`, constructed at `:390`); unwrapped by `IssueAsync` (`:84-85`) and by `RotateAsync` (`:120-121`), each of which passes `SessionId` to the caller's `mintAccessToken` callback and puts `RefreshToken` into the response.

### SignInLinkProfile
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SignInLinks` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:71` · Level 0 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: the name an invitation creates the account with when the invited address has no account yet (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:68-71`).
- **Depends on**: [PiiAttribute](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#piiattribute) on both members; otherwise only `string`.
- **Concept**: the personal-data marking is taught at [PiiAttribute](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#piiattribute). The one detail worth seeing here is the `[property: Pii]` target: on a positional record parameter an unqualified attribute lands on the constructor parameter, so the explicit `property:` target is what puts the marker on the generated `FirstName` and `LastName` properties that tooling actually reflects over.
- **Walkthrough**: one positional declaration, `SignInLinkProfile(string FirstName, string LastName)` (`ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:71`).
- **Where it's used**: passed as the optional `profile` argument of [ISignInLinkTokenService](#isigninlinktokenservice)`.IssueAsync` (`ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:38`, supplied only for an invitation, doc `:26-29`), stored with the token by [SignInLinkTokenService](#signinlinktokenservice), and handed back on redemption as [SignInLinkGrant](#signinlinkgrant)`.Profile`, which [RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>](group-14-module-system-composition.md#redeemsigninlinkhandlerbasetuser-tcommand) reads to provision the account.

### SignInLinkPurpose
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SignInLinks` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:59` · Level 0 · enum

- **What it is**: why a sign-in link was sent. Each purpose has its own lifetime and its own active token (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:58`).
- **Depends on**: nothing.
- **Concept**: keying a single-use token by address AND purpose. The interface remarks (`ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:12-17`) give the reason: one active token per address and purpose, so asking for a sign-in link does not silently invalidate an outstanding invitation for the same address.
- **Walkthrough**: `SignIn = 0` (`:62`), the account owner asked for a link from the sign-in page, short-lived; `Invite = 1` (`:65`), an organizer invited the address, long-lived, and may create the account. The explicit values pin the numbering.
- **Where it's used**: selects the lifetime in [SignInLinkSettings](#signinlinksettings)`.LifetimeFor` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkSettings.cs:58-59`), is the second key of every token in [SignInLinkTokenService](#signinlinktokenservice) (which enumerates both values at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkTokenService.cs:47`), and comes back on redemption in [SignInLinkGrant](#signinlinkgrant). `SendSignInLinkHandlerBase` issues `SignIn`; an invitation is issued as `Invite` through [ISignInLinkTokenService](#isigninlinktokenservice) directly (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/SendSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:32`).

### SessionStampingTokenService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:737` · Level 1 · class (private sealed, nested)

- **What it is**: a pass-through [ITokenService](#itokenservice) that appends up to three claims to every access token minted while it is armed (the current refresh session's `sid`, an `mfa` claim when a second factor verified this request, and an `auth_time` claim carrying the sign-in instant) and behaves as the plain inner service the rest of the time. It is a `private sealed class` nested inside [AuthSessionIssuer](#authsessionissuer) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:737`).
- **Depends on**: [ITokenService](#itokenservice) (the contract it implements and the inner instance it wraps, `AuthSessionIssuer.cs:737`), [AuthClaimTypes](#authclaimtypes) for the `sid`, `mfa` and `auth_time` claim names (`:776`, `:781`, `:787`), and the BCL (`System.Security.Claims`, `System.Globalization.CultureInfo`).
- **Concept introduced: a decorator used to make a new claim additive.** `[Rubric §2, Design Patterns]` assesses idiomatic pattern use, and this is the Decorator pattern applied to a very specific compatibility problem. Access tokens need to name the session they belong to (and, when relevant, the second factor that satisfied a step-up and the instant the user actually signed in), but the claim set is produced by the app's own `CreateAccessToken` hook. The obvious fix, adding parameters to that hook, is a compile break in every consumer for claims the app has no decision to make about; the type's own remarks say exactly this (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:732-736`). Wrapping the token service instead means the issuer arms the wrapper around the hook call and the claims appear in tokens minted by subclasses that were never edited. `[Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]` is the payoff: an additive protocol change with a zero-line consumer diff, three times over.
- **Walkthrough**: a primary constructor takes the `inner` service (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:737`).
  - `Guid? CurrentSessionId { get; set; }` (`:740`) is the session arming switch: a session id stamps, `null` mints unchanged.
  - `string? CurrentMultiFactorMethod { get; set; }` (`:746`) is the second-factor arming switch, set only when a second factor really verified for this request (doc `:742-745`).
  - `DateTimeOffset? CurrentAuthTime { get; set; }` (`:749`) is the sign-in-instant switch. The remarks on the issuer's arming method explain why plain mutable properties are safe for all three (`:161-162`): the issuer is resolved per request (scoped, like the store it saves through) and one request mints one token at a time.
  - `AccessTokenLifetime` (`:752`) and `RefreshTokenLifetime` (`:755`) forward straight to `inner`, so the lifetime callers read is still the JWT settings' value.
  - `GenerateAccessToken(...)` (`:758-793`) is the only member with behavior. When no switch is armed it delegates verbatim (`:765-768`). Otherwise it copies the app's `additionalClaims` into a new `List<Claim>` (`:770`, so the caller's sequence is never mutated), then independently appends `AuthClaimTypes.SessionId` formatted as `sessionId.ToString("D", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)` when `CurrentSessionId` is set (`:772-777`, the `"D"` format being the canonical hyphenated Guid form `ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.FindSessionId` parses back, see [ClaimsPrincipalExtensions](#claimsprincipalextensions)), `AuthClaimTypes.MultiFactor` set to the raw method string when `CurrentMultiFactorMethod` is set (`:779-782`), and `AuthClaimTypes.AuthTime` as Unix seconds typed `ClaimValueTypes.Integer64` when `CurrentAuthTime` is set (`:784-790`), before delegating with the extended list (`:792`). The three claims are independent: a token can carry any combination of them.
  - `GenerateRefreshToken()` (`:796`) and `GetPrincipalFromExpiredToken(string token)` (`:799-800`) are plain forwards.
- **Why it's built this way**: putting the stamping behind an `ITokenService` rather than inside the caller's own method keeps the app hook's signature and semantics untouched while still guaranteeing the claims on the tokens the framework's own flows mint. The escape hatch still applies: an app that mints from its own injected `ITokenService` reference produces a valid token with none of the three claims, and can restore them by overriding `CreateAccessTokenForSession` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:821-822`).
- **Where it's used**: constructed once per issuer instance (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:67`) and exposed as [IAuthSessionIssuer](#iauthsessionissuer)`.TokenService` (`:77`), which [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser) surfaces to subclasses as its protected `TokenService` property (`AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:120`). All three switches are armed and disarmed by the four-argument `AuthSessionIssuer.MintForSession` (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:173-190`, with the `finally` at `:184-189` guaranteeing all three disarm even when the hook throws), which the base calls from `CreateAccessTokenForSession` with its `_multiFactorMethod` and `_authenticatedAt` fields (`AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:822`; `_authenticatedAt` is read from the presented token's `auth_time` on a refresh, `:455`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: the type's own summary (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:727-731`) still describes only the `sid` claim; the `mfa` and `auth_time` behavior is documented on the properties and visible in `GenerateAccessToken`.

### SignInLinkGrant
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SignInLinks` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:76` · Level 1 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: what a redeemed sign-in token grants: the [SignInLinkPurpose](#signinlinkpurpose) it was issued for and, for an invitation that carried one, the [SignInLinkProfile](#signinlinkprofile) to provision the account with (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:73-76`).
- **Depends on**: [SignInLinkPurpose](#signinlinkpurpose), [SignInLinkProfile](#signinlinkprofile).
- **Concept**: the redemption result carries the token's purpose rather than a bare success, so the caller decides what the link may do (sign in an existing account, or also create one) from what was actually issued, never from what the redeeming client claims.
- **Walkthrough**: one positional declaration, `SignInLinkGrant(SignInLinkPurpose Purpose, SignInLinkProfile? Profile)` (`ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:76`).
- **Where it's used**: the success value of [ISignInLinkTokenService](#isigninlinktokenservice)`.ValidateAndConsumeAsync` (`ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:52`), produced by [SignInLinkTokenService](#signinlinktokenservice) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkTokenService.cs:90`) and read by [RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>](group-14-module-system-composition.md#redeemsigninlinkhandlerbasetuser-tcommand) after the consume at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:97`.

### SignInLinkSettings
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SignInLinks` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkSettings.cs:10` · Level 1 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the options class for sign-in links (ADR-116), bound from the `Authentication:SignInLinks` configuration section (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkSettings.cs:6-13`). It carries the master switch, the page the link opens, the two lifetimes, the throttles, and the two small pieces of behavior that depend on them.
- **Depends on**: [SignInLinkPurpose](#signinlinkpurpose); `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations` (`[Range]`) and `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis` (`[SuppressMessage]`).
- **Concept introduced: a capability that is registered but off.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether a security-sensitive feature fails closed. `Enabled` defaults to `false` (`SignInLinkSettings.cs:20`), so registering the capability changes nothing until a host turns it on, and turning it off again makes every outstanding link inert without waiting for it to expire (doc `:15-19`). The second security decision lives in `ComposeLink`: the address and the token ride in the URL fragment, which is never sent to a server, so the live token stays out of access logs, request telemetry and `Referer` headers, and a mail scanner that prefetches the link with a GET never sees, and so never spends, the token (remarks `:68-73`). The shape follows the same fail-fast stance: every numeric knob is range-validated, and the registration validates on start (see Where it's used), matching the fail-fast contract of [ADR-070](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.html).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `SectionName = "Authentication:SignInLinks"` (`:13`).
  - `Enabled` (`:20`), default `false`.
  - `SignInUrl` (`:31`), default empty, deliberately not required (matching `EmailConfirmationSettings.ConfirmationUrl`, see [EmailConfirmationSettings](#emailconfirmationsettings)) so an unconfigured host still boots; with it empty no link can be composed and nothing is sent (doc `:22-26`). The `CA1056` suppression (`:27-30`) explains why it is a `string`: the empty default is not a valid `System.Uri`.
  - `SignInLifetimeMinutes` (`:35`), `[Range(1, 1440)]`, default 15; `InviteLifetimeMinutes` (`:39`), `[Range(1, 43200)]`, default 20160 (14 days).
  - `MaxValidationAttempts` (`:45`), `[Range(1, 100)]`, default 5: wrong tokens tolerated for one address before its outstanding tokens are discarded.
  - `MaxRequestsPerEmail` (`:49`), `[Range(1, 100)]`, default 3, within `RequestWindowMinutes` (`:53`), `[Range(1, 1440)]`, default 60.
  - `LifetimeFor(purpose)` (`:58-59`): the invite lifetime for `Invite`, the sign-in lifetime otherwise.
  - `ComposeLink(email, token)` (`:74-77`): `null` when `SignInUrl` is blank, otherwise `{SignInUrl}#email=...&token=...` with both values passed through `Uri.EscapeDataString`.
- **Why it's built this way**: the defaults make the cheap mistake safe (an unconfigured host boots and sends nothing; an unlisted host never issues links), and the fragment rule is the same one the password-reset link uses (`ForgotPasswordHandlerBase.ComposeResetLink`, cited in the remarks at `:69-70`), so both emailed-token flows keep the token off the wire. Recorded in [ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html).
- **Where it's used**: bound by `AddSignInLinks` with `.Bind(...)`, `.ValidateDataAnnotations()` and `.ValidateOnStart()` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:109-112`); injected as `IOptions<SignInLinkSettings>` into [SignInLinkTokenService](#signinlinktokenservice) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkTokenService.cs:42`), [SendSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>](group-14-module-system-composition.md#sendsigninlinkhandlerbasetuser-tcommand) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/SendSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:48`) and [RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>](group-14-module-system-composition.md#redeemsigninlinkhandlerbasetuser-tcommand) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:62`). ADC's architecture tests pin the invitation lifetime (`MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Privacy/InvitationLifetimeTests.cs`).

### SignInLinkErrors
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SignInLinks` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkErrors.cs:9` · Level 2 · class (static)

- **What it is**: the failures the sign-in-link workflow returns, declared once so the redeem handler, the authentication service and a client all match on the same literals (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkErrors.cs:5-8`).
- **Depends on**: [Error](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error).
- **Concept**: an error catalog (a static class of codes plus factory methods) is the same shape as [EmailConfirmationErrors](#emailconfirmationerrors). What is specific here is the deliberate collapse: `InvalidLink` is "the single rejection every failing redemption collapses to" (`:20`), so a caller probing addresses or tokens cannot tell unknown from expired from mismatched from spent from disabled. `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses that non-disclosure; the one distinct refusal, `SecondFactorRequired`, is reachable only after a valid token was spent, so it tells the mailbox owner, not a sweeper (remarks `:34`).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `InvalidLinkCode = "Authentication.InvalidSignInLink"` (`:12`) and `InvalidLink(source)` (`:23-26`): `Error.Unauthorized`, "The sign-in link is invalid or has expired. Please request a new one."
  - `SecondFactorRequiredCode = "Authentication.SignInLinkSecondFactorRequired"` (`:15`) and `SecondFactorRequired(source)` (`:35-38`): `Error.Unauthorized`. A link proves only that the caller reads the mailbox, so honoring it for an account with a second factor would let the mailbox alone bypass that factor (doc `:28-31`).
  - `NotSupportedCode = "Authentication.SignInLinkNotSupported"` (`:18`) and `NotSupported(source)` (`:43-46`): `Error.Failure`, returned by an authentication service that has not adopted sign-in links.
- **Where it's used**: `NotSupported` is the default body of the sign-in-link member on [IAuthenticationService](#iauthenticationservice) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IAuthenticationService.cs:180`); [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser) returns `InvalidLink` and `SecondFactorRequired` from `SignInVerifiedEmailOwnerAsync` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:569`, `:582`); [RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>](group-14-module-system-composition.md#redeemsigninlinkhandlerbasetuser-tcommand) returns `InvalidLink` from each failing branch (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:148`, `:186`, `:213`, `:249`, `:299`); and [SignInLinkTokenService](#signinlinktokenservice) returns it from `ValidateAndConsumeAsync` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkTokenService.cs:135`).

### IAuthSessionIssuer
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/IAuthSessionIssuer.cs:27` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the contract that issues, rotates and revokes the access/refresh token pair behind a signed-in device. Its summary (`IAuthSessionIssuer.cs:8-13`) lists what it owns: the multi-device [RefreshSession](#refreshsession) rows (hashed at rest), BR-205 rotation with BR-206 reuse detection, the per-user live-session cap, and the `sid`/`mfa` claims stamped on the access token minted for a session. It also lists the user's sign-in history and records a native client's device metadata on a live session.
- **Depends on**: [ITokenService](#itokenservice), [AuthenticationResponse](#authenticationresponse), [RefreshSessionSummaryResponse](#refreshsessionsummaryresponse), [SignInSummaryResponse](#signinsummaryresponse), [DeviceMetadata](#devicemetadata), [RefreshSessionSettings](#refreshsessionsettings) (referenced from the docs), `Result`/`Result<T>` (the Result pattern taught in the primer), and the `UserIdentifierType` alias.
- **Concept introduced: splitting "who is signed in" from "what they are handed".** `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` assesses whether each type has one reason to change. The remarks (`IAuthSessionIssuer.cs:16-20`) draw the line explicitly: credentials, lockout, the second factor and the app's own gates stay with [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser), which calls the issuer only once a caller has been proved, and the base's own summary states the same split from the other side (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:50`: "This class decides who is signed in; IAuthSessionIssuer decides what they are handed"). The access token's claim set still belongs to the app, so the issuer takes it as a `Func<Guid, string> mintAccessToken` callback: the session id the token must carry exists only once the session has been opened or rotated. `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses credential lifecycle handling; the rotation and reuse rules are stated on the contract itself, not left to an implementation. `[Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]` shows in how the contract grew: the `auth_time` overload of `MintForSession` is a default interface member, so an implementation written before it keeps compiling.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `TokenService` (`IAuthSessionIssuer.cs:35`): the [ITokenService](#itokenservice) an app mints through. While the issuer is minting for a session it appends `sid` (and `mfa` when a second factor verified); at any other time it is the plain registered service (doc at `:29-34`).
  - `IssueAsync(userId, mintAccessToken, ipAddress, userAgent, ct)` (`:47`): opens a new session, evicting the oldest live one when the per-user cap is full, persists it and returns the pair; the user's other sessions are untouched (`:37-40`).
  - `RotateAsync(userId, refreshToken, mintAccessToken, ipAddress, userAgent, ct)` (`:71`): BR-205 rotation. An unknown or expired token fails alone, and so does a token whose session was revoked by a sign-out or evicted by the session cap (that device simply lost its session). A token already rotated, already flagged as reuse, or rotated first by a concurrent request is the BR-206 reuse signal and revokes every live session the user holds; a revoked row with any other or no recorded reason is treated as reuse too. Every rejection carries the same `Auth.InvalidRefreshToken` error (`:54-62`).
  - `MintForSession(sessionId, multiFactorMethod, mintAccessToken)` (`:87`): runs the callback with `TokenService` armed to stamp `sid` and, when not null, `mfa` (`:79-82`).
  - `MintForSession(sessionId, multiFactorMethod, authenticatedAt, mintAccessToken)` (`:105-106`): the same, also stamping `auth_time`: `authenticatedAt` when given (a refresh carrying the presented token's sign-in instant over unchanged), otherwise the instant of the sign-in `IssueAsync` is opening, and none outside it (`:89-93`). Its default body ignores `authenticatedAt` and delegates to the three-argument member, so an older implementation mints no `auth_time`, and passkey registration (which requires one) stays refused on that host (remarks `:100-104`).
  - `SignOutAsync(userId, refreshToken, ct)` (`:117`): revokes the one live session behind the presented token when it belongs to the user; when the token is absent or identifies no live session of this user, every live session is revoked instead (`:108-111`).
  - `SignOutEverywhereAsync(userId, ct)` (`:123`): revokes every live session and saves.
  - `ListActiveAsync(userId, currentSessionId, ct)` (`:133`): live sessions newest first, with expired-but-unrevoked rows left out because a device list must not offer a device that can no longer authenticate (`:125-127`).
  - `ListSignInsAsync(userId, currentSessionId, ct)` (`:147`): the sign-in history, one row per sign-in (a rotation chain, however many times it rotated), live and ended alike, newest first, capped at the newest 50, each with how it ended, covering what the store retains (`RefreshSessionSettings.RetentionDays`) (`:138-141`).
  - `RevokeSessionAsync(userId, sessionId, ct)` (`:162`): another account's session id and a never-existing id both answer `Auth.SessionNotFound`; an already-revoked session writes nothing and answers the not-found failure `Auth.SessionAlreadyRevoked`, so the client can say the device was already signed out (`:152-157`).
  - `RecordDeviceAsync(userId, sessionId, device, ct)` (`:176`): records the [DeviceMetadata](#devicemetadata) a native client reported on its own session (named by the access token's `sid`), replacing what was there, and saves; rotation carries it to every successor. Another account's id, a missing id, and a revoked or expired session all answer `Auth.SessionNotFound` and write nothing (`:164-170`).
- **Why it's built this way**: the remarks (`IAuthSessionIssuer.cs:23-24`) give the lifetime rule: scoped, like the session store it writes through, so a sign-in and its session insert share the request's unit of work. Keeping the session rules behind one interface means the authentication workflow never touches a session row. The multi-device session model is recorded in [ADR-097](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.html) and the rotation scheme in [ADR-050](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/050-jwt-refresh-token-rotation.html).
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [AuthSessionIssuer](#authsessionissuer); registered `TryAddScoped` in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:182`; injected into [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser) (`AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:79`), which delegates to it from `TokenService` (`:120`), refresh (`RotateAsync`, `:460`), sign-out (`:487`, `:503`), session listing (`:515`), sign-in history (`:527`), revocation (`:542`), issuance (`IssueAsync`, `:740`) and `CreateAccessTokenForSession` (the four-argument `MintForSession`, `:822`). `AuthControllerBase` takes it as a `[FromServices]` parameter and calls `RecordDeviceAsync` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/AuthControllerBase.cs:293`, `:313`). ADC's `AuthenticationService` takes it as a constructor argument and passes it to the base (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/AuthenticationService.cs:58,67`).

### ISignInLinkTokenService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SignInLinks` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:18` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the contract that issues and redeems the single-use tokens behind sign-in links (ADR-116), on the design [IEmailConfirmationTokenService](#iemailconfirmationtokenservice) uses: the token material lives outside the database, hashed at rest, with a per-address request throttle and a per-token validation-attempt cap (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:6-11`).
- **Depends on**: [SignInLinkPurpose](#signinlinkpurpose), [SignInLinkProfile](#signinlinkprofile), [SignInLinkGrant](#signinlinkgrant), `Result<T>` from the primer.
- **Concept introduced: a token keyed by address, not by account.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses how emailed bearer tokens are issued and spent. The remarks (`ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:12-17`) explain the key choice: an invitation is issued to an address that may have no account yet, and redeeming it is what creates one, so the token cannot be keyed by a user id. One active token per address and purpose means a new link of one purpose replaces only the outstanding link of that purpose. Redemption is validate-and-consume in one call, so a token never redeems twice, and every failure collapses to one generic error (`:48-50`).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `IssueAsync(email, purpose, profile = null, ct)` (`:35`): issues a token for the normalized address, replacing any token of the same purpose already outstanding (`:20-23`). `profile` is supplied only for an invitation; a plain sign-in link never creates an account (`:26-29`). Returns the raw token to email, or a failure when the per-address request throttle is exceeded (`:31-34`).
  - `ValidateAndConsumeAsync(email, token, ct)` (`:52`): validates the token against the address's outstanding tokens and consumes the one it matches, returning the [SignInLinkGrant](#signinlinkgrant); unknown, expired, mismatched and attempt-capped all collapse to the same error (`:41-51`).
- **Why it's built this way**: reusing the email-confirmation token design keeps one reviewed shape for every emailed single-use token in the framework. Recorded in [ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html).
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [SignInLinkTokenService](#signinlinktokenservice) and registered `TryAddScoped` by `AddSignInLinks` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:115`; the remarks at `:104-105` note that registering it issues nothing until the app wires the handlers and a controller and sets `Authentication:SignInLinks:Enabled`). Injected into [SendSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>](group-14-module-system-composition.md#sendsigninlinkhandlerbasetuser-tcommand) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/SendSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:46`) and [RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>](group-14-module-system-composition.md#redeemsigninlinkhandlerbasetuser-tcommand) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:60`, consumed at `:97`). ADC issues invitations through it directly in `SendSignInLinkInternalCommandHandler` (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/SendSignInLink/`).

### RefreshSessionDevice
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/RefreshSessionDevice.cs:11` · Level 5 · class (internal static)

- **What it is**: one extension method that shapes the device columns of a [RefreshSession](#refreshsession) into the [DeviceMetadata](#devicemetadata) the session responses carry, shared by the device list, the sign-in history and the administrator's view so the three cannot drift (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/RefreshSessionDevice.cs:6-10`).
- **Depends on**: [RefreshSession](#refreshsession), [DeviceMetadata](#devicemetadata).
- **Concept**: a single mapping owned in one place, the same reason the primer gives for shared helpers. The detail worth noticing is how "nothing recorded" is detected: a private static `Empty` instance of seven nulls (`:13`) is compared with `==` (`:33`), which works because `DeviceMetadata` is a `sealed record` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/DeviceMetadata.cs:24`) and so compares by value.
- **Walkthrough**: `ToDeviceMetadata(this RefreshSession session)` (`RefreshSessionDevice.cs:22`) builds a `DeviceMetadata` from `DeviceId`, `DeviceName`, `DeviceModel`, `DeviceManufacturer`, `DevicePlatform`, `DeviceFormFactor` and `DeviceType` (`:24-31`), and returns `null` when it equals `Empty` (`:33`), so a response says "no device" for every browser session and every row anonymized for an erasure rather than carrying an object of seven nulls (doc `:15-19`).
- **Where it's used**: [AuthSessionIssuer](#authsessionissuer)`.ListActiveAsync` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:257`), [SignInHistory](#signinhistory) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/SignInHistory.cs:163`) and [UserSessionsAdministrationService](#usersessionsadministrationservice) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserSessionsAdministrationService.cs:49`).

### SoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SoftDeletedUsers` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUsers/SoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:13` · Level 6 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the framework's [ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter](#isoftdeletedusermarkerwriter): writes the deleted-or-locked marker for `SoftDeletedUserCache.MarkerDurationFor` of the host's access-token lifetime, and removes it on an unlock (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUsers/SoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:6-10`).
- **Depends on**: [ICacheService](group-09-caching.md#icacheservice) (the shared store the marker lives in) and [ITokenService](#itokenservice) (for `AccessTokenLifetime`), both primary-constructor parameters (`:13`); [SoftDeletedUserCache](#softdeletedusercache) for the key, the duration rule and the write and remove operations.
- **Concept**: the abstraction is taught at [ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter](#isoftdeletedusermarkerwriter). This class shows how thin the implementation can be once the duration rule and the cache key live in [SoftDeletedUserCache](#softdeletedusercache): two one-line delegations.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `MarkDeletedAsync` (`:16-21`): `SoftDeletedUserCache.MarkDeletedForAsync(cache, userId, SoftDeletedUserCache.MarkerDurationFor(tokenService.AccessTokenLifetime), ct)`, so the marker outlives any access token this host could still accept.
  - `ClearMarkerAsync` (`:24-25`): `SoftDeletedUserCache.ClearMarkerAsync(cache, userId, ct)`.
- **Why it's built this way**: the summary records the one assumption: the default bearer clock skew, because this layer cannot read the host's (`:8-9`). It is registered through a factory rather than a type registration (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:49-54`); the comment there explains that a Development host validates every registration at build, and only a factory defers the writer's dependencies to the moment it is resolved, so a host that issues no tokens (and never resolves this) still starts. See [ADR-047](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/047-soft-deleted-user-session-revocation.html).
- **Where it's used**: resolved wherever [ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter](#isoftdeletedusermarkerwriter) is injected (see that section). Covered by `SoftDeletedUserMarkerWriterTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/SoftDeletedUsers/`).

### SignInHistory
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/SignInHistory.cs:20` · Level 7 · class (internal static)

- **What it is**: the reader that turns a user's refresh-session rows into a sign-in history: the store aggregates the rotation chains and this shapes each one into a [SignInSummaryResponse](#signinsummaryresponse). Shared by the self-service list and the administrator's, so both read a history the same way (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/SignInHistory.cs:7-13`).
- **Depends on**: [IRefreshSessionStore](#irefreshsessionstore) (`GetRecentSignInsAsync`, `FindByIdAsync`), [RefreshSessionSignIn](#refreshsessionsignin), [RefreshSession](#refreshsession), [SignInSummaryResponse](#signinsummaryresponse), [SignInEndReasons](#signinendreasons), [SignInHistoryEntryKind](#signinhistoryentrykind), optionally [IViewAsGrantStore](#iviewasgrantstore) and [ViewAsGrant](#viewasgrant); [RefreshSessionDevice](#refreshsessiondevice) for the device column.
- **Concept introduced: a history row is a rotation chain, not a row.** `[Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]` assesses whether a read is bounded. Every refresh rotates the session into a new row, so a naive history would list one entry per refresh and grow with activity. Here a sign-in is the chain: it starts at its earliest retained row and was last active at its newest row's issue instant, and the newest row (the head) decides how it ended (remarks `:14-19`). The store does the aggregation and caps it at `MaxEntries` (`:23`, 50), so the read is bounded by sign-ins, never by how many times each rotated. `[Rubric §11, Security]` applies to the view-as rows: each support view of the account appears in the holder's own history, without the staff user's device or address (`:59-62`).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `MaxEntries = 50` (`:23`).
  - `ReadAsync(store, userId, now, currentSessionId, ct, viewAsGrants = null)` (`:37`): reads the capped aggregate (`:45`), resolves which sign-in the caller is in (`:46`), shapes it (`:49`), and when a view-as grant store is present reads the account's recent grants with the same cap (`:55`) and merges them (`:56`).
  - `Merge(history, grants, now)` (`:68`): pure; concatenates the shaped grants, orders by `StartedAt` then `SignInId` descending, and takes `MaxEntries` (`:72-78`).
  - `SummarizeViewAs` (`:80`): a grant row spans the grant; ended grants report `SignInEndReasons.ViewAsEnded` (`:84-87`), past-expiry ones `SignInEndReasons.Expired` (`:88-91`); IP and user agent are null, `IsCurrent` is false, and the kind is `SignInHistoryEntryKind.ViewAs` (`:93-102`).
  - `Summarize(signIns, now, currentSignInId)` (`:110`): pure; shapes each chain and applies the same ordering and cap (`:114-120`).
  - `ResolveCurrentSignInAsync` (`:127`): the caller's `sid` is normally its chain's head, since each rotation mints the token for the successor, so it is matched against the heads with no read (`:139-143`); otherwise (an access token minted before a sibling rotated) one user-scoped primary-key lookup finds it and returns its `SignInId`, or its own `Id` for a chain's first row (`:145-146`, doc `:122-126`).
  - `Summarize(signIn, now, currentSignInId)` (`:149`): last-active is the head's `CreatedAt`, IP and user agent come from the head, `IsCurrent` matches the resolved sign-in (`:162`), and `Device` comes from `head.ToDeviceMetadata()` (`:163`).
  - `DescribeEnd(head, now)` (`:166`): a revoked head reports its instant and recorded reason as-is, because the session reasons and `SignInEndReasons` share their values (`:168-173`); otherwise a head past `ExpiresAt` reports `Expired`, and a live one reports no end (`:175`).
- **Why it's built this way**: the shaping functions are pure and take `now` as a parameter, so the history is testable without a clock or a store, and the one shared reader keeps the self-service and administrator views identical. The model is recorded in [ADR-097](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.html); the view-as rows in [ADR-137](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.html).
- **Where it's used**: [AuthSessionIssuer](#authsessionissuer)`.ListSignInsAsync` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:271`) and [UserSessionsAdministrationService](#usersessionsadministrationservice) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserSessionsAdministrationService.cs:64`). ADC's E2E view-as tests exercise the "Viewed by support" rows (`MMCA.ADC/Tests/E2E/MMCA.ADC.E2E.Tests/Workflows/Identity/Administration/ViewAsTests.cs`).

### AuthSessionIssuer
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:54` · Level 8 · class (sealed, partial)

- **What it is**: the framework's [IAuthSessionIssuer](#iauthsessionissuer): multi-device refresh sessions, hashed at rest (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:14-16`). Every issue opens its own [RefreshSession](#refreshsession), so signing in on a second device leaves the first one signed in (`:19-20`).
- **Depends on**: [ITokenService](#itokenservice) (mints both tokens), [IRefreshSessionStore](#irefreshsessionstore) (the session rows), `IOptions<`[RefreshSessionSettings](#refreshsessionsettings)`>` (the per-user cap, the reuse grace and the lost-response window), `TimeProvider` (every session instant), an optional `ILogger<AuthSessionIssuer>` and an optional [IViewAsGrantStore](#iviewasgrantstore), all primary-constructor parameters (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:54-60`, doc `:42-53`); [RefreshSession](#refreshsession), [AuthenticationResponse](#authenticationresponse), [RefreshSessionSummaryResponse](#refreshsessionsummaryresponse), [SignInSummaryResponse](#signinsummaryresponse), [DeviceMetadata](#devicemetadata) and `Error`/`Result` from the primer. Its private helpers are [IssuedSession](#issuedsession) and [SessionStampingTokenService](#sessionstampingtokenservice); it reads history through [SignInHistory](#signinhistory) and device columns through [RefreshSessionDevice](#refreshsessiondevice). The class is `partial` because its two log methods are `[LoggerMessage]` source-generated (`:645-658`).
- **Concept introduced: refresh-token rotation with family revocation on reuse, a grace window for races, and an opt-in recovery for lost responses.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses how bearer credentials are issued, stored and revoked. The class remarks (`AuthSessionIssuer.cs:17-41`) state the model: the store holds only `RefreshSession.HashToken` digests; rotation revokes the presented session and links it to its successor; presenting an already-rotated token lands on that revoked row, which is the reuse signal that revokes the user's whole live family (BR-206); two requests presenting the same live token at once are covered by the same rule because the rotation is claimed atomically through `IRefreshSessionStore.TryRotateAsync`; and an expired session is not a reuse signal. Both paths share one carve-out (`:26-29`): a token rotated less than [RefreshSessionSettings](#refreshsessionsettings)`.ReuseGraceSeconds` ago (default 10) is a rotation race between sibling requests, answered `409 Conflict` (`Auth.RefreshSuperseded`) with nothing revoked; past the grace it is a replay, unless lost-response recovery is configured (`RefreshSessionSettings.LostResponseRecoveryMinutes`, off by default) and the presented row's successor was never presented, in which case that successor is rotated in its place (`:29-31`). A token whose row was revoked by a sign-out, a session-cap eviction or an earlier reuse sweep is not a new theft signal either: that device simply lost its session, so only that request fails. A swept row is dead by construction, so revoking the family again on it would only sign the user out of the sessions they re-established, on demand of anyone holding a swept token (`:391-394`); a genuine replay lands on a rotated row and still revokes the family. The practical effect: a stolen-and-replayed token costs the attacker the session and costs the user only a re-sign-in, while a double-fired refresh from two tabs, or a refresh whose response never reached the client, does not sign anyone out.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - **Fields** (`:67`, `:74`): the nested [SessionStampingTokenService](#sessionstampingtokenservice) wrapped around the injected token service, exposed as `TokenService` (`:77`), and `_signInInstant`, armed only while `IssueAsync` mints a new session's first access token so that token carries `auth_time` (doc `:69-73`).
  - **Lifetimes** (`:79-83`): `AccessTokenLifetime` and `RefreshTokenLifetime` read the token service and fall back to 15 minutes and 7 days when the value is non-positive, so the expiry reported to clients matches the JWT's actual `exp`; a host that binds `JwtSettings` through `AddCommonAuthentication` fails startup on such a value, so the fallback covers test doubles and token services configured outside that binding (`:35-39`).
  - **`IssueAsync`** (`:86`): opens the session first (`OpenSessionAsync`, `:99`), unwraps it with `TryGetValue` (`:100`), saves (`:105`), then sets `_signInInstant` to `now` (`:109`) and calls `mintAccessToken(issued.SessionId)` (`:113`) inside a `try` whose `finally` clears it (`:117-120`). The comment at `:97-98` says why the order matters: the token carries the session's id in `sid`, and a session has an id only once created; the comment at `:107-108` says why the instant is stamped here: opening a session is an interactive sign-in, and every refresh carries it over.
  - **`OpenSessionAsync`** (`:469`): generates a refresh token, creates the row through `RefreshSession.Create` with `now + RefreshTokenLifetime` (`:476-483`), runs `EnforceSessionCapAsync` (`:490`), stages the insert without saving (`:491`) and returns an [IssuedSession](#issuedsession) (`:493`).
  - **`EnforceSessionCapAsync`** (`:705`): reads the user's un-revoked rows, keeps the ones active now, orders oldest first (`CreatedAt`, then `Id`), and revokes from the front with `ReasonSessionCap` until there is room for one more (loop at `:714`). Its summary (`:696-704`) records the default cap of 10, the 1-1000 startup range, and that expired-but-unrevoked rows do not count and age out through `RefreshSessionCleanupService`.
  - **`RotateAsync`** (`:124`): `ResolveRotatableSessionAsync` (`:135`), then `RotateSessionAsync` (`:143`), each result unwrapped with `TryGetValue`, then the mint with the successor's id (`:154`), so the client's current-device marker follows the rotation (comment `:150-152`).
  - **`ResolveRotatableSessionAsync`** (`:398`): a blank token, an unknown hash, or a row of another user fails alone (`:404-416`). A revoked row (`:418-457`) splits four ways: if `IsReuseSignal` is false (signed out, cap-evicted, or already swept by an earlier reuse event) it fails alone (`:420-427`); if it was rotated inside the grace (`IsWithinRotationGrace`) it answers `RefreshSupersededError` with nothing revoked (`:429-434`); if `FindRecoverableSuccessorAsync` finds a never-presented live successor, that successor is logged and returned as the session to rotate (`:436-445`), and if a sibling just recovered it the answer is `RefreshSupersededError` (`:447-452`); otherwise `RevokeFamilyOnReuseAsync` revokes the family before failing (`:454-456`). An expired row fails alone (`:459-461`). Its summary (`:382-397`) explains why the unknown-hash case must not revoke the family (otherwise anyone holding one of this user's expired access tokens could sign them out everywhere by posting a random token) and why a swept row must not either.
  - **`FindRecoverableSuccessorAsync`** (`:619`): returns nothing unless recovery is configured, the presented row was revoked as `Rotated` inside the window and has a successor hash (`:624-632`); looks the successor up by hash and requires the same user (`:634-638`); a still-live successor is the recovery, and a non-live one counts as superseded only when it was itself rotated within the grace (`:640-642`). A successor that was ever presented would itself be revoked, which is exactly the two-holders signal that must keep revoking the family (summary `:609-618`).
  - **`RotateSessionAsync`** (`:510`): builds the successor through `session.CreateSuccessor`, which continues the presented session's `SignInId` so the sign-in history folds a rotation chain into one row (`:518-526`), then asks the store to claim the rotation via `TryRotateAsync` (`:533-535`). A lost claim (`:537-565`) means a concurrent request spent this token first, but the tracked copy was read before that claim and still looks live, so the row is re-read untracked through `IRefreshSessionStore.FindByIdUntrackedAsync` (`:543-545`): a sign-out, cap eviction or reuse sweep of the same row fails alone (`:546-552`), a rotation inside the grace answers `RefreshSupersededError` (`:554-557`), and anything else (rotated longer ago than the grace, or unreadable) gets the replay answer through `RevokeFamilyOnReuseAsync` and `Auth.InvalidRefreshToken` (`:562-564`). Rotation replaces one session with one, so the cap is not re-evaluated (`:498`).
  - **`IsReuseSignal`** (`:579`) and **`IsWithinRotationGrace`** (`:599`): the first treats a revoked row as reuse when it has a successor hash (`:581-584`) or any reason other than signed-out, session-cap or reuse-detected (`:586-588`), the conservative answer for rows the code does not recognize; the second is true only for the `Rotated` reason, with a positive grace and `now - RevokedAt` under it (`:601-606`). A row flagged as reuse, signed out or evicted never reaches the grace check, because `IsReuseSignal` fails it alone first, however recent.
  - **`RevokeFamilyOnReuseAsync`** (`:666`) and **`RevokeLiveSessionsAsync`** (`:677`): the second revokes every un-revoked row with the given reason and returns how many it revoked (`:683-693`); the first uses it with `ReasonReuseDetected`, saves, and logs the user id and the count (`:668-672`). The log message deliberately omits the client IP and user agent, which are personal data and would put a device fingerprint into every log sink (comment `:653-654`).
  - **`InvalidRefreshTokenError`** (`:365`) and **`RefreshSupersededError`** (`:376`): `Error.Unauthorized("Auth.InvalidRefreshToken", ...)` is what every failing branch returns except the races, so a caller cannot tell unknown from expired from replayed (doc `:359-364`); a race answers `Error.Conflict("Auth.RefreshSuperseded", ...)` so the client keeps its session and retries with the winner's token (`:371-380`).
  - **`MintForSession`** (`:164` and `:173`): the three-argument overload forwards with `authenticatedAt: null` (`:164-165`); the four-argument one arms the nested [SessionStampingTokenService](#sessionstampingtokenservice) with the session id, the second-factor method, and `authenticatedAt ?? _signInInstant` (`:177-179`), runs the callback, and disarms all three in a `finally` (`:184-189`). A null `authenticatedAt` outside `IssueAsync` mints no `auth_time` rather than inventing a sign-in (remarks `:168-172`).
  - **`SignOutAsync`** (`:193`): revokes only a live session of this user found by token hash (`:197-214`); anything else degrades to revoking every live session rather than reporting success for a revocation that reached nothing (comment `:203-206`, fallback `:217-218`). `SignOutEverywhereAsync` (`:222`) always revokes everything.
  - **`ListActiveAsync`** (`:236`): one query for un-revoked rows, then an in-memory filter to the active ones, newest first, flagging the caller's own session and attaching its device metadata through `ToDeviceMetadata` (`:244-258`).
  - **`ListSignInsAsync`** (`:267`): delegates to [SignInHistory](#signinhistory)`.ReadAsync` with the clock's current instant and the optional view-as grant store (`:271-277`); the read is bounded by the 50-sign-in cap, never by how many times each sign-in rotated (remarks `:262-265`).
  - **`RevokeSessionAsync`** (`:293`): the ownership check is the user-scoped `FindByIdAsync` query (`:298`), so another account's id and a missing id produce the same `Auth.SessionNotFound` (`:299-306`); an already-revoked row writes nothing and answers the not-found failure `Auth.SessionAlreadyRevoked` (`:308-315`), so the client can say the device was already signed out; the session is the caller's own, so the answer reveals nothing about another account (remarks `:280-292`).
  - **`RecordDeviceAsync`** (`:330`): the same user-scoped lookup (`:338`); a missing, revoked or expired session answers `Auth.SessionNotFound` (`:339-346`), since a client reporting on a dead session has nothing left to describe (remarks `:324-329`); otherwise `session.RecordDevice(device)` (`:348`), a failure returned as-is, then save (`:354`).
- **Why it's built this way**: every timestamp comes from the injected `TimeProvider`, so rotation, expiry, the grace window and the recovery window are testable without a clock, and every user-visible failure on the refresh path collapses to one error (the exceptions being the deliberate, retryable 409s) so the endpoint leaks nothing about which rule fired. A lost concurrent rotation is re-read and judged by the same two predicates as a direct lookup, which keeps one rule for one observable situation. The `auth_time` stamping exists for step-up checks such as passkey registration ([ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html)). The multi-device model, rotation and reuse detection are recorded in [ADR-097](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.html) and [ADR-050](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/050-jwt-refresh-token-rotation.html); the view-as rows in [ADR-137](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.html).
- **Where it's used**: registered as the scoped [IAuthSessionIssuer](#iauthsessionissuer) in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:182`; consumed through that interface by [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser) and `AuthControllerBase`. Constructed directly in the Common test suites, among them `AuthSessionIssuerSignInHistoryTests.cs`, `AuthSessionIssuerDeviceTests.cs`, `AuthSessionIssuerLostResponseRecoveryTests.cs` and `AuthSessionIssuerReuseGraceTests.cs` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/Sessions/`), `AuthenticationServiceBaseTests.cs`, `AuthenticationServiceIdentityCompletionsTests.cs` and `AuthenticationServiceLegalAcceptanceTests.cs` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/`), `PasskeyTestHost.cs` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys.Tests/`) and `AuthControllerBaseSessionDeviceTests.cs` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Controllers/Auth/`), and in ADC's `AuthenticationServiceTests.cs` (`MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application.Tests/Users/`).

### RecoveryCodeSet
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorService.cs:97` · Level 0 · record

- **What it is**: a two-field record pairing a freshly generated set of plaintext recovery codes with their stored hashes.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party.
- **Concept**: a plaintext/hash pair returned once, at generation time only, so the plaintext never has to be persisted or re-derived.
- **Walkthrough**: `Codes` (`ITwoFactorService.cs:98`) is the plaintext shown to the user once; `Hashes` (line 86) is what the store keeps.
- **Why it's built this way**: keeping the plaintext out of any store means a database compromise cannot recover usable recovery codes, only their hashes.
- **Where it's used**: returned by [ITwoFactorService](#itwofactorservice).`GenerateRecoveryCodes()`, consumed by `TotpTwoFactorService.cs` and exercised in `MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/TwoFactorHandlerBaseTests.cs`.

### TwoFactorOutcome
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:73` · Level 0 · enum

- **What it is**: the result of a second-factor challenge: `NotEnrolled = 0`, `VerifiedTotp = 1`, `VerifiedRecoveryCode = 2` (`ITwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:76,79,82`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party.
- **Concept**: same explicitly-numbered, wire-stable outcome-enum shape used throughout the domain event taxonomy (see `DomainEntityState` in group-02); `NotEnrolled = 0` is the default/no-op value, matching that convention.
- **Walkthrough**: three values; `NotEnrolled` means the account has no active second factor so nothing was challenged, `VerifiedTotp` means a time-based code from the authenticator app verified, `VerifiedRecoveryCode` means a single-use recovery code verified and was spent.
- **Why it's built this way**: collapsing the challenge result to one enum lets `AuthenticationServiceBase` decide, in one switch, whether to continue sign-in unchanged (`NotEnrolled`) or stamp an `mfa` claim on the issued token (the two verified cases).
- **Where it's used**: returned by [ITwoFactorAuthenticator](#itwofactorauthenticator).`ChallengeAsync`, read by `AuthenticationServiceBase.cs` (7 sites) and `TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs` (7 sites), and by the disable/regenerate handler bases.

### TwoFactorSettings
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorSettings.cs:15` · Level 0 · class

- **What it is**: the options class bound to `Authentication:TwoFactor`, controlling the TOTP parameters (issuer, digits, period, clock-skew window) and the recovery-code and secret sizing.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations` (`[Range]`, `[Required]`, `[StringLength]`).
- **Concept**: the same config-bound settings shape as [EmailConfirmationSettings](#emailconfirmationsettings); no new concept.
- **Walkthrough**: `SectionName` (`TwoFactorSettings.cs:18`) is `"Authentication:TwoFactor"`. `Issuer` (line 26) defaults to `"MMCA"` and labels the account in the authenticator app; its summary (lines 20-23) says a host sets its own application name there. `Digits` (line 30) defaults to 6. `PeriodSeconds` (line 34) defaults to 30. `VerificationWindowSteps` (line 46) defaults to 1, and its remarks (lines 40-44) explain the trade-off: one step widens acceptance to roughly ninety seconds to tolerate clock skew, while a larger window multiplies how many codes are live at once for an attacker guessing. `RecoveryCodeCount` (line 50) defaults to 10. `RecoveryCodeByteLength` (line 57) defaults to 10 bytes (eighty bits). `SecretByteLength` (line 61) defaults to 20 bytes, the RFC 4226 recommendation.
- **Why it's built this way**: every size and window is a documented security/usability trade-off rather than an arbitrary constant, per [ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html).
- **Where it's used**: bound and validated by `AddTwoFactorAuthentication(configuration)` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:49-50`), read by [TotpTwoFactorService](#totptwofactorservice) and [TwoFactorAuthenticator](#twofactorauthenticator) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/`).

### ViewAsSettings
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.ViewAs` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsSettings.cs:34` · Level 0 · class

- **What it is**: the options class bound to the `ViewAs` section that switches read-only view-as support access on and decides which host owns the grant table, how long grant rows are kept, and which data source holds them.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations` (`[Range]`, `[Required]`).
- **Concept**: the same config-bound, startup-validated settings shape as [TwoFactorSettings](#twofactorsettings) ([ADR-070](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.html)). The feature it configures, a staff user seeing the app as one account sees it through a short-lived read-only token, is described by [ADR-137](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.html) and walked through at [ViewAsService](#viewasservice).
- **Walkthrough**: `SectionName` (`ViewAsSettings.cs:37`) is `"ViewAs"`. `Enabled` (line 40) defaults to `false`; the class remarks (lines 10-15) list what "off" means: the grant and end endpoints answer 404, the always-present guard middleware refuses any view-as token with 401, the grant table is in no model (so no migration appears), and sign-in history shows no view-as rows. Lines 17-20 list what a host that turns it on must also do: register an [IViewAsSubjectResolver](#iviewassubjectresolver), grant `users:view-as` to its staff role, add the `ViewAsGrants` migration on the Identity database, and disclose staff access in its privacy notice. `HostsGrantStore` (line 49) defaults to `true`; in a multi-service host only the Identity service keeps it, and the others set it `false` and learn that a grant ended from a marker in the shared `ICacheService` (remarks lines 23-31, which also state that a service unable to read that cache refuses view-as requests, failing closed). `RetentionDays` (line 56, `[Range(1, 3650)]` at line 55) defaults to 90, matching the field-level audit trail's retention. `DataSourceName` (line 63) defaults to `"Default"`.
- **Why it's built this way**: off by default with no table mapped means a host that never opts in carries neither the endpoints nor the schema, and the explicit `HostsGrantStore` split keeps the grant table in one database per [ADR-137](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.html).
- **Where it's used**: bound in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:193-194`, read by [ViewAsService](#viewasservice) (the retention sweep), `EFViewAsGrantStore`, `ApplicationDbContext`, `DesignTimeDbContextHelper`, and the `AuthControllerBase`, `UsersAdminControllerBase` and `ViewAsGrantsAdminControllerBase` controllers in `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/`.

### ViewAsSubject
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.ViewAs` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsSubject.cs:15` · Level 0 · record

- **What it is**: the facts about one account that a view-as token is minted from, plus the two flags that make an account unviewable.
- **Depends on**: `UserIdentifierType`; the `[Pii]` attribute on its personal fields.
- **Concept**: a small app-supplied read model that lets Common stay ignorant of the consumer's user entity; the consumer fills it through [IViewAsSubjectResolver](#iviewassubjectresolver).
- **Walkthrough**: positional members `UserId`, `Email`, `Role`, `FullName`, `IsDeleted` (`ViewAsSubject.cs:16-20`), with `Email` (line 17) and `FullName` (line 19) marked `[property: Pii]`. `IsServiceAccount` (line 27) flags the service account behind a machine client ([ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html)), which has no person to support. `IsLocked` (line 34) flags a locked account: a lock writes the soft-deleted-user marker (ADR-047), so every host would refuse the token on its first call. Both are `init` properties that default to `false`.
- **Why it's built this way**: carrying the refusal facts on the subject lets [ViewAsService](#viewasservice) decide every refusal in one place before any grant row is written.
- **Where it's used**: returned by [IViewAsSubjectResolver](#iviewassubjectresolver).`FindAsync`, consumed by [ViewAsService](#viewasservice) (the refusal checks and the token claims), built in ADC by `MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/Administration/ViewAsSubjectResolver.cs`.

### ITwoFactorService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorService.cs:16` · Level 1 · interface

- **What it is**: the TOTP/authenticator-app abstraction: mints secrets, builds the provisioning URI, verifies codes, and generates/hashes/matches recovery codes.
- **Depends on**: [RecoveryCodeSet](#recoverycodeset) (return type of `GenerateRecoveryCodes`).
- **Concept introduced**: a service interface that isolates the cryptographic mechanics of TOTP (RFC 6238-style time-based codes) from the account-state orchestration that lives in [ITwoFactorAuthenticator](#itwofactorauthenticator). `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` (assesses single-responsibility separation): this interface only knows about codes and secrets, never about a user account or a store.
- **Walkthrough**: `GenerateSecret()` (`ITwoFactorService.cs:22`) mints a fresh Base32 secret. `BuildProvisioningUri(secret, accountName)` (line 37) builds the `otpauth://totp/...` URI an authenticator app scans as a QR code; it is deliberately returned as `string` rather than `System.Uri` (the `[SuppressMessage]` at lines 33-36 explains that round-tripping through `Uri` would re-normalize the percent-encoding the app parses). `VerifyCode(secret, code)` (line 46) checks a code within the configured number of time steps on each side of the current one. The overload `VerifyCode(secret, code, out matchedStep)` (line 59) verifies exactly the same way and also reports which time step matched (Unix seconds divided by the period, or 0 when nothing matched), so a caller that keeps per-account state can refuse a replay of a code it already accepted inside the same window. `GenerateRecoveryCodes()` (line 66) returns a fresh [RecoveryCodeSet](#recoverycodeset). `HashRecoveryCode(code)` (line 74) hashes one plaintext code the way the store keeps it. `TryMatchRecoveryCode(code, storedHashes, out matchedHash)` (line 83) compares in fixed time to avoid a timing side-channel on which stored hash matched.
- **Why it's built this way**: keeping code verification, secret generation, and recovery-code hashing behind one narrow interface means [ITwoFactorAuthenticator](#itwofactorauthenticator) and the handler bases never touch a raw cryptographic primitive directly. Replay protection stays out of this interface too: the service only reports the matched step, and the stateful "accept each step once" rule lives in the caller.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [TotpTwoFactorService](#totptwofactorservice) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpTwoFactorService.cs:59` for the step-reporting overload), consumed by the enrollment/regeneration handler bases in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/` and by [TwoFactorAuthenticator](#twofactorauthenticator), which calls the step-reporting overload (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:81`) and then rejects any step at or below the last one it cached for that user (`TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:198`). Registered as a singleton in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:55`.

### IViewAsSubjectResolver
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.ViewAs` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/IViewAsSubjectResolver.cs:8` · Level 1 · interface

- **What it is**: the one-method extension point through which the consuming app reads an account's [ViewAsSubject](#viewassubject).
- **Depends on**: [ViewAsSubject](#viewassubject), `UserIdentifierType`.
- **Concept**: a consumer-implemented port: Common owns the view-as workflow, the app owns its user table.
- **Walkthrough**: `FindAsync(userId, cancellationToken)` (`IViewAsSubjectResolver.cs:14`) returns the subject, or `null` when no such account exists.
- **Why it's built this way**: Common does not register an implementation (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:192` says the account reader is the consumer's), and [ViewAsService](#viewasservice) takes it as an optional constructor argument, so an enabled host that forgot it gets a `ViewAs.NotConfigured` failure rather than a DI error.
- **Where it's used**: called by [ViewAsService](#viewasservice).`StartAsync`; implemented in ADC by `ViewAsSubjectResolver` (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/Administration/ViewAsSubjectResolver.cs:24`) and registered in that module's `DependencyInjection.cs`.

### TwoFactorErrors
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorErrors.cs:15` · Level 2 · class

- **What it is**: the static `Error`-factory class for the two-factor flow: challenge-required, challenge-invalid, not-enrolled, enrollment-missing, and recent-sign-in-required.
- **Depends on**: `Error`.
- **Concept**: same convention as [EmailConfirmationErrors](#emailconfirmationerrors); no new concept.
- **Walkthrough**: five codes (`TwoFactorErrors.cs:18,21,24,27,33`). `TwoFactorRequired(source)` (lines 38-41) is `Error.Unauthorized`, asking the caller to supply a code or a recovery code. `TwoFactorInvalid(source)` (lines 51-54) is also `Error.Unauthorized`; its remarks (lines 46-50) note it is deliberately the same message for a wrong TOTP code and a wrong recovery code, since telling them apart would leak whether a presented value was recovery-code shaped. `TwoFactorNotEnrolled(source)` (lines 59-62) and `TwoFactorEnrollmentMissing(source)` (lines 67-70) are both `Error.Conflict`, for an action attempted on an account with no active factor and on an enrollment that was never started, respectively. `RecentSignInRequired(source)` (lines 80-83) is `Error.Forbidden` with code `Authentication.TwoFactorRecentSignInRequired` (line 33): starting or confirming enrollment from a session whose interactive sign-in (`auth_time`) is older than the recent-sign-in window. Its remarks (lines 75-79) explain that enrollment adds a way into the account, so it asks for the same recent sign-in as registering a passkey, and that a refresh never renews `auth_time`, so only a new sign-in clears it.
- **Why it's built this way**: `Conflict` versus `Unauthorized` is used to distinguish "your account state does not support this action" from "your credentials did not verify", and `Forbidden` marks "you are signed in, but not recently enough for this", matching the semantics the rest of the auth surface uses for those error kinds.
- **Where it's used**: raised by `ConfirmTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase.cs`, `DisableTwoFactorHandlerBase.cs` and `RegenerateRecoveryCodesHandlerBase.cs` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/`), by [TwoFactorAuthenticator](#twofactorauthenticator) and `AuthenticationServiceBase.cs`; `RecentSignInRequired` is raised by `TwoFactorControllerBase` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/TwoFactor/TwoFactorControllerBase.cs:136,170`). Asserted in `TwoFactorHandlerBaseTests.cs`, `TwoFactorAuthenticatorTests.cs`, `TwoFactorControllerBaseTests.cs` and `AuthErrorCodesAlignmentTests.cs`.

### ITwoFactorAuthenticator
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:24` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the account-level orchestration for the second-factor challenge at sign-in, one level above [ITwoFactorService](#itwofactorservice)'s pure cryptographic operations.
- **Depends on**: `UserIdentifierType`, [TwoFactorOutcome](#twofactoroutcome), [TwoFactorErrors](#twofactorerrors), `Result<T>`.
- **Concept**: the service-orchestrates-over-a-crypto-primitive layering also seen with [IEmailConfirmationTokenService](#iemailconfirmationtokenservice) versus its store; no new concept.
- **Walkthrough**: `ChallengeAsync(userId, code, cancellationToken)` (`ITwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:40-43`) returns [TwoFactorOutcome](#twofactoroutcome).`NotEnrolled` when the account has no active second factor (sign-in continues unchanged, no `mfa` claim), the verified outcome when a code satisfies the challenge, or a failure: [TwoFactorErrors](#twofactorerrors).`TwoFactorRequiredCode` when a code was needed and none arrived, [TwoFactorErrors](#twofactorerrors).`TwoFactorInvalidCode` when one arrived and did not verify (doc comment lines 32-39).
- **Why it's built this way**: returning an outcome enum rather than a bare boolean lets `AuthenticationServiceBase` distinguish "no second factor configured" from "verified", which matters for whether it stamps an `mfa` claim on the issued token.
- **Enrollment confirmation**: `VerifyEnrollmentCodeAsync(userId, secret, code, cancellationToken)` (`ITwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:65-69`) returns a plain `bool` and verifies a code against the account's PENDING secret under the same single-use time-step guard as `ChallengeAsync` (doc comment lines 45-64). The `secret` it receives (param doc lines 57-61) is the pending secret as [ITwoFactorStore](#itwofactorstore) holds it, in the protected form [ITwoFactorSecretProtector](#itwofactorsecretprotector).`Protect` produced; the shipped implementation unprotects it before verifying. `ChallengeAsync` answers [TwoFactorOutcome](#twofactoroutcome).`NotEnrolled` until the factor is active, so the confirm step cannot use it.
