### PasswordComplexity
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/PasswordComplexity.cs:18` · Level 0 · class (static partial)

- **What it is**: the one definition of the strong-password rule: the two length bounds, four
  source-generated character-class regexes, and an `Evaluate` predicate that combines them
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/PasswordComplexity.cs:5-18`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; BCL `System.Text.RegularExpressions` and the
  `[GeneratedRegex]` source generator (`PasswordComplexity.cs:1,34`).
- **Concept introduced, one rule evaluated on both sides of the wire.** `[Rubric §24, Forms,
  Validation & UX Safety]` assesses validation parity: the client form must give the verdict the
  API would. The doc comment states the purpose directly (`PasswordComplexity.cs:5-10`): the server
  validator ([StrongPasswordRules<T>](group-06-validation.md#requiredstringrulest-optionalstringrulest-emailrulest-positiveintrulest-positivedecimalrulest-nonnegativeintrulest-requiredidrulest-tid-optionalpositiveidrulest-tid-passwordrulest-strongpasswordrulest)
  in MMCA.Common.Application) and the client attribute
  ([PasswordComplexityAttribute](group-15-common-ui-framework.md#passwordcomplexityattribute) in
  MMCA.Common.UI) both read this type, so they cannot disagree on the same input. It lives in Shared
  because Shared is the one project both of those layers may reference (UI depends on Shared only).
  The character classes are Unicode-aware (`PasswordComplexity.cs:11-16`): an accented or CJK letter
  counts as a letter, never as the "special" character.
- **Walkthrough**: `MinimumLength` is `8` (`PasswordComplexity.cs:28`) and `MaximumLength` is `128`
  (`PasswordComplexity.cs:31`), both `const int` measured in UTF-16 code units, so they are usable in
  attribute arguments. Four `public static partial Regex` properties are source-generated by
  `[GeneratedRegex]`, each with a 1000 ms match timeout: `Uppercase` (`\p{Lu}`,
  `PasswordComplexity.cs:34-35`), `Lowercase` (`\p{Ll}`, `:38-39`), `Digit` (`\p{Nd}`, `:42-43`), and
  `SpecialCharacter` (`[^\p{L}\p{Nd}]`, anything that is neither a letter nor a decimal digit,
  `:49-50`). `Evaluate(string? password)` (`PasswordComplexity.cs:52-57`) returns `true` only when the
  input is non-null, at least `MinimumLength` long, and matches all four regexes. It deliberately does
  **not** check `MaximumLength`: the upper bound is a separate rule with its own message on both
  sides (`PasswordComplexity.cs:52-56`).
- **Why it's built this way**: a client rule and a server rule written separately are two copies of
  one policy that drift independently. Exposing the regexes (not only `Evaluate`) lets the
  server's FluentValidation chain keep one message per failed class, while the client attribute asks
  the single yes/no question. Source-generated regexes avoid runtime regex construction, and the
  match timeout bounds evaluation of untrusted input.
- **Where it's used**: `StrongPasswordRules<T>` feeds both length constants and all four regexes into
  its rule chain
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Validation/CommonValidationRules.cs:195-200`);
  [PasswordComplexityAttribute](group-15-common-ui-framework.md#passwordcomplexityattribute) calls
  `Evaluate`, leaving empty input to `[Required]`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/PasswordComplexityAttribute.cs:25`);
  [RegisterModel](group-15-common-ui-framework.md#registermodel) and
  [ResetPasswordModel](group-15-common-ui-framework.md#resetpasswordmodel) pair that attribute with
  `[StringLength(PasswordComplexity.MaximumLength)]` to supply the separate upper-bound rule
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/RegisterModel.cs:27-28`,
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/ResetPasswordModel.cs:25-26`); pinned by
  `MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared.Tests/Auth/PasswordComplexityTests.cs`.
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: the server's error messages still hard-code the numbers ("at least 8
  characters", "longer than 128 characters") rather than interpolating the constants
  (`CommonValidationRules.cs:195-196`), and so does the attribute's default message
  (`PasswordComplexityAttribute.cs:19`); changing a bound means editing those strings too. The
  plain `PasswordRules<T>` sibling in the same file still uses literal `8`/`128`
  (`CommonValidationRules.cs:179-180`) and does not read this type.

### Totp
> MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · `MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/Totp.cs:24` · Level 0 · class (internal static)

- **What it is**: RFC 6238 time-based one-time passwords over HMAC-SHA1 with RFC 4226 dynamic
  truncation, "the variant every authenticator app implements"
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/Totp.cs:8-11,24`).
- **Depends on**: BCL only: `HMACSHA1.HashData`, `BinaryPrimitives`, `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`
  and `MemoryMarshal` from `System.Security.Cryptography`, `System.Buffers.Binary` and
  `System.Runtime.InteropServices`.
- **Concept introduced, a one-time code is an HMAC of the clock.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses
  whether credentials are verified without side channels. A TOTP code is the HMAC of a shared secret over
  a counter, where the counter is "the whole Unix seconds of the instant divided by the period", so a
  code is live for exactly one period (`Totp.cs:13-17`). The server holds the same secret, recomputes the
  code for the current step and its neighbors, and compares. **Comparison is fixed time**: every candidate
  step is computed and compared with `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`, without stopping at a
  match, so the reply time does not say which step matched (`Totp.cs:18-22`). `[Rubric §32, Dependency &
  Supply-Chain]` applies as for [Base32](#base32): the algorithm is about a hundred lines of BCL calls
  rather than a package.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `Compute(key, utcInstant, periodSeconds, digits)` (`Totp.cs:32-33`) computes the code for the step
    containing an instant.
  - `Verify(key, code, utcInstant, periodSeconds, digits, windowSteps, out matchedStep)` (`:47-75`)
    null-checks its inputs (`:56-57`), takes the current step (`:59`) and the presented code's bytes
    (`:60`), then walks every candidate step, computing the expected code and comparing in fixed time; the
    `&& !matched` guard records the first match without leaving the loop early (`:64-72`). `matchedStep`
    is zero when nothing matched.
  - `TimeStep` (`:77-82`) rejects a non-positive period and divides whole Unix seconds by it.
  - `Candidates` (`:84-97`) yields the current step, then each earlier step out to the window but never
    below step zero (`currentStep >= offset`, `:88`), then each later step.
  - `ComputeForStep` (`:99-124`) bounds `digits` to 1..9 (`:101-102`), writes the step as a big-endian
    64-bit counter into a stack buffer (`:104-105`), HMAC-SHA1s it (`:107-110`, with a scoped `CA5350`
    suppression whose justification is that authenticator apps speak HMAC-SHA1 and HMAC does not rely on
    SHA-1 collision resistance), applies the RFC 4226 section 5.3 dynamic truncation (the low nibble of
    the last byte picks four bytes, read big endian with the top bit cleared, `:112-115`), and reduces
    modulo `10^digits`, left-padding with zeros (`:117-123`).
- **Why it's built this way**: two-factor authentication is opt-in
  ([ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html)); the algorithm
  is `internal` to Infrastructure, so Application, Domain and Shared take no dependency for it and
  [TotpTwoFactorService](#totptwofactorservice) is its only production caller.
- **Where it's used**: `TotpTwoFactorService.VerifyCode`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpTwoFactorService.cs:87-94`);
  checked against the RFC test vectors by
  `MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpRfcVectorTests.cs`.
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: replay inside the window is not this type's concern; it only reports the
  matched step, and [TwoFactorAuthenticator](#twofactorauthenticator) refuses a step it already accepted.

### ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute.cs:18` · Level 0 · class (sealed attribute)

- **What it is**: a marker for a read-only gRPC service, or a single method of one, that may be called
  under a view-as token. gRPC is always POST, so without this mark
  [ViewAsGuardMiddleware](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#viewasguardmiddleware) refuses every view-as
  read that fans out over gRPC
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute.cs:3-10,18`).
- **Depends on**: BCL `Attribute`; `AttributeUsage(Class | Method, AllowMultiple = false, Inherited = true)`
  (`ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute.cs:17`).
- **Concept introduced, an exemption the host asserts and nothing verifies.** `[Rubric §11, Security]`
  assesses whether a read-only mode is enforced by construction. The guard treats a POST to a marked
  endpoint as safe for the HTTP METHOD rule only: any other method is still refused, `ViewAs:Enabled` and
  the grant-liveness check still apply, and the command decorator still refuses every command
  (`ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute.cs:6-9`). The remarks are candid that the mark "is an assertion the
  host makes, which nothing can verify", so a host applies it deliberately and only to code that performs
  no write; there is no exemption by content type and none for gRPC in general (`:11-16`). See
  [ADR-137](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.html).
- **Walkthrough**: an empty `sealed class` deriving from `Attribute` (`:18`).
- **Why it's built this way**: it lives in Shared "so a gRPC service project can apply it without taking
  a reference on the API package" (`ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute.cs:14-15`).
- **Where it's used**: read from the routed endpoint's metadata by `ViewAsGuardMiddleware`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:119`); ADC's
  services tests check the posture of its gRPC endpoints against it
  (`MMCA.ADC/Tests/Services/MMCA.ADC.Services.Tests/Live/GrpcViewAsPostureTests.cs`).

### ClaimsPrincipalExtensions
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:18` · Level 1 · class (static)

- **What it is**: the one place the framework reads identity claims off a `ClaimsPrincipal`: the raw
  user-id value, the parsed user id, the caller's roles, an explicit permission claim, the
  refresh-session id, whether a second authentication factor was presented, whether the request comes
  from a view-as token, which roles were withheld pending a second factor, and the sign-in instant
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:6-18`).
- **Depends on**: [AuthClaimTypes](#authclaimtypes) for the claim names it reads
  (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:27` `Subject`, `:98` `Permission`, `:112` `SessionId`, `:129,148`
  `MultiFactor`, `:138` `ViewAsActor`, `:165,175` `MultiFactorWithheldRole`, `:191` `AuthTime`); the
  solution-wide `UserIdentifierType` alias; BCL `System.Security.Claims` and `System.Globalization`
  (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:1-2`).
- **Concept introduced, one reader for a claim that arrives under two names.** `[Rubric §11,
  Security]` assesses whether identity resolution is correct and uniform, and `[Rubric §15,
  Best Practices & Code Quality]` assesses whether a fragile detail is centralized or copy-pasted. The trap is
  ASP.NET Core's inbound claim mapping. Tokens carry the user identifier in the standard `sub` claim
  only, but that single value reaches readers under two different claim types depending on which
  pipeline produced the principal (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:8-16`):
  - the JWT bearer handler maps inbound `sub` onto `ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier`, the long
    `http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/...` URI;
  - a handler that materializes an identity straight from a token's claims leaves the raw `sub` in
    place. [SessionCookieAuthenticationHandler](#sessioncookieauthenticationhandler) is exactly that
    case: it builds `new ClaimsIdentity(jwt.Claims, ...)` from the decoded token
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/SessionCookies/SessionCookieAuthenticationHandler.cs:60-61`).

  A reader that hard-codes either name works under one pipeline and silently returns "anonymous" under
  the other, and "silently anonymous" in an authorization path is the worst failure shape available.
  Routing every framework reader through `FindUserIdValue` makes both shapes resolve identically, and
  means a consumer that changes its claim mapping does not lose the current user
  (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:13-15`). `FindAuthTime` applies the same two-shape rule to `auth_time`.
  Note the deliberate use of C#'s classic `this`-parameter extension methods here rather than the
  `extension(T)` blocks the codebase uses for DI registration: these are plain static helpers on a BCL
  type.
- **Walkthrough**: twelve extension methods, all null-tolerant by construction (every parameter is
  `ClaimsPrincipal?`, so a null principal yields null, empty, or false rather than throwing).
  - `FindUserIdValue(this ClaimsPrincipal?)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:26-28`) is the primitive:
    `principal?.FindFirst(AuthClaimTypes.Subject)?.Value ?? principal?.FindFirst(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)?.Value`.
    Raw `sub` wins, the mapped `NameIdentifier` is the fallback, and a principal carrying neither
    yields `null`.
  - `GetUserId(this ClaimsPrincipal?)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:40-44`) parses that value into
    the module's `UserIdentifierType` and returns `null` when the claim is absent or unparsable. It
    parses through `IParsable<TSelf>.TryParse` in `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`, which the remarks
    justify twice over (`:34-38`): it matches the writer (claims are formatted invariantly) and it
    stays correct if the solution-wide identifier alias changes shape, so the helper does not have to
    be rewritten when an app moves from `int` to `Guid`.
  - `GetRoleValues(this ClaimsPrincipal?)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:60-68`) returns every role
    value the principal carries under any of three claim types: the standard `ClaimTypes.Role` URI,
    or the raw `role`/`roles` claim an identity provider emits with inbound-claim mapping off. The
    remarks mark it SECURITY: it is the framework's **one** definition of "the caller's roles",
    because the narrower BCL `ClaimsPrincipal.IsInRole(string)` sees only the identity's own role
    claim type and can therefore disagree with the authorization handler about who is privileged.
    The rule is scoped to access decisions (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:55-57`): every role read
    that gates access goes through here, while the UI NavMenu's BCL `IsInRole` calls only decide
    which nav links are shown, not what the caller may do.
  - `HasRole(this ClaimsPrincipal?, string)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:76-78`) is
    `GetRoleValues().Contains(role, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`, guarded against a blank role.
  - `HasPermissionClaim(this ClaimsPrincipal?, string)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:95-98`) checks
    for an [AuthClaimTypes](#authclaimtypes)`.Permission` claim matching the given permission,
    independently of role. The remarks mark it SECURITY too: both authorization gates, the HTTP
    policy handler and the CQRS pipeline gate, read it, so a grant the minting host stored and
    emitted as a claim is honored identically at both boundaries; in a multi-service deployment the
    claim is the only way such a grant reaches a service that does not own the grant table. It is
    additive, never a denial: a principal without the claim still passes on a role the registry
    grants.
  - `FindSessionId(this ClaimsPrincipal?)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:110-114`) reads the `sid`
    claim and `Guid.TryParse`s it. The remarks make the degradation explicit (`:104-108`): `null` is an
    ordinary answer, not an error, because tokens issued before `sid` shipped carry no such claim, and
    every reader treats its absence as "the caller's own session is unknown". Nothing authenticates on
    this value.
  - `HasMultiFactor(this ClaimsPrincipal?)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:128-129`) is
    `principal?.FindFirst(AuthClaimTypes.MultiFactor) is not null`. The remarks mark it SECURITY:
    presence is the whole test, and absence denies rather than falling back to a role check, because
    only the sign-in flow stamps the claim, and only after a code verified.
  - `IsViewAs(this ClaimsPrincipal?)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:137-138`) is the same presence test
    on `ViewAsActor`: `true` means the principal comes from a view-as token and the request is read-only.
  - `FindMultiFactorMethod(this ClaimsPrincipal?)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:147-148`) returns the
    value of the `MultiFactor` claim, or `null` when the principal carries none, for audit and UI copy
    such as "signed in with a recovery code".
  - `GetMultiFactorWithheldRoles(this ClaimsPrincipal?)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:162-165`) returns
    the values of every `MultiFactorWithheldRole` marker in recorded order, or an empty list. The remarks
    are precise that a withheld role is **not held**: `GetRoleValues` and `HasRole` do not see it, and
    this member exists so a caller can say "set up two-factor authentication to use this role" instead of
    treating the account as one without the role (`:155-159`).
  - `HasMultiFactorWithheldRole(this ClaimsPrincipal?)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:174-175`) is the
    presence test for at least one such marker.
  - `FindAuthTime(this ClaimsPrincipal?)` (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:189-197`) reads the raw
    `auth_time` first and falls back to `ClaimTypes.AuthenticationInstant`, the type the JWT bearer
    handler's inbound claim map renames it to (`:182-186`), then parses whole Unix seconds into a
    `DateTimeOffset`. It returns `null` for a token minted before the claim shipped and for a view-as
    token.
- **Why it's built this way**: [TokenService](#tokenservice) records the other half of the story in a
  comment (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TokenService.cs:140-143`): a
  duplicate custom user-id claim used to ride alongside `sub`, which meant two values that could
  disagree and two claim names every reader had to know. Collapsing the writer to one claim
  (`TokenService.cs:146`) is only safe because one reader absorbs the mapping difference, which is this
  type. The `sid` half comes from
  [ADR-097](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.html), the view-as
  test from [ADR-137](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.html),
  and the sign-in instant from
  [ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html).
- **Where it's used**: broadly, and always instead of a hand-rolled claim lookup.
  [CurrentUserService](#currentuserservice) resolves the ambient user id through `GetUserId()`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:20`);
  [ClaimBasedUserIdProvider](#claimbaseduseridprovider) uses `FindUserIdValue()` to key SignalR
  connections
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/ClaimBasedUserIdProvider.cs:15`); the
  [IdempotencyFilter](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#idempotencyfilter) uses it to scope an
  idempotency key to a caller
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Idempotency/IdempotencyFilter.cs:540`);
  [CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#currentusertargetingcontextaccessor)
  uses it for feature-flag targeting
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/FeatureManagement/CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor.cs:121`);
  the opt-in "UserPolicy" rate-limit partition keys on `httpContext.User?.Identity?.Name` directly
  rather than on `GetUserId()`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:197-202`);
  [AuthControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#authcontrollerbase) uses `FindSessionId()` to
  tell the session list which row is the caller's own
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/AuthControllerBase.cs:262`);
  [AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>](#authenticationservicebasetuser) uses `GetUserId()` on the
  principal recovered from an expired access token during rotation and `FindAuthTime()` to carry the
  sign-in instant forward
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:425,455`);
  `PasskeyStepUp` judges recent sign-in with `FindAuthTime()`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyStepUp.cs:27`); and
  [TestPrincipal](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#testprincipal) writes `sub` precisely so test
  principals resolve the same way real ones do
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.UI/Infrastructure/TestPrincipal.cs:19,27`).
  `HasPermissionClaim` backs both [PermissionAuthorizationHandler](#permissionauthorizationhandler)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:31`)
  and the CQRS [AuthorizationGate](group-05-cqrs-pipeline.md#authorizationgate)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/Decorators/AuthorizationGate.cs:48`), whose
  `IRequiresMfa` check is `HasMultiFactor` (`AuthorizationGate.cs:60`); `IsViewAs` backs
  [ViewAsGuardMiddleware](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#viewasguardmiddleware)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:58`) and the
  view-as command decorator
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/Decorators/ViewAsCommandDecorator.cs:38`);
  the withheld-role readers back [MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler](#multifactorroleauthorizationhandler)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:67-69`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: MMCA.Store's Sales UI module defines its own unrelated
  `ClaimsPrincipalExtensions` in a different namespace
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.UI/Extensions/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:9`);
  do not confuse the two when reading a `using` list. Also note `GetUserId` returns a nullable value
  type, so `is { } userId` pattern-matching (as the framework's controllers use, for example
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/TwoFactor/TwoFactorControllerBase.cs:100`)
  is the idiomatic call shape, not a `!` dereference.

### TotpTwoFactorService

> MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · `MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpTwoFactorService.cs:33` · Level 2 · class

- **What it is**: the RFC 6238 TOTP implementation of `ITwoFactorService`: secret generation,
  provisioning-URI construction, code verification, and recovery-code generation/hashing/matching
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpTwoFactorService.cs:9-12,33-164`).
- **Depends on**: [`ITwoFactorService`](#itwofactorservice) (the contract it implements);
  [`TwoFactorSettings`](#twofactorsettings) injected as `IOptions<TwoFactorSettings>`;
  [`RecoveryCodeSet`](#recoverycodeset) as its return shape; the internal [Totp](#totp) (RFC 6238 over
  HMAC-SHA1) and [Base32](#base32) (RFC 4648) in the same folder, no third-party package;
  `System.Security.Cryptography` (`RandomNumberGenerator`, `SHA256`, `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`).
- **Concept introduced, constant-time comparison for a secret the caller does not control the timing
  of.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether the codebase avoids timing side channels around secret
  comparison. `TryMatchRecoveryCode` never exits its scan early on a match: the loop "runs to the end so
  the answer takes the same time whichever code in the list was presented"
  (`TotpTwoFactorService.cs:145-146`), and each comparison itself goes through
  `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals` rather than `==` or `SequenceEqual` (`:147`). A byte-for-byte
  comparison that stops at the first differing byte leaks how many leading bytes an attacker guessed
  correctly across repeated attempts; a fixed-time comparison over a full linear scan removes that
  channel entirely. The type remarks add why the recovery hash is a plain SHA-256 rather than a key
  derivation: the codes are high-entropy random values, not user-chosen secrets, so stretching buys
  nothing an attacker cannot skip and would cost a derivation per stored code on every sign-in
  (`:14-20`).
- **Walkthrough**: `internal sealed class` with a primary constructor taking
  `IOptions<TwoFactorSettings> settings` (`:33`), caching `.Value` once (`:35`).
  - `GenerateSecret()` returns `Base32.Encode` of `RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(_settings.SecretByteLength)`
    (`:38-39`).
  - `BuildProvisioningUri` rejects a blank secret or account name, URL-escapes the issuer and account
    name, and formats the standard `otpauth://` URI a QR code encodes: the algorithm is fixed at `SHA1`,
    while digit count and period are read from settings (`:42-53`). The remarks explain why it is composed
    in one visible place: the `issuer:account` label and the redundant `issuer` parameter, which older
    authenticator apps read, are part of what a user's app has to accept (`:26-30`).
  - `VerifyCode` comes in two overloads. The two-argument form is a one-line forward to the
    three-argument form, discarding the step (`:56`). The three-argument form reports the matched TOTP
    time step through `out long matchedStep`, initialized to `0` so every early `false` leaves it
    defined (`:59-61`). It returns `false` for a blank secret or code (`:62-65`), then decodes the
    stored secret with `Base32.Decode`, catching `ArgumentException` and returning `false` rather than
    throwing when the value is not valid Base32: "a stored secret that is not Base32 can never mint a
    code, so it verifies nothing. That is a data fault, not a caller fault" (`:67-78`). A secret that
    decodes to no key (padding alone, or fewer than eight bits) verifies false for the same reason
    (`:80-85`). It then calls `Totp.Verify` with `DateTime.UtcNow`, the configured period and digit
    count, and a window of `_settings.VerificationWindowSteps` steps on each side of now, every candidate
    compared in fixed time, writing the step the code matched into `matchedStep` (`:87-94`). The window
    tolerates clock drift between the server and the user's authenticator app; the reported step is what
    lets [`TwoFactorAuthenticator`](#twofactorauthenticator) refuse a replay of the same code inside that
    window. The `secret` it receives is plaintext: unprotecting the stored value is the caller's job
    ([DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector](#dataprotectiontwofactorsecretprotector)).
  - `GenerateRecoveryCodes` produces `_settings.RecoveryCodeCount` codes, each a Base32-encoded random
    byte string of `_settings.RecoveryCodeByteLength` bytes with the `=` padding trimmed, alongside
    their SHA-256 hashes computed by `HashRecoveryCode` (`:98-114`). Base32 rather than Base64: "the
    alphabet has no case ambiguity and no characters a user has to guess at while copying a code off
    paper" (`:105-106`). Only the hashes and the caller-facing codes are returned as a `RecoveryCodeSet`
    (`:113`); nothing persists the plaintext codes here.
  - `HashRecoveryCode` normalizes the code (keeps letters and digits, upper-cases) then SHA-256-hashes
    it to an upper-case hex string (`:117-122`).
  - `TryMatchRecoveryCode` normalizes and hashes the presented code once, skips `null` stored entries,
    then fixed-time-compares it against every stored hash, returning the matched hash (not the code)
    through an `out` parameter (`:125-154`).
  - `NormalizeCode` is the shared helper both verification paths route through: it strips whitespace and
    separators a user types or a password manager inserts and upper-cases what remains, "so a code is
    matched the way it was generated" (`:156-163`).
- **Why it's built this way**: two-factor authentication is opt-in
  ([ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html)), registered by
  `AddTwoFactorAuthentication(config)`. The one-time-password algorithm and the Base32 codec are
  internal Infrastructure types rather than a package, so Application, Domain and Shared take no
  dependency for them, and this type, rather than anything in Application, is what computes and
  verifies codes.
- **Where it's used**: registered in DI
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:55`, a
  `TryAddSingleton`) as the `ITwoFactorService` implementation behind `AddTwoFactorAuthentication(config)`
  (`DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:47`), and consumed by
  [`TwoFactorAuthenticator`](#twofactorauthenticator) for both TOTP and recovery-code verification.
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: `internal sealed`, so it is reached only through the `ITwoFactorService`
  abstraction; a consumer cannot construct or type-check against this class directly.

### RoleValue

> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/RoleValue.cs:26` · Level 3 · class (abstract)

- **What it is**: the abstract base for a role value object. It stores one canonical string, gives it
  case-insensitive value equality and hashing, and offers a shared validation helper against a
  per-app set of known role names
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/RoleValue.cs:6-26`).
- **Depends on**: [`Result`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and
  [`Error`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error) from `MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions`
  (`RoleValue.cs:2`), plus `System.Collections.Frozen` from the BCL (`RoleValue.cs:1`). Its doc
  comments point at [`RoleNames`](group-24-identity-module.md#rolenames) for the canonical strings (`RoleValue.cs:9`) and at
  `ICurrentUserService.IsInRole` for the comparison semantics it matches (`RoleValue.cs:17`).
  Conceptually a value object (see [`ValueObject`](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#valueobject))
  but deliberately not derived from that base, for a reason the next bullet unpacks.
- **Concept introduced, a value object as an abstract class with type-guarded equality.**
  `[Rubric §4, Domain-Driven Design]` assesses whether identity-less concepts are modeled as value
  objects rather than bare primitives, and `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` applies to how an open hierarchy is
  left safe to extend. A role has no database identity: two "Organizer" values are the same role, so
  the type is defined by its value, which is exactly the value-object shape. Two design decisions
  make this base unusual, and both are written into the source:
  1. **No `IEquatable<T>` on the base** (`RoleValue.cs:18-24`). The remarks cite Sonar S4035: an
     unsealed type implementing `IEquatable<T>` breaks the equality contract, because a subclass
     instance compared through the base-typed interface can report an equality the derived type
     would reject. Instead equality is the plain `object.Equals` override, and it is type-guarded:
     `GetType() == other.GetType()` before the value comparison (`RoleValue.cs:91-94`), so a role of
     one concrete type is never equal to a same-valued role of another. A *sealed* derived type is
     then free to layer a strongly-typed `IEquatable<TSelf>` plus `==`/`!=` on top, which is what
     ADC's `UserRole` does
     (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Domain/Users/UserRole.cs:18,78-84`).
  2. **It does not derive from [`ValueObject`](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#valueobject)**, and
     that is a fitness-rule consequence, not an oversight. `ValueObjectsAreImmutableSealedInShared`
     requires every concrete class whose base type starts with
     `MMCA.Common.Shared.ValueObjects.ValueObject` to be sealed, immutable, *and* to live in the
     Shared layer
     (`MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Domain/ArchitectureRules.Immutability.cs:56-72`).
     A concrete role type lives in its app's Domain layer
     (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Domain/Users/UserRole.cs:6`), so deriving
     from `ValueObject` would fail that rule in every app. Keeping the base in `MMCA.Common.Shared`
     with its own equality also keeps it dependency-free and therefore usable from Blazor WebAssembly
     and UI code as well as Domain (`RoleValue.cs:12-17`). The same trade-off is made by
     [`Enumeration<TEnumeration>`](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#enumerationtenumeration), whose
     own remarks name `RoleValue` as the shipped precedent
     (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/ValueObjects/Enumeration.cs:34`).

  `[Rubric §11, Security]` applies too, because role strings arrive as JWT claim values whose casing
  is not under this codebase's control. Every comparison here is `OrdinalIgnoreCase`, so an
  authorization check does not silently miss on `"organizer"` against `"Organizer"`.
- **Walkthrough**: a get-only `Value` (`RoleValue.cs:29`) assigned by the protected constructor
  (`RoleValue.cs:33`), so an instance is immutable and only a derived type can create one. The static
  `Validate(role, knownRoles, source)` (`RoleValue.cs:43`) null-guards the supplied set
  (`RoleValue.cs:45`), then returns `Result.Success()` when the role is known, otherwise a
  [`Result`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) failure carrying an
  [`Error`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error) of kind `Invariant`, coded `User.Role.Invalid`,
  with the caller's method name as `source` and `role` as `target` (`RoleValue.cs:47-53`). The
  membership test is the private `IsKnown` (`RoleValue.cs:64-66`) and it is more careful than it
  first looks: the fast path is the supplied set's own `Contains` (correct and O(1) for the intended
  `OrdinalIgnoreCase` sets, with a `role ?? string.Empty` coalesce so a null role becomes a clean
  failure rather than a `NullReferenceException`), and a miss falls back to an explicit
  case-insensitive `Any` scan, so a set built with the *default* ordinal comparer still validates
  case-insensitively as the contract promises (`RoleValue.cs:56-63`). Role sets hold a handful of
  entries, so the fallback is negligible and only ever runs on a miss. The protected generic
  `BuildLookup<TRole>(params TRole[] roles)` (`RoleValue.cs:76`) freezes the supplied singletons into
  a case-insensitive `FrozenDictionary` keyed by `Value` (`RoleValue.cs:81-84`), so a derived type
  can back its `FromString`/`IsValid` members with interned instances instead of re-allocating on
  every parse. `ToString` returns the value (`RoleValue.cs:88`), and `GetHashCode` uses the
  ordinal-ignore-case hash (`RoleValue.cs:97`) so it stays consistent with `Equals`, which is the
  contract any dictionary or `HashSet` key depends on.
- **Why it's built this way**: the abstract-class-plus-type-guard shape is how you share equality
  behavior across an open hierarchy of value objects without violating the equality contract, and the
  S4035 rationale is documented inline (`RoleValue.cs:18-24`) so a future reader does not
  "helpfully" add `IEquatable<T>` to the base. The comparer-agnostic `IsKnown` fallback exists
  because `Validate` accepts any `IReadOnlySet<string>`: the type cannot see how the caller built the
  set, so it enforces its own promise instead of trusting the caller's comparer. That behavior is
  pinned by test, including the default-comparer case
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared.Tests/Auth/RoleValueTests.cs:24`), the
  `OrdinalIgnoreCase` case (`RoleValueTests.cs:36`), a null role (`RoleValueTests.cs:65`), and a null
  role set throwing (`RoleValueTests.cs:73`).
- **Where it's used**: the two apps consume it differently, and the difference is instructive.
  ADC derives a full sealed value object, [`UserRole`](group-24-identity-module.md#userrole), which
  fixes three roles (Organizer, Attendee, ContentEditor), interns them through `BuildLookup`
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Domain/Users/UserRole.cs:21-34`), exposes
  `FromString` returning a `Result<UserRole>` and `IsValid` over that frozen lookup
  (`UserRole.cs:52-66`), and adds a case-insensitive `IsOrganizer` for raw claim strings
  (`UserRole.cs:76`) plus the sealed-type `IEquatable<UserRole>` and `==`/`!=` operators the base
  leaves to subclasses (`UserRole.cs:78-90`). Store's `UserRole` is a **static class**, not a
  subclass: it fixes Admin and Customer as string properties over an `OrdinalIgnoreCase` set and
  calls the shared `RoleValue.Validate` helper for its `IsValid`
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Domain/Users/UserRole.cs:14,26-30,37`), so
  it inherits the rule set (case-insensitive membership, the `User.Role.Invalid` code) without
  inheriting the type. Both key their known-role sets off the [`RoleNames`](group-24-identity-module.md#rolenames) constants,
  and [`PermissionRegistryBuilder`](#permissionregistrybuilder) keeps its role keys on the same
  case-insensitive comparer to match
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/PermissionRegistryBuilder.cs:11`).

### DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector
> MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · `MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector.cs:15` · Level 4 · class (internal sealed)

- **What it is**: the default [ITwoFactorSecretProtector](#itwofactorsecretprotector), which encrypts a
  TOTP secret at rest with the host's ASP.NET Core data-protection key ring under the purpose
  `MMCA.Common.Auth.TwoFactor.Secret.v1`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector.cs:8-13,15`).
- **Depends on**: [ITwoFactorSecretProtector](#itwofactorsecretprotector) (the contract); the framework's
  `Result<T>` and `Error`; `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection` (`IDataProtectionProvider`,
  `IDataProtector`); BCL `CryptographicException`.
- **Concept introduced, an unreadable secret is a result, not an exception.** `[Rubric §11, Security]`
  assesses whether secrets are protected at rest; `[Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]`
  assesses whether a key-management fault degrades instead of crashing a hot path. A multi-replica host
  needs the shared key ring
  ([ADR-069](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/069-shared-data-protection-key-ring.html)), or a
  replica cannot read a secret another one wrote, and the remarks require that this "surfaces as a
  failed unprotect, never as an exception" (`DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector.cs:10-12`).
  `Unprotect` therefore returns `Result<string>` and maps both failure exceptions to one coded failure.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `Purpose` (`:18`), `"MMCA.Common.Auth.TwoFactor.Secret.v1"`, documented as part of the stored format,
    "so it never changes" (`:17`); the protector is created from it once (`:23`).
  - `SecretUnreadableCode` (`:21`), `"Authentication.TwoFactorSecretUnreadable"`.
  - `Protect(string)` (`:26-30`) throws on null or empty and returns the protected payload.
  - `Unprotect(string)` (`:33-52`) answers a blank input as unreadable (`:35-38`), returns
    `Result.Success` with the plaintext (`:40-43`), and catches `CryptographicException` (`:44-47`) and
    `FormatException` (`:48-51`) into the same failure.
  - `Unreadable()` (`:54-58`) builds `Error.Failure(SecretUnreadableCode, "The two-factor secret cannot be
    unprotected with this host's key ring.", nameof(Unprotect))`.
- **Why it's built this way**: the sign-in path treats an unreadable secret as "no time-based code can
  verify" and keeps the recovery codes usable, so the owner still has a way in
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:77-78`);
  that is only possible because this type answers with a `Result` rather than throwing.
- **Where it's used**: registered with `TryAddSingleton` behind `AddTwoFactorAuthentication(config)`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:59`), so a host can
  register its own protector first; consumed by [TwoFactorAuthenticator](#twofactorauthenticator).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: Not determinable from source read for this section: which caller
  invokes `Protect` when an enrollment stores the secret; the type is referenced directly only by its DI
  registration and by tests.

### TwoFactorAuthenticator

> MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · `MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:43` · Level 5 · class

- **What it is**: the `ITwoFactorAuthenticator` implementation that turns a raw code plus a user's
  stored two-factor state into one of four challenge outcomes
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:43-208`).
- **Depends on**: [`ITwoFactorService`](#itwofactorservice) (code verification and
  recovery-code matching); [`ITwoFactorStore`](#itwofactorstore) (loading state and
  consuming a recovery code); [`ITwoFactorSecretProtector`](#itwofactorsecretprotector) (unprotecting
  the stored secret before a code is verified against it); [`ICacheService`](group-09-caching.md#icacheservice)
  (remembering the last accepted TOTP time step per account); [`TwoFactorSettings`](#twofactorsettings)
  via `IOptions<T>` (period and window size); [`IDistributedLock`](group-05-cqrs-pipeline.md#idistributedlock)
  (serializing both code paths per account); [`TwoFactorErrors`](#twofactorerrors);
  [`TwoFactorOutcome`](#twofactoroutcome); the framework's `Result<T>`; the
  `UserIdentifierType` alias.
- **Concept introduced, a challenge is answered with an outcome enum, not a bare boolean.** `[Rubric §1,
  SOLID]` and `[Rubric §11, Security]` both bear on the shape of `ChallengeAsync`'s return: `Result<TwoFactorOutcome>`
  distinguishes "not enrolled" (a success carrying `TwoFactorOutcome.NotEnrolled`, not a failure) from a
  missing code, an invalid code, and the two ways a valid one can be accepted, `VerifiedTotp` versus
  `VerifiedRecoveryCode`. Collapsing those five states into one boolean would force the caller to
  re-derive which one happened from side effects, and a login path that cannot tell "not enrolled" from
  "denied" cannot decide whether to prompt for enrollment or reject the sign-in.
- **Walkthrough**: `internal sealed class` taking `ITwoFactorService`, `ITwoFactorStore`,
  `ITwoFactorSecretProtector`, `ICacheService`, `IOptions<TwoFactorSettings>`, and `IDistributedLock` as
  primary constructor parameters (`:43-49`), with two static lock timings: `StepLockTimeToLive` of 10
  seconds (`:51`) and `StepLockWait` of 5 seconds (`:53`). It implements `ChallengeAsync(userId, code,
  cancellationToken)` (`:56-87`) and `VerifyEnrollmentCodeAsync` (`:90-105`).
  - Loads the user's `state` from the store first (`:61`). If the state is missing or
    `IsTwoFactorEnabled` is false, the challenge succeeds trivially with `NotEnrolled`: "an account that
    never enrolled, and an account whose row vanished between the password check and here, are both
    'nothing to challenge'" (`:63-69`).
  - An enrolled account with no presented code fails with `TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorRequired` (`:71-75`).
  - The code is checked first against the stored TOTP secret, but only after
    `secretProtector.Unprotect` succeeds with a non-empty plaintext; the plaintext goes to the
    `out long matchedStep` overload of `ITwoFactorService.VerifyCode`, and a match is not accepted
    outright but handed to `AcceptTimeStepOnceAsync` with the step it matched (`:79-84`). "A stored
    secret this host cannot unprotect verifies no time-based code; the recovery codes stay usable, so
    the owner still has a way in" (`:77-78`).
  - Otherwise the challenge goes to `RedeemRecoveryCodeOnceAsync` (`:86`).
  - `VerifyEnrollmentCodeAsync(userId, secret, code, cancellationToken)` (`:90-105`) checks the first
    code of an enrollment against a candidate `secret` that is not yet stored. The candidate arrives
    protected: a blank secret, one that does not unprotect to a non-empty plaintext, or a code that fails
    `VerifyCode` against the plaintext returns `false` (`:96-101`); a match is passed through the same
    `AcceptTimeStepOnceAsync` and returns whether that step was accepted (`:103-104`), so the code that
    confirms enrollment cannot then be replayed as the first sign-in challenge.
  - The private `RedeemRecoveryCodeOnceAsync` (`:117-151`) takes the same per-account lock the
    time-based path takes, `lock:{StepKey(userId)}` with `StepLockTimeToLive` and `StepLockWait`, and
    answers a submission that cannot take it with `TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorInvalid` (`:122-128`).
    Inside the lock it **re-reads** the state and fails as invalid when the account is gone, no longer
    enrolled, or the code matches no stored hash through `ITwoFactorService.TryMatchRecoveryCode`
    (`:130-139`). A match is then **consumed**, not just verified: `store.ConsumeRecoveryCodeAsync`
    persists the redemption, and if that persistence fails, the challenge is answered as a failure rather
    than a success: "letting the sign-in through would hand out a code that is still live" (`:141-149`).
    Only a persisted consumption returns `VerifiedRecoveryCode`. Re-reading inside the lock is what makes
    two concurrent redemptions of one code yield exactly one success: the second reads the state after
    the first spent it (`:107-112`).
  - The private static `StepKey(userId)` (`:156-157`) builds the per-account key
    `twofactor:laststep:{userId}` that both paths lock on (`:153`).
  - The private `AcceptTimeStepOnceAsync` makes a TOTP code single use (`:167-188`). It takes the
    distributed lock on `lock:{key}` (`:176-178`), because "the read, the compare and the write below are
    one critical section: without it, two submissions of one code that both read before either writes
    would both pass" (`:174-175`). A submission that cannot take the lock within the wait gets a null
    handle and fails with `TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorInvalid` (`:179-182`), never a second success. Holding
    the handle in an `await using` block, it delegates to `AcceptIfNewerAsync` (`:184-187`).
  - The private `AcceptIfNewerAsync(key, matchedStep, cancellationToken)` (`:190-207`) reads the last
    accepted step with `GetFromSharedStoreAsync`, deliberately bypassing a local copy: "a step accepted
    on another replica must be seen here, or a replayed code would pass against a stale local copy
    inside its window" (`:195-197`). A matched step not newer than the stored one fails with
    `TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorInvalid` (`:198-201`). Otherwise the step is written back with a lifetime
    of `PeriodSeconds * (2 * VerificationWindowSteps + 2)` seconds, long enough to outlast every step the
    verification window could still accept, and the challenge returns `VerifiedTotp` (`:203-206`).
- **Why it's built this way**: this is the runtime half of the opt-in two-factor feature
  ([ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html)). The type
  remarks give the order: the time-based code is tried first because it is the ordinary path and costs
  one HMAC, and walking the recovery list only on failure keeps a six-digit code from being compared
  against the recovery hashes in the common case (`TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:15-19`). Both kinds of code
  are made one-time inside the challenge rather than left to the caller, because a caller that forgot
  would leave a code live for a second sign-in (`:20-26`). A TOTP code would otherwise stay valid for its
  whole verification window, so a code seen over someone's shoulder could be replayed; remembering the
  last accepted step closes that window. Remembering alone is not enough under concurrency, so the read,
  compare and write of that step, and the match and spend of a recovery code, run under an
  [`IDistributedLock`](group-05-cqrs-pipeline.md#idistributedlock) on the account's step key
  ([ADR-108](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/108-distributed-lock-primitive.html)), and a submission
  that cannot take the lock is answered as invalid, the same shape `PasswordResetTokenService` uses
  (`:27-35`).
- **Where it's used**: registered in DI
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:63`, a `TryAddScoped`)
  as the `ITwoFactorAuthenticator` behind `AddTwoFactorAuthentication(config)`; the resolved instance is
  passed to [`AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>`](#authenticationservicebasetuser), which
  answers `Authentication.TwoFactorRequired` or mints the `mfa` claim depending on the outcome, mapping
  `VerifiedTotp` and `VerifiedRecoveryCode` to the claim's method value
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:899-900`).

### AdministrationPermissions
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.Permissions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/AdministrationPermissions.cs:15` · Level 0 · class (static)

- **What it is**: the seven permission-string constants the framework's own opt-in administration
  controller bases gate on: `ManageUsers` (`"users:manage"`), `ManageRoles` (`"roles:manage"`),
  `ViewAsUsers` (`"users:view-as"`), `ManageFeatures` (`"features:manage"`), `ManageClients`
  (`"clients:manage"`), `ViewAuditTrail` (`"audit:view"`) and `ManageWebhooks`
  (`"webhooks:manage"`)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/AdministrationPermissions.cs:15-55`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; it is a plain `const string` holder consumed by the
  permission-authorization pipeline. Its doc comment points at
  [IPermissionRegistry](#ipermissionregistry) and [PermissionRegistryBuilder](#permissionregistrybuilder)
  as the way these names are granted (`AdministrationPermissions.cs:3-7`).
- **Concept introduced, the framework shipping its own permission vocabulary for the
  administration surface it also ships.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses the authorization
  model for built-in capabilities. The administration controller bases are framework code, so they
  need permission names that exist before any consuming app declares its own; these constants are
  those names, defined once so the base controllers and every host that wires a role to them agree
  on the string. They follow the same `area:capability` naming as a host's own permissions, and
  the remarks record the failure direction: a host that mounts one of the bases but grants none of
  these permissions serves endpoints that deny everyone (`AdministrationPermissions.cs:3-14`).
- **Walkthrough**: seven `public const string` fields, each documented with the operation it gates
  (`AdministrationPermissions.cs:17-54`): `ManageUsers` (`:18`) for listing, inspecting, locking,
  unlocking and re-roling accounts; `ManageRoles` (`:21`) for listing roles and editing their stored
  permission grants; `ViewAsUsers` (`:27`) for read-only view-as of another account for at most 15
  minutes, where an account holding it can never itself be viewed, so staff cannot view each other;
  `ManageFeatures` (`:33`) for listing feature flags and setting or clearing their stored overrides;
  `ManageClients` (`:40`) for creating, rotating, promoting and revoking machine clients, documented
  as to be granted as sparingly as `ManageUsers` because creating a client creates a
  service-account user; `ViewAuditTrail` (`:46`) for reading recorded entity change history; and
  `ManageWebhooks` (`:54`) for the outbound webhook subscription lifecycle, documented as to be
  granted as sparingly as the data the subscribed events carry.
- **Why it's built this way**: part of the opt-in identity completions
  ([ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html)), extended by
  each later opt-in surface: view-as
  ([ADR-137](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.html)),
  feature-flag overrides
  ([ADR-031](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/031-feature-flag-management.html)), machine clients
  ([ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html)),
  the audit trail ([ADR-075](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/075-audit-trail.html)) and outbound
  webhooks
  ([ADR-142](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/142-outbound-webhooks-and-delivery-lane.html)).
  Naming them in the framework is what lets each shared controller base carry its own
  `[HasPermission]` attribute, so a host adopting a built-in screen grants a role the constant rather
  than inventing its own string (`AdministrationPermissions.cs:9-14`).
- **Where it's used**: the controller bases carry them as class or action attributes:
  [RolesAdminControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#rolesadmincontrollerbase)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/RolesAdminControllerBase.cs:60`),
  [UsersAdminControllerBase<TUserDto>](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#usersadmincontrollerbasetuserdto)
  (`ManageUsers` at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/UsersAdminControllerBase.cs:67`,
  `ViewAsUsers` on its view-as action at `UsersAdminControllerBase.cs:161`),
  [ViewAsGrantsAdminControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#viewasgrantsadmincontrollerbase)
  (`ViewAsGrantsAdminControllerBase.cs:39`),
  [FeatureFlagsControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#featureflagscontrollerbase)
  (`FeatureFlagsControllerBase.cs:37`),
  [AuditHistoryControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#audithistorycontrollerbase)
  (`AuditHistoryControllerBase.cs:47`),
  [MachineClientsControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#machineclientscontrollerbase)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/MachineClients/MachineClientsControllerBase.cs:38`)
  and
  [WebhookSubscriptionsControllerBase](group-04-events-outbox.md#webhooksubscriptionscontrollerbase)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Webhooks/WebhookSubscriptionsControllerBase.cs:39`).
  [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice) refuses a client role that grants `ViewAsUsers`,
  `ManageUsers`, `ManageRoles` or `ManageClients`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:52-57`);
  [ViewAsService](#viewasservice) checks `ViewAsUsers` on the subject's role
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsService.cs:193`);
  [StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService](#storedpermissionroleadministrationservice) refuses to
  grant `ManageRoles` through a stored row, since it guards the role-administration surface itself
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/Administration/StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs:147-151`),
  and `RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs` disables that permission in the edit UI for the same reason
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:260,272`).
  In ADC, [IdentityPermissions](group-24-identity-module.md#identitypermissions) aliases
  `ManageUsers`, `ManageRoles`, `ViewAsUsers` and `ManageClients`
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Shared/Authorization/IdentityPermissions.cs:26,41,52,64`),
  `IdentityPermissionGrants` grants `ViewAuditTrail`
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Shared/Authorization/IdentityPermissionGrants.cs:50`),
  and `IdentityUIModule` uses `ManageUsers` and `ManageClients` as the `RequiredPermission` of its
  Support Access and Machine Clients nav entries
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/IdentityUIModule.cs:39,44`).

### CreateMachineClientRequest
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/CreateMachineClientRequest.cs:15` · Level 0 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: the body of the create-machine-client call: a `Name`, the `Role` the
  service-account user behind the client is created with, and an optional `SecretExpiresOn`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/CreateMachineClientRequest.cs:3-15`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; BCL `DateTime`.
- **Concept**: a machine client is a program that authenticates with a client id and secret
  (the OAuth client credentials grant) and acts as a dedicated service-account user
  ([ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html)).
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses least privilege: the request carries a role rather than a
  permission list, so the client's tokens carry exactly that role's permissions, and the doc comment
  records that a role granting `users:view-as`, `users:manage`, `roles:manage` or `clients:manage`
  is refused (`CreateMachineClientRequest.cs:7-11`).
- **Walkthrough**: three positional members (`CreateMachineClientRequest.cs:15`): `Name`, documented
  as 1 to 100 characters (`:6`); `Role` (`:7-11`); `SecretExpiresOn`, a UTC instant, defaulting to
  `null` for no expiry (`:12-14`).
- **Why it's built this way**: the refusal list in the comment is enforced server-side by
  [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice)'s `ForbiddenPermissions`, which names the matching
  [AdministrationPermissions](#administrationpermissions) constants
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:52-57`),
  so a program can never be minted with the power to create more programs or impersonate staff.
- **Where it's used**: the `[FromBody]` of
  [MachineClientsControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#machineclientscontrollerbase)`.CreateAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/MachineClients/MachineClientsControllerBase.cs:75-76`),
  passed on to [IMachineClientService](#imachineclientservice); sent from the UI by
  [MachineClientAdmin](group-15-common-ui-framework.md#machineclientadmin) through
  `MachineClientAdminService`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/MachineClientAdminService.cs`).

### IPermissionCatalog
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.Permissions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionCatalog.cs:24` · Level 0 · interface

- **What it is**: the read-only enumeration half of the permission model: every role the compiled
  registry grants something to, and every permission it grants to anyone, both sorted ordinally
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionCatalog.cs:24-31`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; it is a companion abstraction to
  [IPermissionRegistry](#ipermissionregistry).
- **Concept introduced, separating "does this role grant that permission" from "what roles and
  permissions exist at all".** `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` applies to interface segregation:
  [IPermissionRegistry](#ipermissionregistry) answers a per-request authorization question,
  `IPermissionCatalog` answers an administration-screen enumeration question, and a consumer that
  only needs to render a permission-grant matrix does not have to depend on the authorization
  interface at all.
- **Walkthrough**: two get-only properties, `Roles` and `Permissions`, both
  `IReadOnlyList<string>`.
- **Why it's built this way**: [PermissionRegistry](#permissionregistry) already holds the closed set
  of roles and permissions compiled into the host, so the catalog is a second, narrower interface
  the same class implements explicitly, rather than a second source of truth that could drift.
- **Where it's used**: implemented explicitly by [PermissionRegistry](#permissionregistry); read by
  `StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/Administration/StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs`),
  `PermissionCatalogResponse`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Responses/PermissionCatalogResponse.cs`), and
  `AuthorizationExtensions`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs`);
  registered alongside [IPermissionRegistry](#ipermissionregistry) in both `MMCA.Common.Application`
  and `MMCA.Common.Infrastructure` `DependencyInjection.cs`.

### IPermissionRegistry
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.Permissions` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionRegistry.cs:14` · Level 0 · interface

- **What it is**: the abstraction that maps roles to the fine-grained permissions they grant, and the
  single place that knows which roles confer which capabilities
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionRegistry.cs:3-14`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; its remarks reference [RoleNames](group-24-identity-module.md#rolenames) for the
  case-insensitivity rule.
- **Concept introduced, permission (capability) authorization over role checks.** `[Rubric §11,
  Security]` assesses the authorization model, and `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` assesses dependency inversion:
  endpoints depend on an abstraction, not on a role name. Instead of scattering
  `[Authorize(Roles = "Organizer")]` across endpoints, code authorizes against a *permission* (a
  capability such as `sessions:manage`) and this registry translates a principal's roles into the
  permissions they hold. The payoff is decoupling: adding a role or reshaping who-can-do-what is a
  registry change, not an edit to every endpoint (`IPermissionRegistry.cs:4-7`). The remarks also fix
  the comparison rules (`IPermissionRegistry.cs:9-13`): role lookups are case-insensitive, permission
  values are compared ordinally, and implementations are expected to be immutable and thread-safe.
  Those three sentences are what let the implementation be a frozen, lock-free structure.
- **Walkthrough**: two members. `GetPermissions(string role)` (`IPermissionRegistry.cs:21`) returns
  the permission set for a role, or an empty set for an unknown role, never a throw
  (`IPermissionRegistry.cs:16-18`). `HasPermission(IEnumerable<string> roles, string permission)`
  (`IPermissionRegistry.cs:29`) answers whether *any* of a principal's roles grants the permission:
  the hot path the authorization handler calls per request.
- **Why it's built this way**:
  [ADR-020](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/020-permission-based-authorization.html) records the
  decision. An empty-set-on-miss contract keeps callers branchless, and pushing the who-grants-what
  knowledge behind one interface is the capability-security expression of the framework's habit of
  hiding decision logic behind an abstraction.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [PermissionRegistry](#permissionregistry) (built via
  [PermissionRegistryBuilder](#permissionregistrybuilder)); registered as a lazily-built singleton by
  [AuthorizationExtensions](#authorizationextensions)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:78`) and
  injected into [PermissionAuthorizationHandler](#permissionauthorizationhandler)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:14`).

### MachineClientResponse
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientResponse.cs:15` · Level 0 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: one machine client as the administration surface lists it: its `ClientId`,
  `Name`, `ServiceAccountUserId`, `CreatedOn`, `SecretExpiresOn`, `RevokedOn`, `LastUsedOn` and
  `HasSecondarySecret`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientResponse.cs:3-23`).
- **Depends on**: the `UserIdentifierType` alias for `ServiceAccountUserId`
  (`MachineClientResponse.cs:18`, see the primer on identifier-type aliases); BCL `Guid`, `DateTime`.
- **Concept**: the read model of a machine client
  ([ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html)).
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses data minimization on admin surfaces: the secret hashes are
  deliberately absent, because nothing an operator does with a client needs them
  (`MachineClientResponse.cs:3-6`).
- **Walkthrough**: eight positional members (`MachineClientResponse.cs:15-23`). `ClientId` is the
  value a program presents as `client_id` (`:7`); the three nullable instants mean "no expiry",
  "still active" and "never used" when `null` (`:11-13`); `HasSecondarySecret` says a rotated secret
  is waiting to be promoted (`:14`), which is the state an operator needs to see between a rotate and
  a promote.
- **Why it's built this way**: a flat, hash-free projection lets the same record answer list,
  promote and revoke, and be nested inside
  [MachineClientSecretResponse](#machineclientsecretresponse) when a secret is issued.
- **Where it's used**: built by [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice)'s private `ToResponse`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:239`)
  and returned from it (`MachineClientService.cs:208,236`); listed by
  [MachineClientsControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#machineclientscontrollerbase)`.GetAllAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/MachineClients/MachineClientsControllerBase.cs:49-53`);
  rendered by [MachineClientAdmin](group-15-common-ui-framework.md#machineclientadmin).

### MachineTokenErrorResponse
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/MachineTokenErrorResponse.cs:11` · Level 0 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: the error body of `POST auth/token` in the RFC 6749 section 5.2 shape, a single
  `error` member, plus the three error codes the endpoint can send
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/MachineTokenErrorResponse.cs:5-21`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; `System.Text.Json.Serialization.JsonPropertyNameAttribute`
  (`MachineTokenErrorResponse.cs:1`).
- **Concept**: speaking a standard's wire format. `[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]` assesses
  whether contracts follow the conventions their clients expect: an OAuth client library parses
  `{"error": "..."}`, so the property is pinned to the snake-case name with `[property:
  JsonPropertyName("error")]` (`MachineTokenErrorResponse.cs:11`) rather than left to the host's
  camel-case policy. `[Rubric §11, Security]` applies too: no `error_description` is sent, so a
  refusal never says which half of the credential was wrong (`MachineTokenErrorResponse.cs:8`).
- **Walkthrough**: the positional `Error` (`:11`) and three `public const string` codes:
  `InvalidClient` (`"invalid_client"`, `:14`) for an unknown, revoked, expired, wrong-secret or
  refused-role client; `UnsupportedGrantType` (`"unsupported_grant_type"`, `:17`) for any grant other
  than `client_credentials`; `InvalidRequest` (`"invalid_request"`, `:20`) when no grant type is sent.
- **Why it's built this way**: collapsing every authentication failure into `invalid_client` keeps
  the endpoint from acting as an oracle for which client ids exist
  ([ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html)).
- **Where it's used**:
  [MachineTokenControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#machinetokencontrollerbase) maps
  [MachineClientErrors](#machineclienterrors) codes to `400` with `UnsupportedGrantType` or
  `InvalidRequest`, and every other failure to `401` with `InvalidClient`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/MachineClients/MachineTokenControllerBase.cs:120-130`).

### MachineTokenResponse
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/MachineTokenResponse.cs:13` · Level 0 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: the success body of `POST auth/token` for the client credentials grant, in the
  RFC 6749 section 5.1 shape: `access_token`, `token_type`, `expires_in`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/MachineTokenResponse.cs:5-16`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; `JsonPropertyNameAttribute` (`MachineTokenResponse.cs:1`).
- **Concept**: the success sibling of
  [MachineTokenErrorResponse](#machinetokenerrorresponse), with the same standard-wire-name
  reasoning (`[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]`). There is deliberately no refresh token: a
  program holds its secret and asks again (`MachineTokenResponse.cs:6-8`).
- **Walkthrough**: three positional members, each pinned to its snake-case name
  (`MachineTokenResponse.cs:14-16`): `AccessToken`, the signed token; `TokenType`, always `Bearer`
  (`:11`); `ExpiresIn`, the lifetime in seconds as an `int` (`:12`).
- **Why it's built this way**: omitting a refresh token removes a long-lived credential from the
  machine flow, since the client secret already lets the program mint a new access token
  ([ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html)).
- **Where it's used**: built by [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice) with `"Bearer"` and
  the configured lifetime in whole seconds
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:119`);
  returned by
  [MachineTokenControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#machinetokencontrollerbase)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/MachineClients/MachineTokenControllerBase.cs:50`).

### PasskeyOptionsResponse
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyOptionsResponse.cs:20` · Level 0 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: the first leg of a passkey ceremony: a `FlowId` and the WebAuthn `Options` the
  browser hands to `navigator.credentials.create` (registration) or `navigator.credentials.get`
  (sign-in)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyOptionsResponse.cs:5-20`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; `System.Text.Json.JsonElement` (`PasskeyOptionsResponse.cs:1`).
- **Concept introduced, the two-leg WebAuthn ceremony.** Passkeys
  ([ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html)) are
  public-key credentials held by the user's device. The server first issues a random challenge
  wrapped in options (this record), the browser has the authenticator sign it, and a second request
  ([PasskeyRegisterRequest](#passkeyregisterrequest) or [PasskeySignInRequest](#passkeysigninrequest))
  sends the result back naming the same flow. `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses replay resistance:
  the challenge behind `FlowId` is kept for five minutes and burned on the first completion, so a
  replayed completion is refused even when its signature is valid (`PasskeyOptionsResponse.cs:9-13`).
- **Walkthrough**: `FlowId`, the opaque handle of the stored challenge (`:15`); `Options`, a raw
  `JsonElement` in the `PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptionsJSON` or
  `PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptionsJSON` shape with binary members base64url-encoded (`:16-19`).
- **Why it's built this way**: carrying the options as a `JsonElement` passes the WebAuthn library's
  JSON straight through to the browser without a parallel C# model of the spec's option tree.
- **Where it's used**: built by [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice) for both ceremonies
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyService.cs:68,190`);
  returned by [PasskeysControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#passkeyscontrollerbase)
  `BeginRegistrationAsync` and `BeginSignInAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Passkeys/PasskeysControllerBase.cs:65-69,233-236`);
  consumed in the UI by `AuthUIService`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs`).

- **What it is**: the second leg of a passkey registration: the `FlowId` the options were issued

  `navigator.credentials.create` in the `RegistrationResponseJSON` shape (`:10-13`); `Name`, a label
  such as "Work laptop", defaulting to `null`, where a blank name becomes a default label (`:14-18`).

  options; the name is optional so registration never blocks on a label.
- **Where it's used**: the `[FromBody]` of the
  [PasskeysControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#passkeyscontrollerbase) registration

  handled by [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice); sent from
  [PasskeysPanel](group-15-common-ui-framework.md#passkeyspanel).

### PasskeyResponse
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyResponse.cs:15` · Level 0 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: one row of the caller's passkey list: `Id`, `Name`, `CreatedOn`, `LastUsedOn`

  the list stays useless to anyone reading it over the user's shoulder (`PasskeyResponse.cs:6-9`).

  rename and delete are addressed to (`:11`); `Name` (`:12`); `CreatedOn` (`:13`); `LastUsedOn`,
  `null` if the passkey never signed the user in (`:14`).

  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyService.cs:220`) and

  [PasskeysControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#passkeyscontrollerbase)`.ListAsync`

### MachineClientSecretResponse
> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientSecretResponse.cs:13` · Level 1 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: a machine client together with a secret just issued for it: the answer to a create
  (the primary secret) or a rotate (the secondary secret)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientSecretResponse.cs:3-13`).
- **Depends on**: [MachineClientResponse](#machineclientresponse).
- **Concept**: show-once secrets. `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses credential storage: only the
  secret's SHA-256 hash is stored, so this response is the only place the plaintext ever appears,
  and a client that loses it rotates (`MachineClientSecretResponse.cs:6-9`).
- **Walkthrough**: two positional members (`MachineClientSecretResponse.cs:13`): `Client`, the
  hash-free client row, and `ClientSecret`, base64url-encoded (`:12`).
- **Why it's built this way**: wrapping rather than extending
  [MachineClientResponse](#machineclientresponse) keeps the plaintext out of every other response
  shape, so no list or detail endpoint can leak it by accident
  ([ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html)).
- **Where it's used**: built by [MachineClientService](#machineclientservice) on create and rotate
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:169,189`);
  returned by
  [MachineClientsControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#machineclientscontrollerbase)
  `CreateAsync` and `RotateAsync`
