  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Shared/Users/UserListDTO.cs`).

### PasskeySettingsValidator
> MMCA.Common.Passkeys · `MMCA.Common.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/PasskeySettingsValidator.cs:12` · Level 1 · class

- **What it is**: the startup validator for the `Passkeys` configuration section. It checks the
  relying-party settings a WebAuthn ceremony needs, but only when passkeys are switched on
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/PasskeySettingsValidator.cs:12-62`).
- **Depends on**: [PasskeySettings](#passkeysettings) (the bound options); `IValidateOptions<T>` and
  `ValidateOptionsResult` from `Microsoft.Extensions.Options`; `System.Uri` (BCL).
- **Concept introduced: a disabled feature validates nothing.** `[Rubric §33, Developer Experience]`
  assesses how quickly a misconfiguration surfaces and how clearly it is explained. `Validate` returns
  success immediately when `Enabled` is false (`:28-31`), so a host that registers the package but leaves
  passkeys off never has to supply a relying party. When it is on, every problem is collected into one
  list (`:33`) and reported together (`:60`), and each message names the configuration key and gives an
  example value, for instance "the registrable domain, for example example.com" (`:36`). This is the
  fail-fast configuration contract of
  [ADR-070](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.html) applied to one
  settings type.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `IsAbsoluteOrigin` (`:17-22`), `internal static`: an origin passes when `Uri.TryCreate` parses it as
    absolute, the scheme is `https` or `http`, the path is exactly `/`, and there is no query and no
    fragment. Its doc comment states the test: whether "the browser could report it as a ceremony
    origin" (`:14-16`).
  - `Validate` (`:25-61`) throws on a null options object (`:27`), short-circuits when disabled
    (`:28-31`), then requires `RelyingPartyId` (`:34-37`) and `RelyingPartyName` (`:39-42`), requires at
    least one entry in `Origins` (`:44-47`) and adds one failure per entry that `IsAbsoluteOrigin`
    rejects, quoting the offending value (`:48-53`), and requires `DataSourceName` (`:55-58`).
- **Why it's built this way**: the origin rule matches what the ceremony does with the value: the Fido2
  verifier is configured with each origin cut back to scheme and authority
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/Fido2PasskeyCeremony.cs:136-138`), so a configured
  path, query or fragment would be silently dropped there. Refusing it at startup turns that into a named
  error instead.
- **Where it's used**: registered by
  [PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions](#passkeysservicecollectionextensions) with `TryAddEnumerable`
  next to `ValidateOnStart()`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:41-44`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: `internal sealed`, reached only through the options pipeline.

### KeyedSemaphoreStripe

> MMCA.Common.Shared · `MMCA.Common.Shared.Concurrency` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Concurrency/KeyedSemaphoreStripe.cs:22` · Level 2 · class

- **What it is**: an in-process, per-key mutual-exclusion primitive. Callers ask to serialize on a
  string key; the key is hashed onto one of a fixed number of `SemaphoreSlim` stripes, and the caller
  gets back a [`Releaser`](#releaser) to dispose
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Concurrency/KeyedSemaphoreStripe.cs:22-87`).
- **Depends on**: its own nested [`Releaser`](#releaser); `System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim` (BCL).
- **Concept introduced, lock striping.** `[Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]` assesses how shared
  state is guarded under concurrency and what that guard costs. The naive way to lock per key is a
  `ConcurrentDictionary<string, SemaphoreSlim>`, and the class doc comment lays out why that shape is a
  trap, in the code rather than in tribal memory (`KeyedSemaphoreStripe.cs:8-15`):
  - If you **remove** the entry when the last holder releases, you open a race. Caller A looks the
    semaphore up, then B releases and removes it, then A waits on an object no longer in the table while
    C creates a fresh one and takes that. A and C now both run the guarded section, which is precisely
    what the lock existed to prevent.
  - If you **never remove** it, the table grows without bound, and the keys here are caller-supplied
    (an idempotency key, a parameterized cache key), so that is an attacker-influenced memory leak.

  Striping sidesteps both by never creating or destroying anything: the table is allocated once at the
  declared width and every key maps into it forever. The price is stated honestly in the same comment:
  two unrelated keys can collide on a stripe and briefly serialize against each other. That is harmless
  for the double-check-locking callers this exists for, because each one re-checks its own key's state
  after acquiring (`KeyedSemaphoreStripe.cs:13-15`).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `DefaultWidth = 256` (`:25`), described as "ample concurrency without a meaningful memory cost"
    (`:24`); 256 `SemaphoreSlim` instances is a fixed, small, one-time allocation.
  - The parameterless constructor chains to the width-taking one (`:30-33`). The real constructor
    validates with `ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfLessThanOrEqual(width, 0)` (`:39`), then eagerly
    fills the array with binary semaphores, `new SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)` (`:42-46`). Eager fill is what
    removes every later allocation and every later race: after the constructor there is no mutation of
    the table at all, which is why the type is safe to share without any lock of its own.
  - `Width` is a get-only property (`:50`), exposed so tests can reason about collisions; one test
    computes the exact stripe index a key lands on, precisely so it "cannot flake on the
    one-in-`DefaultWidth` collision"
    (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/SessionCookies/CookieSessionRefresherTests.cs:641,662`).
  - `AcquireAsync` (`:60`) resolves the stripe, awaits `WaitAsync(cancellationToken)` with
    `ConfigureAwait(false)` per
    [ADR-049](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/049-library-configureawait-policy.html) (`:63`), and
    wraps the semaphore in a `Releaser` (`:64`). The parameter doc draws a line worth remembering: the
    token "Cancels the wait, not the work that follows it" (`:58`).
  - `GetStripe` (`:67`) does the hashing:
    `(uint)string.GetHashCode(key, StringComparison.Ordinal) % (uint)Width` (`:73`). Two deliberate
    choices, both commented (`:71-72`). `StringComparison.Ordinal` is passed explicitly rather than
    relying on the default, which keeps the mapping culture-independent. And the comment says the hash
    is reinterpreted as unsigned, by casting to `uint`, rather than passed to `Math.Abs`, because
    `int.MinValue` has no positive counterpart and `Math.Abs` would throw on it.
- **Why it's built this way**: the class is a hoisted shared primitive rather than a private helper
  because five separate call sites needed the same guard.
  [ADR-017](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/017-request-idempotency.html) records its role in the
  idempotency filter explicitly: the striped semaphore is the fallback for a host that registers no
  `IDistributedLock`, and the ADR reproduces the same two-defects argument
  (`Website/docs-src/adr/017-request-idempotency.md:59-65`). The scaling limit is stated there too: a
  process-local lock only serializes duplicates that land on the same replica
  (`017-request-idempotency.md:91-93`), which is why
  [`IDistributedLock`](group-05-cqrs-pipeline.md#idistributedlock) is preferred when present
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Idempotency/IdempotencyFilter.cs:35-38`).
- **Where it's used**: five holders, all `static` or instance fields that live for the lifetime of their
  owner, matching the remark that instances are "intended to be held in a static field for the process
  lifetime" and that stripes are never disposed (`KeyedSemaphoreStripe.cs:18-21`):
  [`IdempotencyFilter`](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#idempotencyfilter) (`IdempotencyFilter.cs:91`),
  [`CookieSessionRefresher`](#cookiesessionrefresher)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/SessionCookies/CookieSessionRefresher.cs:87`),
  [`MemoryCacheService`](group-09-caching.md#memorycacheservice)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Caching/MemoryCacheService.cs:45`), the
  `CacheKeyLocks` holder behind [`ICacheService`](group-09-caching.md#icacheservice)'s
  `GetOrCreateAsync` default implementation
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/ICacheService.cs:217-220`), and the
  `QueryCacheKeyLocks` holder behind
  [`CachingQueryDecorator<TQuery, TResult>`](group-05-cqrs-pipeline.md#cachingquerydecoratortquery-tresult)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/Decorators/CachingQueryDecorator.cs:247-250`).
  [`InProcessDistributedLock`](group-14-module-system-composition.md#inprocessdistributedlock) cites the
  same reasoning in its own doc comment (`InProcessDistributedLock.cs:20`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: .NET randomizes string hash codes per process, so the stripe a given key
  lands on differs between runs. That is invisible to correctness (any key consistently maps to one
  stripe *within* a process) but it means collision behavior cannot be reproduced across processes.

### IRoleAdministrationService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/IRoleAdministrationService.cs:29` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the application-layer contract for a role-permission administration screen: list every role with its compiled and stored permissions, read one role, read the closed catalog of roles and permissions an editor may pick from, and replace one role's stored permissions (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/IRoleAdministrationService.cs:29-77`).
- **Depends on**: `RolePermissionsResponse` and `PermissionCatalogResponse` (both in `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Administration`), and [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and its generic form.
- **Concept introduced: an editor's writable set is a strict subset of its readable catalog.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether an administrative surface can grant more than it should. The remarks on `GetCatalogAsync` (`:311-315`) state that the permission list it returns is the **compiled** catalog, so an editor built from that response can never submit anything `SetStoredPermissionsAsync` would refuse as unknown, and the parameter doc on `SetStoredPermissionsAsync` (`:324-328`) adds the one hard exclusion: no submitted list may include `AdministrationPermissions.ManageRoles`, so a role editor can never grant a role the permission to edit roles.
- **Walkthrough**: four methods.
  - `ListRolesAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:297`) returns one `RolePermissionsResponse` per known role, ordered by role name.
  - `GetRoleAsync(string role, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:305`) reads one role's compiled and stored permissions, matched case-insensitively, or a not-found failure.
  - `GetCatalogAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:318`) returns the two closed sets, roles and permissions, an editor renders from, both sorted ordinally.
  - `SetStoredPermissionsAsync(string role, IReadOnlyList<string> permissions, string? changedBy = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:332-336`) replaces a role's stored permissions and invalidates the cached snapshot, recording an optional `changedBy` principal name on the rows it creates.
- **Why it's built this way**: separating the compiled catalog (`GetCatalogAsync`) from the writable operation (`SetStoredPermissionsAsync`), and stating the `ManageRoles` exclusion as a contract obligation rather than leaving it to each implementation, keeps every host's role editor equally safe against granting itself the permission that edits roles.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by `StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/Administration/StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs`); consumed by `RolesAdminControllerBase` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/RolesAdminControllerBase.cs`) and, through it, by each app's admin roles controller, for example `MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.API/Controllers/AdminRolesController.cs`; registered through `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`.

### IUserAdministrationService<TUserDto>
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/IUserAdministrationService.cs:25` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the application-layer contract for an account administration screen: read one account, read the role it holds, lock or unlock it, and replace its roles (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/IUserAdministrationService.cs:25-73`).
- **Depends on**: the `UserIdentifierType` alias, and [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and its generic form. Generic over `TUserDto`, the app's shape for one account. The list read is not part of this contract: the paged, filtered account list is served by the app's generic paged entity endpoint (see [IUserAdminDTO](#iuseradmindto)).
- **Concept introduced: locking an account is a workflow, not a flag flip.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether an administrative action actually removes access rather than merely marking it removed. The remarks on `SetLockedAsync` (`:48-55`) state the obligation and where it is already met: derive [UserAdministrationServiceBase<TUser, TUserDto>](#useradministrationservicebasetuser-tuserdto) rather than implementing the interface by hand, because a lock must both refuse the account's already-issued access tokens (the soft-deleted user marker, written through [ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter](#isoftdeletedusermarkerwriter)) and revoke its live refresh sessions ([RefreshSessionRevocation](#refreshsessionrevocation)'s `RevokeAllAsync` over [IRefreshSessionStore](#irefreshsessionstore)), or the lock only takes effect once the current access token expires; an unlock clears the marker. "The base does all three."
- **Walkthrough**: four methods.
  - `GetAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:33`) reads one account, or a not-found failure.
  - `GetRoleAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:43`) returns the account's current role name, or the same not-found failure. Its summary names the reader: `UsersAdminControllerBase` uses it "to refuse administering an account whose role grants a permission the caller does not hold" (`:35-39`), and the controller calls it at `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/UsersAdminControllerBase.cs:393`.
  - `SetLockedAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, bool locked, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:60`) locks or unlocks an account.
  - `SetRolesAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, IReadOnlyList<string> roles, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:69-72`) replaces the complete set of roles an account holds.
- **Why it's built this way**: generic over `TUserDto` so each app's admin DTO can carry app-specific columns without the framework knowing about them, while the security-relevant lock behavior (marker plus session revocation) lives once in a framework base class that the contract's remarks point implementers at, rather than being left to whichever app implements the interface first.
- **Where it's used**: consumed by `UsersAdminControllerBase` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/UsersAdminControllerBase.cs`); implemented through [UserAdministrationServiceBase<TUser, TUserDto>](#useradministrationservicebasetuser-tuserdto) by each app's `UserAdministrationService`, for example `MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/Administration/UserAdministrationService.cs:37-43`, and registered through `MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/DependencyInjection.cs`.

### IUserSessionsAdministrationService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/IUserSessionsAdministrationService.cs:11` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the read-only contract an administrator uses to see who is signed in: one user's live sessions, that user's sign-in history, the set of users holding any live session, and a per-user live-session count for a roster page (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/IUserSessionsAdministrationService.cs:11-58`).
- **Depends on**: [RefreshSessionSummaryResponse](#refreshsessionsummaryresponse), [SignInSummaryResponse](#signinsummaryresponse), the `UserIdentifierType` alias, and [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and its generic form.
- **Concept introduced: "signed in" is a question about refresh sessions, answered by a narrow read contract.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether administrators can observe session state without being handed the means to mutate it. Revocation stays on the existing session paths ([RefreshSessionRevocation](#refreshsessionrevocation)); this interface only reads, and the history method's doc says so in as many words: "View only, like the session list" (`:28`). A live session means not revoked and not expired at the injected clock's now, so the three live-session answers agree on one definition.
- **Walkthrough**: four methods.
  - `GetSessionsAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:21-23`) returns the user's live sessions, newest first, each with `IsCurrent` false because an administrator is never on the viewed user's device. No sessions, or no such user, yields an empty list.
  - `GetSignInsAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:34-36`) returns the user's sign-in history: one row per sign-in, ended ones included with how they ended, newest first, capped at the newest 50, each with `IsCurrent` false. A user with no retained sessions, or no such user, yields an empty list (`:25-29`).
  - `GetSignedInUserIdsAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:44-45`) returns each user holding at least one live session exactly once, in no particular order; a consumer's roster uses it as the "signed in" filter.
  - `CountLiveSessionsAsync(IReadOnlyCollection<UserIdentifierType> userIds, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` (`:55-57`) counts live sessions per requested user in one store query. A user with none is absent from the result rather than a zero entry, and an empty request answers empty without querying the store.
- **Why it's built this way**: the roster page needs a count for a whole page of users at once, so the batch method exists to avoid one store query per row, and the "absent, never zero" rule keeps the result a sparse map a caller can test with a plain lookup.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [UserSessionsAdministrationService](#usersessionsadministrationservice) and registered in `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:186`; consumed by `UsersAdminControllerBase` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/UsersAdminControllerBase.cs`) and by ADC's `UserListEntityQueryService` (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UserListEntityQueryService.cs`). See [ADR-097](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.html).

### MachineClientSettingsValidator
> MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · `MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.MachineClients` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientSettingsValidator.cs:15` · Level 4 · class

- **What it is**: the startup validator for the `MachineClients` configuration section: it bounds the
  machine access-token lifetime, requires a data source name, and, when machine clients are enabled,
  checks that the app registered the service-account provisioner they depend on
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientSettingsValidator.cs:15-45`).
- **Depends on**: [MachineClientSettings](#machineclientsettings) (the bound options and its
  `MinAccessTokenMinutes`/`MaxAccessTokenMinutes` bounds);
  [IServiceAccountProvisioner](#iserviceaccountprovisioner); `IServiceProvider` and
  `IServiceProviderIsService` (Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection); `IValidateOptions<T>`.
- **Concept introduced: a validator that checks the container, not just the values.** `[Rubric §33,
  Developer Experience]` assesses how early and how clearly a misconfiguration is reported. Beyond the
  value checks, this validator takes the root `IServiceProvider` in its primary constructor (`:15`) and,
  when `Enabled` is true, asks `IServiceProviderIsService` whether `IServiceAccountProvisioner` is
  registered (`:35-37`). A missing registration becomes a startup failure whose message spells out the
  fix, `services.AddScoped<IServiceAccountProvisioner, ...>()` (`:39-40`), instead of a resolution
  error on the first token request. `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether credentials stay revocable:
  the lifetime bound's own message gives the reason for the ceiling, "a longer token would outlive the
  revocation marker" (`:27`). Both follow
  [ADR-070](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.html); machine
  clients themselves are
  [ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html).
- **Walkthrough**: one method, `Validate` (`:18-44`), collecting failures into one list (`:22`).
  - `AccessTokenMinutes` outside `MinAccessTokenMinutes` to `MaxAccessTokenMinutes` fails, with the
    message built through `string.Create(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, ...)` (`:23-28`).
  - A blank `DataSourceName` fails (`:30-33`). Neither this check nor the lifetime check depends on
    `Enabled`.
  - The provisioner check runs only when `Enabled` is true and the container exposes
    `IServiceProviderIsService`; if the container does not, the check is skipped rather than failed
    (`:35-41`).
  - All failures are returned together through `ValidateOptionsResult.Fail` (`:43`).
- **Why it's built this way**: the provisioner is the one dependency an app must supply itself (the
  message describes it as the app's implementation over its User aggregate, `:40`), so it is the most
  likely thing to be forgotten when a host flips `MachineClients:Enabled`.
- **Where it's used**: registered with `TryAddEnumerable` as an `IValidateOptions<MachineClientSettings>`
  singleton (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.MachineClients.cs:45`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: `internal sealed`, reached only through the options pipeline.

### StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService

> MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · `MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/Administration/StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs:45` · Level 5 · class

- **What it is**: the `IRoleAdministrationService` implementation that lets an operator list roles, read
  or replace a role's stored permissions, and view the compiled permission catalog, layered over the
  code-compiled permission registry
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/Administration/StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs:45-282`).
- **Depends on**: [`IPermissionRegistry`](group-08-auth.md#ipermissionregistry) (the compiled grants);
  [`IPermissionCatalog`](group-08-auth.md#ipermissioncatalog) (the closed list of declared permissions);
  [`IPermissionGrantStore`](group-08-auth.md#ipermissiongrantstore) (persisted grants);
  [`IPermissionGrantCache`](group-08-auth.md#ipermissiongrantcache) and
  [`IPermissionGrantCacheInvalidator`](group-08-auth.md#ipermissiongrantcacheinvalidator);
  `PermissionGrantSettings` (`KnownRoles`) via `IOptions<T>`;
  [`AdministrationPermissions`](group-08-auth.md#administrationpermissions) (`ManageRoles`); the
  framework's `Result<T>` and `Error` factories.
- **Concept introduced, a layered grant surface that refuses to let stored data override the permission
  that guards it.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether an authorization surface can be used to
  escalate its own access, and `[Rubric §4, DDD]`/`[Rubric §1, SOLID]` the separation between the
  compiled and stored halves of a permission set. `SetStoredPermissionsAsync` refuses to grant
  `AdministrationPermissions.ManageRoles` from a stored row, and the error message states the two-sided
  reason: granting it from a data row would make access to role administration itself a matter of data,
  while deleting the row "would lock every operator out of the screen that could restore it"
  (`StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs:147-153`). That permission is only ever compiled in,
  through a host's own permission registry.
- **Walkthrough**: constructed with the registry, catalog, store, cache, invalidator, and settings as
  primary constructor parameters (`:45-51`).
  - `ListRolesAsync` groups all stored grants by role, case-insensitively (`:59-64`), unions the result
    with the compiled and configured role universes via the private `RoleUniverse` helper (`:66`), and
    returns one `RolePermissionsResponse` per role pairing its compiled permissions (`CompiledPermissions`)
    with its stored ones (`:68-76`).
  - `GetCatalogAsync` returns every known role alongside the full compiled `catalog.Permissions`
    deliberately, not whatever happens to be stored: "widening it with whatever happens to be stored
    would let one typo legitimize itself" (`:87-89`).
  - `GetRoleAsync` first resolves the caller's spelling through the private `CanonicalRole` helper
    (`:102`), reads stored and compiled permissions under that canonical name, and returns not found when
    the private `IsKnownRole` rule fails (`:106`), so "a role
    the host has never named ... does not exist as far as this surface is concerned" rather than being
    reported as an empty, plausible-looking role (rule documented at `:229-233`). The response echoes the canonical spelling (`:111`).
  - The private `IsKnownRole` helper is the single existence rule: a role exists when the registry
    compiles at least one permission for it, or when it belongs to the `RoleUniverse` (catalog roles,
    configured `KnownRoles`, or a role that already carries a stored grant) (`:238-240`).
  - `SetStoredPermissionsAsync` applies that same existence rule first, before anything is validated or
    written, reading the role's current stored grants once (`:134-136`): "a set must not be the route by
    which a typo becomes a role", whether with an empty list (answering success for a role that does not
    exist) or a non-empty one (creating it). Every read, write and invalidation uses one canonical spelling
    from `CanonicalRole` (`:134`), so a route value cased differently from the stored rows cannot write a
    second casing beside them or revoke nothing on a case-sensitive collation (`:130-133`). It then trims
    and de-duplicates the desired set
    (`:141-143`), rejects `ManageRoles` as above, rejects any permission absent from
    `catalog.Permissions` with the unknown names listed in the error (`:156-168`), then diffs the
    desired set against the current one read earlier (`:170`): grants what is newly desired, revokes
    what was dropped, short-circuiting on the first store failure either way (`:177-196`). The two
    loops sit in a `try` whose `finally` invalidates the role's permission cache on every exit, failure
    and exception included (`:175-201`): each grant and revoke "commits on its own, so a failure or a
    throw part-way through leaves earlier rows already written", and invalidating only on success would
    leave the process "serving the pre-edit snapshot until the next refresh" (`:172-174`). On success it
    returns the fresh `RolePermissionsResponse` (`:205`), keyed by the canonical role.
  - The private `RoleUniverse` helper unions the compiled catalog's roles, the configured `KnownRoles`,
    and whatever roles the store's own rows name, case-insensitively and sorted (`:215-221`).
  - The private `CompiledPermissions` helper reads "through the SAME registry the authorization path
    uses" and subtracts what the cache already reports, so the two lists a role response carries stay
    disjoint (`:267-281`).
  - The private `CanonicalRole` helper trims the name and looks it up case-insensitively in the `RoleUniverse`
    (catalog spelling first, then configured `KnownRoles`); a role named only by stored rows keeps the
    caller's trimmed spelling and the store folds it to the stored one (`:242-259`).
- **Why it's built this way**:
  [ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html) documents
  `AddStoredPermissionGrants(config)` as the opt-in that layers a `PermissionGrant` table over the
  compiled registry; `MMCA.Common/CLAUDE.md`'s Authorization section describes the same union-only
  layering through
  [`LayeredPermissionRegistry`](group-08-auth.md#layeredpermissionregistry) "without changing the
  decorators' contract", the principle this service's `ManageRoles` refusal exists to protect.
- **Where it's used**: registered in DI
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:195`, a
  `TryAddScoped`) behind `AddStoredPermissionGrants(config)` (`DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:175`) as the
  `IRoleAdministrationService` implementation; consumed
  through `RolesAdminControllerBase`, which is itself gated on
  `AdministrationPermissions.ManageRoles` (`MMCA.Common/CLAUDE.md`, "Identity completions" section).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: `internal sealed`, so it is reached only through the
  `IRoleAdministrationService` abstraction.

### Fido2PasskeyCeremony
> MMCA.Common.Passkeys · `MMCA.Common.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/Fido2PasskeyCeremony.cs:17` · Level 8 · class

- **What it is**: the [IPasskeyCeremony](#ipasskeyceremony) implementation that builds WebAuthn
  registration and sign-in options and verifies the browser's attestation and assertion responses,
  using the Fido2 .NET library's `Fido2` verifier
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/Fido2PasskeyCeremony.cs:17-169`).
- **Depends on**: [IPasskeyCeremony](#ipasskeyceremony), [PasskeySettings](#passkeysettings),
  [PasskeyAttestation](#passkeyattestation), [PasskeyStoredKey](#passkeystoredkey),
  [PasskeyErrors](#passkeyerrors), [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and `Error`;
  externally the Fido2 library (`Fido2`, `Fido2Configuration`, `Fido2VerificationException` and its
  request/response types) and `System.Text.Json`.
- **Concept introduced: the WebAuthn library stays behind one internal class.** `[Rubric §32,
  Dependency & Supply-Chain]` assesses how far a third-party dependency reaches into the codebase. Every
  Fido2 type is used here and nowhere in the contract: the ceremony takes and returns JSON strings,
  `JsonElement`, byte arrays and the framework's own records, so the application layer's
  [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice) never sees the library, and the extension method's remarks note that
  a host that never references this package "carries no WebAuthn library"
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:23-26`).
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses how verification failures are handled: every library refusal is
  caught as `Fido2VerificationException` and returned as a validation `Result` carrying the library's
  error code (`:75-78`, `:124-127`), and malformed input never reaches the library (`:52-56`,
  `:102-106`). See [ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `Verifier` (`:20`) is built on first use through the `field ??=` backing-field form; the comment
    says why: "a host with passkeys disabled never reads the relying-party settings" (`:19`). `Create`
    (`:130-140`) maps `RelyingPartyId`, `RelyingPartyName` and the origins, each cut back with
    `GetLeftPart(UriPartial.Authority)` into a case-insensitive set (`:136-138`), and passes
    `metadataService: null` (`:140`).
  - `CreateRegistrationOptions` (`:23-41`) requests a new credential for the given user handle, names
    and excluded credential ids, so "the browser refuses to create a second passkey on an authenticator
    that already holds one for this account" (`:31-33`). It requires a resident (discoverable) key, prefers
    user verification, and asks for no attestation (`:34-39`).
  - `VerifyRegistrationAsync` (`:44-79`) deserializes the attestation (null on a non-object or bad JSON,
    `:145-156`), refuses it as "malformed attestation" (`:52-56`), then calls `MakeNewCredentialAsync`
    with the original options JSON and the caller's credential-id uniqueness callback (`:60-67`). Success
    becomes a [PasskeyAttestation](#passkeyattestation) of id, public key, sign count and transport names
    (`:69-73`).
  - `CreateSignInOptions` (`:82-87`) asks for an assertion with an empty `AllowedCredentials` list, so the
    authenticator offers whichever discoverable passkeys it holds for the relying party.
  - `ReadCredentialId` (`:90-91`) pulls the raw credential id from an assertion, or null, so the caller
    can look up the stored key before verifying.
  - `VerifyAssertionAsync` (`:94-128`) calls `MakeAssertionAsync` with the stored public key and signature
    counter, and an ownership callback that requires the assertion's user handle to equal the stored
    credential's `UserHandle` byte for byte (`:117-118`). It returns the new signature counter (`:122`).
  - `TransportName` (`:159-168`) maps each `AuthenticatorTransport` to the WebAuthn spelling the browser
    reports (`usb`, `nfc`, `ble`, `smart-card`, `hybrid`, `internal`), falling back to `ToString()`.
- **Why it's built this way**: discoverable credentials with an empty allow list give a usernameless
  sign-in, and `AttestationConveyancePreference.None` with no metadata service means the server does not
  try to verify the authenticator's make and model. Not determinable from source: the rationale for
  skipping attestation is not stated in this file.
- **Where it's used**: registered as a singleton `IPasskeyCeremony` by
  [PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions](#passkeysservicecollectionextensions), whose comment notes the
  verifier "holds only the bound relying-party settings"
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:46-47`);
  consumed by [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: `internal sealed`, reached only through `IPasskeyCeremony`.

### UserAdministrationServiceBase<TUser, TUserDto>
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserAdministrationServiceBase.cs:52` · Level 8 · class

- **What it is**: the abstract base that implements
  [IUserAdministrationService<TUserDto>](#iuseradministrationservicetuserdto) once for every app: load,
  save, revoke and log live here, while the app supplies the handful of aggregate-specific steps
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserAdministrationServiceBase.cs:52-297`).
- **Depends on**: [IUnitOfWork](group-07-persistence-ef-core.md#iunitofwork),
  [IRefreshSessionStore](#irefreshsessionstore), `TimeProvider`,
  [ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter](#isoftdeletedusermarkerwriter) and `ILogger` (primary constructor,
  `:52-57`); `TUser` constrained to
  [AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType>](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#auditableaggregaterootentitytidentifiertype)
  over `UserIdentifierType` (`:58`); [RefreshSessionRevocation](#refreshsessionrevocation);
  [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and `Error`.
- **Concept introduced: the security steps are fixed, the domain steps are abstract.** `[Rubric §2,
  Design Patterns]` assesses whether a pattern is applied where it earns its keep; this is a template
  method. The public methods own the order of operations, and the app overrides only `MapToDto`,
  `IsLocked`, `ApplyLockState`, `GetRole`, `ApplyRole` and `CreateExactlyOneRoleError` (abstract,
  `:202-255`) plus, optionally, `ValidateRequestedRole` (virtual, defaulting to success, `:243`).
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether an administrative change actually takes access away. On a
  lock the base writes the soft-deleted user marker first and then revokes every refresh session, and
  the comment explains the order: the marker "is what refuses the access tokens already issued, and the
  session revocation below only stops new ones being minted" (`:122-129`). A role change also revokes
  sessions, because "the role travels in the access token" (`:190-193`). See
  [ADR-047](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/047-soft-deleted-user-session-revocation.html).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `GetAsync` (`:61-73`) and `GetRoleAsync` (`:77-89`) read through `GetReadRepository` and return
    `MapToDto(user)` or `GetRole(user)`, or a not-found error built by `NotFound`, which stamps the
    calling method as source and `typeof(TUser).Name` as target (`:257-258`).
  - `SetLockedAsync` (`:98-137`) loads through the tracking `GetRepository` (`:103-110`), records
    `wasLocked = IsLocked(user)` (`:112`), calls `ApplyLockState` with the clock's UTC now and returns its
    failure before anything is saved (`:114-118`), then saves (`:120`). A lock writes the marker and
    revokes sessions (`:122-129`); an unlock clears the marker only when the account was actually locked
    (`:130-133`). It logs the change (`:135`).
  - `SetRolesAsync` (`:147-197`) refuses anything but exactly one role with the app's
    `CreateExactlyOneRoleError` (`:152-155`), runs `ValidateRequestedRole` before the account is loaded
    (`:157-161`), loads it, applies the role, and compares `GetRole` before and after ordinally. An
    unchanged role returns success with nothing saved and nothing revoked, because "re-submitting the
    same value must not sign the account out" (`:181-186`). A change is saved, sessions are revoked, and
    the old and new roles are logged (`:188-195`).
  - `WriteMarkerAsync` and `ClearMarkerAsync` (`:260-284`) swallow any exception except cancellation and
    log a warning, since the lock or unlock is already saved and "a cache fault must not report it as
    failed" (`:268`). The warnings state the consequence: already-issued tokens keep working until they
    expire, or the unlocked account's tokens are refused until the marker expires (`:292-296`).
  - Four `[LoggerMessage]` source-generated log methods (`:286-296`), which is why the class is
    `partial`.
- **Why it's built this way**: the remarks on `CreateExactlyOneRoleError` explain why the app owns the
  whole error, code included: the API's error localizer
  ([ADR-027](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/027-multi-locale-i18n.html)) keys text by code, so a
  framework-emitted code "would take the framework's translation and replace the app's message"
  (`:250-254`). The interface's own remarks direct implementers here rather than to a hand-written
  implementation (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/IUserAdministrationService.cs:48-55`).
- **Where it's used**: derived by ADC's `UserAdministrationService`
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/Administration/UserAdministrationService.cs:37-43`,
  closed over `User` and `UserAdminDTO`); reached through `UsersAdminControllerBase`; tested by
  `UserAdministrationServiceBaseTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/Administration/UserAdministrationServiceBaseTests.cs`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: the marker write and clear are best-effort by design, so a cache outage
  during a lock leaves the account's current access tokens valid until expiry; only the log warning
  records it.

### UserSessionsAdministrationService
> MMCA.Common.Application · `MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserSessionsAdministrationService.cs:17` · Level 8 · class

- **What it is**: the `IUserSessionsAdministrationService` implementation, a thin read over the refresh-session store, plus the sign-in history read (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserSessionsAdministrationService.cs:17-103`).
- **Depends on**: [IUserSessionsAdministrationService](#iusersessionsadministrationservice), [IRefreshSessionStore](#irefreshsessionstore), [RefreshSessionSummaryResponse](#refreshsessionsummaryresponse), [SignInSummaryResponse](#signinsummaryresponse), [SignInHistory](#signinhistory), the optional [IViewAsGrantStore](#iviewasgrantstore), `TimeProvider`, the `UserIdentifierType` alias, and [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result).
- **Concept introduced: liveness is decided against an injected clock, not the store's idea of now.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether session state is evaluated consistently. Every method reads `timeProvider.GetUtcNow().UtcDateTime` (`:33`, `:67`, `:79`, `:98`) and applies it, so tests can pin the clock and all answers share one definition of live.
- **Walkthrough**: `public sealed class` with a primary constructor taking `IRefreshSessionStore`, `TimeProvider`, and an optional `ViewAs.IViewAsGrantStore?` defaulting to null (`:17-20`).
  - `GetSessionsAsync` (`:29-53`) loads the user's un-revoked rows with `GetUnrevokedByUserAsync`, keeps those where `UserId` matches and `IsActiveAt(now)` holds (the store returns expired-but-unrevoked rows on purpose, so expiry is filtered in memory), orders by `CreatedAt` then `Id` descending, and projects each to a `RefreshSessionSummaryResponse` with `IsCurrent: false` and the row's `ToDeviceMetadata()` (`:48-49`). No user lookup is made, so an unknown user is an empty list rather than a 404, revealing nothing the `GET Admin/Users/{userId}` endpoint does not (`:23-28`).
  - `GetSignInsAsync` (`:60-73`) delegates to `SignInHistory.ReadAsync` with the store, the user, the clock's now, `currentSessionId: null` and the view-as grant store (`:64-70`): "the same store-aggregated read the account holder's own history uses", with no current sign-in because an administrator is never on the viewed user's device (`:56-59`). Passing the grant store is what lets the history show each time support viewed the account ([ADR-137](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.html)).
  - `GetSignedInUserIdsAsync` (`:76-83`) delegates to `GetUserIdsWithLiveSessionsAsync(now)`.
  - `CountLiveSessionsAsync` (`:86-102`) rejects a null argument, answers an empty dictionary for an empty request without touching the store (`:92-96`), and otherwise calls `CountLiveSessionsByUserAsync(userIds, now)` (`:99`).
- **Why it's built this way**: it reuses the same store reads as the account holder's own devices and history pages rather than adding a parallel query path, and keeps the empty-request short circuit here so every caller gets it.
- **Where it's used**: registered with `TryAddScoped` at `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:186`; exercised by `UserSessionsAdministrationServiceTests` and `UserSessionsAdministrationServiceSignedInTests` under `MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/Administration/`, and by `ViewAsSignInHistoryTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsSignInHistoryTests.cs`). See [ADR-097](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.html).

### ClaimBasedUserIdProvider
> MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · `MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Context` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/ClaimBasedUserIdProvider.cs:11` · Level 8 · class

- **What it is**: a two-line SignalR `IUserIdProvider` that tells the hub infrastructure which user a
  connection belongs to, by reading the identity claim off the connection's principal
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/ClaimBasedUserIdProvider.cs:6-10`).

- **Concept**: `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses that identity is derived from the validated token and
  never from client-supplied input, and `[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]` assesses whether that derivation
  is centralized once. SignalR keys its user-targeted sends on whatever string an `IUserIdProvider`
  returns; the built-in provider reads `ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier`. This framework mints the user id
  only into `sub` (see [`TokenService`](#tokenservice),

  survives as `sub` or arrives mapped to `NameIdentifier` depends on which handler authenticated the
  connection. Routing through the shared extension is what makes both shapes resolve identically, so a
  consumer that changes its inbound claim mapping does not silently start delivering zero
  notifications.
- **Walkthrough**: the entire type is `GetUserId(HubConnectionContext connection)`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/ClaimBasedUserIdProvider.cs:14-15`), an
  expression body returning `connection?.User.FindUserIdValue()`. Two null paths are handled without a
  branch: a null connection short-circuits to `null`, and `FindUserIdValue` is an extension on a
  nullable `ClaimsPrincipal` that returns `null` when neither claim is present
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:26-28`). An
  unauthenticated connection therefore has no user id, and SignalR treats it as belonging to no user
  rather than failing connection setup.
- **Why it's built this way**: the value returned here is compared as a *string* against the string a
  sender passes to `Clients.User(...)`, so both sides must format the identifier the same way. The raw
  claim value is used verbatim on this side, and the sender formats with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Notifications/Push/SignalRPushNotificationSender.cs:19`),
  matching the invariant formatting the token writer used
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TokenService.cs:146`). Keeping the whole
  provider to one delegating line is what makes that three-way agreement checkable at a glance.
- **Where it's used**: registered as
  `services.TryAddSingleton<IUserIdProvider, ClaimBasedUserIdProvider>()`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Notifications.cs:78`), in the
  same block that swaps the null notification implementations for the SignalR-backed ones (`:64-66`). SignalR's
  connection manager calls it on every connection, and it is what makes
  [`SignalRPushNotificationSender`](group-10-notifications.md#signalrpushnotificationsender) reach the
  right sockets on [`NotificationHub`](group-10-notifications.md#notificationhub)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Notifications/Push/SignalRPushNotificationSender.cs:17-21`
  for the single-user send and `:25-34` for the batched multi-user send).

### CurrentUserService
> MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · `MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Context` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:17` · Level 9 · class

- **What it is**: the per-request implementation of [`ICurrentUserService`](#icurrentuserservice). It
  answers "who is calling" by reading claims off the current HTTP request's principal: the raw
  `ClaimsPrincipal`, the typed user id, the role, and any other parsable claim by name
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:10-16`).
- **Depends on**: [`ICurrentUserService`](#icurrentuserservice) (the Application port) and
  [`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions`](#claimsprincipalextensions) for the identity read
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:4-5`); externals
  are `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.IHttpContextAccessor`, `System.Security.Claims` and
  `System.Globalization`. The claims it reads are the ones [`TokenService`](#tokenservice) writes.
- **Concept introduced: a scoped identity snapshot, computed lazily and parsed invariantly.**
  `[Rubric §3, Clean Architecture]` applies first: application code needs the caller's identity but
  must not reference `HttpContext`, so the port lives in Application and this HTTP-aware implementation
  lives in Infrastructure, which is the only place `IHttpContextAccessor` appears.
  `[Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]` explains the `Lazy<T>` fields
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:19`, `:21`):
  because the service is registered scoped
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:350`), the claim walk
  happens at most once per request no matter how many handlers, filters and save operations ask.
  `[Rubric §27, i18n]` covers the trap most codebases miss: claim values are machine-written under
  `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`, so they must be *read* invariantly too, or a request running under a
  culture with different separators misreads decimal, double and `DateTime` claims. Both parse paths
  say so explicitly (`:40`, with the comment at `:38-39`, and the identifier parse inside
  `ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.GetUserId` at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:43`).
- **Walkthrough**
  - The primary constructor takes `IHttpContextAccessor httpContextAccessor`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:17`) and is
    captured directly by the lazy initializers, so there is no field boilerplate.
  - `_userId`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:19-20`) defers
    to `ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.GetUserId`, which reads `sub` first and falls back to the mapped
    `ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:26-28`) before
    parsing into `UserIdentifierType`. That indirection is the reason a JWT-bearer request and a
    session-cookie request resolve to the same user.
  - `_role`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:22-23`) caches
    the first `ClaimTypes.Role` claim.
  - `User` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:26`)
    returns the principal, substituting a fresh empty `ClaimsPrincipal` when there is no HTTP context.
    That fallback is what makes the service safe to resolve from a background job or hosted service:
    callers get an anonymous principal instead of a `NullReferenceException`.
  - `UserId` and `Role`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:29`, `:31`) are
    one-line projections of the two lazies, both nullable, both `null` when unauthenticated.
  - `GetClaimValue<T>(string claimType)`
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:35-42`) is
    constrained to `T : struct, IParsable<T>` and calls the static abstract `T.TryParse`, so any
    parsable value type (`int`, `Guid`, `DateTime`) can be lifted out of a named claim without Common
    knowing what the claim means. It returns `null` for an absent or unparsable claim, and unlike
    `UserId`/`Role` it is a fresh lookup on every call.
- **Why it's built this way**: scoped lifetime plus `Lazy<T>` yields a stable per-request identity
  snapshot at minimal cost, while the empty-principal fallback keeps the same abstraction usable
  outside a request. Reading identity through the shared extension rather than a hand-rolled
  `FindFirst("sub")` is the load-bearing part: it is what stops a consumer's claim-mapping choice from
  silently emptying the current user
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:9-16`).
- **Where it's used**: registered as
  `services.TryAddScoped<ICurrentUserService, CurrentUserService>()`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:350`). The
  highest-traffic consumer is
  [`DbContextFactory`](group-07-persistence-ef-core.md#dbcontextfactory), which takes it as a
  constructor dependency
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/DbContexts/Factory/DbContextFactory.cs:53`,
  `:57`) and passes `UserId` into every save so audit fields are stamped with the acting user (`:248`,
  `:291`, `:330`, `:352`, `:414`);
  [`EFRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType>`](group-07-persistence-ef-core.md#efrepositorytentity-tidentifiertype)
  accepts it as an optional dependency
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Repositories/EFRepository.cs:29`).
  Application handlers in both apps inject the port for ownership checks and caller-scoped queries.
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: this class implements four members. `Roles` and `IsInRole` are default
  interface members on the port
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/Auth/ICurrentUserService.cs:45`,
  `:88`), not overridden here, so multi-role behavior is defined on the interface rather than in this
  file. Outside an HTTP request `HttpContext` is null and `UserId` is therefore `null`, which means a
  save performed by a background worker stamps no acting user; nothing in this file substitutes a
  system identity.

### PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions
> MMCA.Common.Passkeys · `MMCA.Common.Passkeys` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:10` · Level 9 · class

- **What it is**: the one public entry point of the `MMCA.Common.Passkeys` package, an `AddPasskeys(configuration)`
  extension member on `IServiceCollection` that registers passkey sign-in
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:10-58`).
- **Depends on**: [PasskeySettings](#passkeysettings), [PasskeySettingsValidator](#passkeysettingsvalidator),
  [IPasskeyCeremony](#ipasskeyceremony) and [Fido2PasskeyCeremony](#fido2passkeyceremony),
  [PasskeyChallenges](#passkeychallenges), [IPasskeyService](#ipasskeyservice) and
  [PasskeyService](#passkeyservice); `IConfiguration`, `TimeProvider`, and the `TryAdd*` helpers of
  Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.
- **Concept introduced: registering a feature is not enabling it.** `[Rubric §33, Developer
  Experience]` assesses whether an opt-in is safe to wire before it is configured. The remarks say
  calling this "alone turns nothing on": with `Passkeys:Enabled` false every passkey endpoint answers 404
  and no context maps the `PasskeyCredentials` table, and a host that never calls it, or never references
  the package, behaves the same way, "needs no migration and carries no WebAuthn library" (`:22-26`).
  The extension-member shape is the DI surface convention of
  [ADR-106](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/106-extension-members-as-public-di-surface.html); the
  feature is [ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html).
- **Walkthrough**: `AddPasskeys` (`:37-56`) throws on a null configuration (`:39`), then:
  - binds `PasskeySettings` to its `SectionName` with `ValidateOnStart()` and adds
    `PasskeySettingsValidator` through `TryAddEnumerable` (`:41-44`), so a bad section fails the host at
    startup ([ADR-070](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.html));
  - registers `Fido2PasskeyCeremony` as a singleton `IPasskeyCeremony`, because "the verifier holds only
    the bound relying-party settings" (`:46-47`);
  - registers `PasskeyChallenges` and `IPasskeyService` as scoped, because the service reads the
    request's passkey store and signs in through the app's scoped authentication service (`:49-52`);
  - adds `TimeProvider.System` with `TryAddSingleton`, so a host's own clock registration wins (`:53`).
- **Why it's built this way**: the remarks list what turning passkeys on still needs from the host: a
  controller deriving from [PasskeysControllerBase](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#passkeyscontrollerbase)
  routed at `auth/passkeys`, the `PasskeyCredentials` migration on the Identity database
  (`DesignTimeDbContextOptions.EnablePasskeys`), and an app `AuthenticationService` deriving from
  `AuthenticationServiceBase`. The passkey store comes from `AddInfrastructure`, and the challenges need
  the shared cache and the distributed lock `AddCaching` registers (`:28-35`;
  [ADR-108](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/108-distributed-lock-primitive.html)). Every
  registration uses a `TryAdd*` form, so a host can replace any piece before calling it.
- **Where it's used**: no call site exists outside the defining file in the scanned source; a host opts in
  by calling `services.AddPasskeys(configuration)`.
